What are the signs and symptoms of Alagille syndrome? Alagille syndrome is a complex multisystem disorder involving the liver, heart, eyes, face, and skeleton. Symptoms typically present in infancy or early childhood. The severity of the disorder varies among affected individuals, even within the same family. Symptoms range from so mild as to go unnoticed to severe enough to require heart and/or liver transplants. One of the major features of Alagille syndrome is liver damage caused by abnormalities in the bile ducts. These ducts carry bile (which helps to digest fats) from the liver to the gallbladder and small intestine. In Alagille syndrome, the bile ducts may be narrow, malformed, and reduced in number. This results in a build-up of bile causing scarring that prevents the liver from working properly. This may lead to jaundice, itchy skin, and deposits of cholesterol in the skin (xanthomas). Alagille syndrome is also associated with several heart problems, including impaired blood flow from the heart into the lungs (pulmonic stenosis). Other heart-related problems include a hole between the two lower chambers of the heart (ventricular septal defect) and a combination of heart defects called tetralogy of Fallot. People with Alagille syndrome may also have distinctive facial features (including a broad, prominent forehead; deep-set eyes; and a small, pointed chin), problems with the blood vessels within the brain and spinal cord (central nervous system) and the kidneys, and an unusual butterfly shape of the bones of the spinal column (vertebrae). Detailed information about the symptoms associated with Allagille syndrome can be accessed through the National Digestive Diseases Information Clearinghouse (NDDIC) and GeneReviews. How is progressive osseous heteroplasia inherited? This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, which means one copy of the altered gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the disorder. People normally inherit one copy of each gene from their mother and one copy from their father. For most genes, both copies are active, or "turned on," in all cells. For a small subset of genes, however, only one of the two copies is active. For some of these genes, only the copy inherited from a person's father (the paternal copy) is active, while for other genes, only the copy inherited from a person's mother (the maternal copy) is active. These differences in gene activation based on the gene's parent of origin are caused by a phenomenon called genomic imprinting. The GNAS gene has a complex genomic imprinting pattern. In some cells of the body the maternal copy of the gene is active, while in others the paternal copy is active. Progressive osseous heteroplasia occurs when mutations affect the paternal copy of the gene. Thus, progressive heteroplasia is usually inherited from the father.

What are the signs and symptoms of Alopecia universalis? Alopecia universalis (AU) is characterized by the complete loss of hair on both the scalp and body. In some cases, AU can be associated with other conditions such as atopic dermatitis, thyroid disorders, and/or nail changes (such as pitting). Anxiety, personality disorders, depression, and paranoid disorders are more common in people with different forms of alopecia areata. How is alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency diagnosed? Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) may first be suspected in people with evidence of liver disease at any age, or lung disease (such as emphysema), especially when there is no obvious cause or it is diagnosed at a younger age. Confirming the diagnosis involves a blood test showing a low serum concentration of the alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) protein, and either: detecting a functionally deficient AAT protein variant by isoelectric focusing (a method for detecting mutations); or detecting SERPINA1 gene mutations on both copies of the gene with molecular genetic testing. (This confirms the diagnosis when the above-mentioned tests are not performed or their results are not in agreement.) Specialists involved in the diagnosis may include primary care doctors, pulmonologists (lung specialists), and/or hepatologists (liver specialists).

How is alpha-thalassemia x-linked intellectual disability syndrome inherited? Alpha-thalassemia x-linked intellectual disability (ATRX) syndrome is caused by a mutation in the ATRX gene and is inherited in an x-linked way. The chance that a relative may have ATRX syndrome depends on whether the mutation in the first affected family member was inherited from his mother or happened by chance (a de novo mutation). If the mutation happened by chance, there is very little risk that other relatives could be affected by this condition. If the mutation was inherited from his mother, each of his mother's sisters has a 50% of being a carrier of ATRX syndrome. If a woman is a carrier of an ATRX mutation, she has a 25% chance of having a son with the mutation who is affected with ATRX syndrome; a 25% chance of having a son who does not have the mutation and does not have ATRX syndrome; a 25% chance of having a daughter with the mutation who is a carrier of ATRX syndrome; and a 25% chance of having a daughter who does not have the mutation and is not a carrier.

How might Alport syndrome be treated? Although there is no one specific treatment for Alport syndrome, the goals of treatment include monitoring and controlling progression of the disease and treating the symptoms. Strict control of blood pressure is very important. Research suggests that ACE inhibitors can help reduce proteinuira and the progression of kidney disease. However, treatment of chronic kidney failure often becomes necessary. This can include dietary modifications, fluid restriction, and other treatments. Ultimately, chronic kidney failure progresses to end-stage kidney disease, requiring dialysis or transplantation. Kidney transplantation in patients with Alport syndrome is usually successful, but some studies have reported that about 10% of transplanted patients develop nephritis in the graft. Other aspects of the condition are addressed as needed. For instance, surgical repair of cataracts (cataract extraction), or repair of the anterior lenticonus in the eye may be needed. Loss of hearing is likely to be permanent. Counseling and education to increase coping skills can be helpful. Learning new skills such as lip reading or sign language may be of some benefit. Hearing aids are helpful. Young men with Alport syndrome should use hearing protection in noisy environments. Genetic counseling may be recommended because of the inherited pattern of the disorder. Additional information related to the treatment of Alport syndrome can be accessed through GeneReviews and eMedicine.

How is amelogenesis imperfecta diagnosed? A dentist can identify and diagnose amelogenesis imperfecta on the basis of the patient's family history and the signs and symptoms present in the affected individual. Extraoral X-rays (X-rays taken outside the mouth) can reveal the presence of teeth that never erupted o that were absorbed. Intraoral X-rays (X-rays taken inside the mouth) show contrast between the enamel and dentin in cases in which mineralization is affected. Genetic testing is available for the genes AMELX, ENAM, and MMP20. You can visit the Genetic Testing Registry to locate laboratories performing genetic testing for these genes. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry is a source of information to find a pediatric dentist. The National Dental Association can also assist people in locating a dentist.

What are the signs and symptoms of Amniotic band syndrome? The symptoms of amniotic band syndrome depend on the severity and location of the constrictions. The mildest constrictions affect only the superficial skin and may not require treatment. Deeper constrictions may block lymphatic vessels, impair blood flow, and require immediate surgical care. When the bands affect the limbs, the lower part of the limbs are most often involved, especially the middle, long, and index fingers of the hand. When the feet are involved, the bands most commonly affect the big toe. Pressure from the bands may result in additional abnormalities, such as underdevelopment of a limb, bone abnormalities, amputations, leg-length discrepancy, and club feet. Constriction bands across the head and face may lead to facial clefts. Severe clefts affecting vital organs are often life-threatening. Is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) inherited? About 90-95% percent of cases of ALS are not inherited and occur in individuals with no history of the condition in their family. The remaining 5-10% of cases are familial, and are thought to be caused by mutations in any one of several genes. The inheritance pattern associated with familial ALS varies depending on the disease-causing gene involved. Most familial cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. This means that only one altered (mutated) copy of the disease-causing gene in each cell is sufficient to cause the condition. In most of these cases, an affected individual has one parent with the condition. When an individual with an autosomal dominant form of ALS has children, each child has a 50% (1 in 2) risk to inherited the mutated copy of the gene and be affected. Less frequently, ALS is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. In autosomal recessive inheritance, both copies of the disease-causing gene (typically one copy inherited from each parent) must have a mutation for the individual to be affected. The parents of an individual with an autosomal recessive condition, who presumably each carry one mutated copy of the gene, are referred to as carriers. Carriers typically do not have any signs or symptoms of the condition. When two carriers for the same condition are having children, each child has a 25% (1 in 4) risk to have the condition, a 50% (1 in 2) risk to be a carrier like each parent, and a 25% risk to not have the condition and not be a carrier. Autosomal recessive forms of ALS may be mistaken for non-inherited (sporadic) forms due to having a negative family history of the condition. In rare cases, ALS is inherited in an X-linked dominant manner. This occurs when the disease-causing gene is located on the X chromosome (a sex chromosome). Although females have 2 X chromosomes, having a mutation in one X chromosome is still sufficient to cause the condition. Males who have a mutation (and only one X chromosome) will have the condition. Usually, males with an X-linked dominant form of ALS experience more severe symptoms than females with the same form. Some individuals who do inherit a mutation known to cause ALS never develop signs and symptoms of ALS, although the reason for this is unclear. This phenomenon is referred to as reduced penetrance.

Is genetic testing available for Andersen-Tawil syndrome? Yes, the Genetic Testing Registry (GTR) provides information about the genetic tests for this condition. The intended audience for the GTR is health care providers and researchers. Patients and consumers with specific questions about a genetic test should contact a health care provider or a genetics professional. How is Andersen-Tawil syndrome diagnosed? The diagnosis of Andersen-Tawil syndrome might be suspected in individuals with either: 1. Two of the following three criteria: Periodic paralysis Symptomatic cardiac arrhythmias or evidence of enlarged U-waves, ventricular ectopy, or a prolonged QTc or QUc interval on electrocardiogram (ECG) Characteristic facial features, dental abnormalities, small hands and feet, and at least two of the following: Low-set ears Widely spaced eyes Small lower jaw (mandible) Fifth-digit clinodactyly (curved pinky finger) Syndactyly or 2. One of the above three criteria in addition to at least one other family member who meets two of the three criteria. The presence of a mutation in the KCNJ2 gene confirms the diagnosis of Andersen-Tawil syndrome.

Anencephaly is a type of neural tube defect characterized by abnormal development of the brain and the bones of the skull. The neural tube is a narrow channel that normally folds and closes between the 3rd and 4th weeks of pregnancy, forming the brain and spinal cord of the embryo. Anencephaly occurs when the 'cephalic' or head end of the neural tube fails to close, causing the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp. Infants with this disorder are born without a forebrain (the front part of the brain) and a cerebrum (the thinking and coordinating part of the brain). The remaining brain tissue is often exposed (not covered by bone or skin). Affected babies are usually blind, deaf, unconscious, and unable to feel pain. Almost all babies with anencephaly die before birth, although some may survive a few hours or a few days after birth. Anencephaly is likely caused by an interaction between genetic and environmental factors, many of which remain unknown.

How might ankylosing spondylitis be treated? The main goal of treatment for people with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is to maximize long-term quality of life. This may involve easing symptoms of pain and stiffness; retaining function; preventing complications (such as contractures); and minimizing the effects of associated conditions. Education, exercise, and medications are all very important in managing AS. An exercise program is recommended for all affected people, and some may need individual physical therapy. Affected people are encouraged to speak with their health care provider before instituting any changes to an exercise regime. Video demonstrations of exercises tailored for ankylosing spondylitis are available for viewing through the National Ankylosing Spondylitis Society in the UK. Medications may include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs); pain relievers; sulfasalazine; and anti-tumor necrosis factor drugs. Steroid injections may be helpful for some people. Most people don't need surgery, but it may be indicated when there is severe, persistent pain or severe limitation in mobility and quality of life. Smoking creates additional problems for people with AS, so affected people who smoke should quit. More detailed information about the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis is available on Medscape's Web site. You may need to register to view the article, but registration is free.

How is anophthalmia plus syndrome diagnosed? A review of the available medical literature does not currently yield information about specific diagnostic criteria for anophthalmia plus syndrome (APS). Because APS is so rarely reported, specific diagnostic criteria may not exist. Anophthalmia and/or microphthalmia with oral-facial clefting occurs in a number of known syndromes; however, the other known syndromes typically have specific other features (such as limb abnormalities, deafness or other organ anomalies). A diagnosis of APS may be considered when an individual has the signs and symptoms most commonly reported in affected individuals, but other known syndromes with overlapping features have been ruled out.

How is antisynthetase syndrome diagnosed? A diagnosis of antisynthetase syndrome is often suspected based on the presence of characteristic signs and symptoms once other conditions that cause similar features have been ruled out. Additional testing can then be ordered to confirm the diagnosis, determine the severity of the condition, and inform treatment. This testing varies based on the signs and symptoms present in each person, but may include: Blood tests to evaluate levels of muscle enzymes such as creatine kinase and aldolase Laboratory tests to look for the presence of autoantibodies associated with antisynthetase syndrome High resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the lungs Electromyography (EMG) Muscle biopsy Pulmonary function testing Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of affected muscles Evaluation of swallowing difficulties and aspiration risk Lung biopsy

Apert syndrome is a disorder mainly characterized by craniosynostosis (premature fusion of skull bones, causing abnormalities in the shape of the head and face) and syndactyly (fusion or webbing or fingers and/or toes). Other signs and symptoms may include distinctive facial features (bulging and wide-set eyes; a beaked nose; an underdeveloped upper jaw leading to crowded teeth and other dental problems; and shallow eye sockets which can cause vision problems); polydactyly; hearing loss; hyperhidrosis (increased sweating); and other symptoms. Cognitive abilities in affected individuals range from normal to mild or moderate intellectual disability. It is caused by mutations in the FGFR2 gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Management typically includes various surgical procedures that are tailored to the affected individual's needs.

Apocrine carcinoma is a cancer of a sweat gland. Apocrine carcionoma most often develops under the arm (the axilla), but it can develop on the scalp or other parts of the body. The cause of apocrine carcinoma is unknown. Apocrine carcinoma usually appears as a single, small, painless bump (nodule) that can vary in color and slowly increases in size. The average age at the time of diagnosis is 62 years of age, and twice as many men are affected than women. Most apocrine carcinomas can be treated and are not fatal. Treatment of apocrine carcinoma is surgery to remove as much of the cancer as possible. Additional treatments such as radiation therapy and chemotherapy have been used to treat this condition, but the usefulness of these treatments is unproven.

How is aquagenic pruritus diagnosed? Criteria for diagnosis include : Severe itching, prickling, stinging, or burning that consistently develops after skin contact with water, regardless of water temperature or salinity; Lack of visible skin manifestations; Reaction within minutes of exposure and lasting anywhere between 10 minutes to 2 hours; Lack of a other skin disease, internal condition, or medication to account for the reaction; and Exclusion of all other physical urticarias, symptomatic dermographism, and polycythemia vera.

answers_clean: The prognosis of adult acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, white blood cell count, chromosomal abnormalities, response to initial treatment, and relapse status . In general, ALL has a better prognosis in adults than in children, with 5-year overall survival rates ranging from 30% to over 80%, depending on the specific subtype of ALL .

AML can affect anyone of any age group but it is more common in adults over 65 years old. Risk factors include exposure to certain chemicals or radiation, smoking, family history of blood disorders, previous treatment with chemotherapy or radiation therapy, and some genetic conditions such as Down syndrome .

The treatment of adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, targeted therapy, stem cell transplantation, or palliative care depending on various factors such as age, overall health status, genetic abnormalities, and response to initial treatment .

Diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) requires a combination of clinical features, laboratory tests, and imaging studies. The most common feature is persistent lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly with absolute lymphocyte count greater than 5 × 109 cells per liter in peripheral blood .

The symptoms of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) typically include fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain or discomfort, fever, frequent infections, an enlarged spleen, increased susceptibility to bleeding and bruising, weakness, bone pain, joint tenderness, skin changes such as pallor, yellowing of the skin (jaundice), redness of the eyes (erythroderma), and easy bruisability .

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). These include studies of new targeted therapies such as dasatinib, bosutinib, nilotinib, ponatinib, ponatini, radotinib, and others . Other ongoing clinical trials involve combination therapy with other drugs or stem cell transplantation. It is recommended that patients with CML consult their healthcare provider about enrolling in any relevant clinical trial.

Hairy cell leukemia (HCL) is a type of cancer that affects white blood cells called lymphocytes or B-cells. The diagnosis of HCL involves several steps including physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging studies such as bone marrow biopsy, and cytogenetic analysis .

Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a type of cancer that affects the bone marrow and blood cells. It occurs when there is an abnormal proliferation of immature white blood cells known as lymphocytes . There are two main types of ALL in children: B-cell precursor ALL and T-cell precursor ALL. The cause of childhood ALL is not fully understood but it may be due to genetic or environmental factors . Symptoms include fatigue, fever, bruising, bleeding, pain, swelling, weight loss, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, coughing, and vomiting. Diagnosis involves a physical examination, blood tests, imaging studies such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and bone marrow aspiration and biopsy. Treatment typically includes chemotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplantation, supportive care, and other approaches depending on the specific subtype and stage of disease .

Childhood acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) can affect anyone but it more commonly affects children between 2-5 years of age with a peak incidence around 4 years of age . Males are slightly more likely to develop ALL than females. While there are some known genetic factors that increase the risk of developing childhood ALL, most cases occur spontaneously without any identifiable cause or family history of cancer.

Diagnosis of childhood acute myeloid leukemia (AML) typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, blood tests, bone marrow aspiration or biopsy, cytogenetic analysis, and molecular testing. The initial assessment includes a physical examination, medical history, and laboratory tests such as complete blood count (CBC), peripheral smear, and urine analysis. If AML is suspected, further diagnostic procedures may be recommended, including imaging studies such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and bone scintigraphy. Bone marrow aspiration or biopsy is also necessary for diagnosis and classification of AML. Cytogenetic analysis can help identify specific chromosomal abnormalities associated with AML, which can aid in determining prognosis and treatment options. Molecular testing using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) can detect mutations in genes that play a role in the development of AML.

An adult soft tissue sarcoma is a type of cancer that arises from mesenchymal cells in adults. These cells can differentiate into various types of connective tissues such as bone, cartilage, fat, muscle, blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, nerve, or fibrous tissue . The most common subtypes include liposarcomas, leiomyosarcomas, myxofibrosarcomas, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas, synovial sarcomas, extraskeletal osteosarcomas, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, angiosarcomas, rhabdomyosarcomas, and gastrointestinal stromal tumors.

The stages of adult soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are classified according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). Staging is important because it helps determine the best treatment approach for each patient and can help predict their prognosis.

The most common symptom of gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) is abdominal pain, which can be present in 60% to 75% of patients . Other common symptoms include gastrointestinal bleeding (42-59%) , anemia or hypochromic microcytic anemia due to chronic blood loss (38-41%) , weight loss (35-45%) , nausea and vomiting (30-40%) , indigestion (20-30%) , diarrhea (10-20%) , constipation (10-20%) , early satiety (10-20%) , palpable mass (10-20%) , dyspepsia (10-15%) , jaundice (10-15%) , fever (10-15%) , postprandial fullness (5-10%) , melena (5-10%) , hematemesis (< 5%) , iron deficiency anemia (< 5%) , and fatigue (< 5%) .

The diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is typically made through a combination of clinical examination, histopathological evaluation of biopsy samples, immunohistochemical staining for human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), and molecular testing such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR). In addition, KS can be diagnosed radiologically by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) scans.

Diagnosis of childhood rhabdomyosarcoma typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies such as ultrasound or MRI, biopsy for histopathological examination, immunohistochemical staining, flow cytometry analysis, and genetic testing.

A childhood soft tissue sarcoma (STS) is a type of cancer that originates from mesenchymal cells in children aged 15 years or younger . These tumors can occur anywhere in the body but most commonly develop in the abdominal cavity, bone, and extraskeletal muscles . The exact cause of STS remains unknown; however, certain genetic conditions such as neurofibromatosis-1 and Li-Fraumeni syndrome have been associated with an increased risk for developing this type of cancer .

The most common types of childhood soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) include rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, osteosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, liposarcoma, fibrosarcoma, and desmoplastic small round cell tumor .

The treatment of childhood vascular tumors depends on various factors such as the type, size, location, and behavior of the tumor. Generally, there are three main approaches to treating these tumors: observation, surgical excision, and chemotherapy.

The diagnosis of adult hodgkin lymphoma is typically made through a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies such as positron emission tomography (PET) or computed tomography (CT), and biopsy with histopathological examination. During the initial workup for suspected lymphoma, it is important to obtain a complete blood count, chemistry panel, urinalysis, and lactate dehydrogenase level. Imaging tests may include CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, PET scan, and ultrasound of any enlarged lymph nodes. A biopsy of an affected lymph node or other tissue is necessary for definitive diagnosis.

Non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs) are a group of hematological malignancies that originate from B or T cells at different stages of their development . They account for about 95% of all types of lymphoid cancers in adults . The most common type of NHL in adults is diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), which accounts for approximately one-third of cases . Other subtypes include follicular lymphoma (FL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Burkitt's lymphoma, peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL), and marginal zone lymphoma (MZL).

The outlook for adult non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) depends on several factors, including the type of NHL, stage at diagnosis, age, overall health status, and treatment received. In general, patients with localized disease have better outcomes than those with more advanced or widespread disease .

The diagnosis of AIDS-related lymphomas is made by combining clinical history, physical examination findings, laboratory tests such as blood counts and viral load testing, imaging studies such as CT or PET scans, and pathological evaluation of biopsy specimens from affected tissues .

The symptoms of mycosis fungoides include red patches or plaques that may be itchy and scaly. As the disease progresses, these lesions can develop into tumors and may spread to other parts of the body such as the scalp, face, trunk, genitals, and soles of the feet.

The treatment of mycosis fungoides (MF) is determined by several factors such as disease stage, age, comorbidities, and patient preference . Low-dose total skin electron therapy (TSE) remains the standard first-line treatment option for patients with early MF who have no visceral involvement or significant immunosuppression . However, TSE can be associated with adverse effects such as skin atrophy, telangiectasia, hyperpigmentation, and hypopigmentation .

There have been several ongoing studies investigating primary central nervous system lymphomas (PCNSLs). One such study is the Radiation Therapy Oncology Group 0126 trial, which aims to evaluate the efficacy of high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplantation in combination with whole brain radiotherapy compared to standard dose methotrexate plus radiation therapy . Another study, the Central Nerval System Lymphoma International Trial (CNSL-IT), is evaluating the use of rituximab as part of first line treatment for PCNSL patients . The European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) has also conducted a phase II trial of combined chemoimmunotherapy using temozolomide, cytarabine, and rituximab for newly diagnosed PCNSL patients .

Diagnosis of childhood Hodgkin lymphoma typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies such as CT scans or PET scans, and biopsy with histopathological examination. The presence of characteristic features in the biopsied tissue, including the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells (the diagnostic hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma) along with other supportive findings, is considered the gold standard for diagnosis. Imaging studies can help identify the location and extent of the disease and may also provide information about potential involvement of distant sites. Staging procedures, which vary depending on the specific stage of the disease, may include bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, lumbar puncture, and additional imaging tests. It's important to note that while these procedures play an essential role in establishing a definitive diagnosis and determining appropriate treatment options, they should be performed by experienced professionals who have received proper training and follow strict safety guidelines to minimize any risks associated with them.

Childhood non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs) refer to malignant tumors of the immune system that arise in children under 15 years old . They account for approximately 4% of all childhood cancers and occur more frequently in males than females . The most common subtypes of NHL in children include Burkitt’s lymphoma, T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), B cell ALL, diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), and Hodgkin’s disease (HD).

The stages of childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) are classified according to the Ann Arbor staging system for adults with some modifications . Stage I is limited disease involving one region or organ; stage II involves two regions or organs on the same side of the diaphragm; stage III involves three or more regions or organs on the same side of the diaphragm or any region or organ on both sides of the diaphragm plus spleen; and stage IV is disseminated disease affecting bone marrow, liver, lungs, or bone.

The diagnosis of anal cancer typically involves a combination of clinical examination, imaging tests such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT), and biopsy for histopathological evaluation. A thorough physical exam should be performed by an experienced clinician, including digital rectal examination (DRE), palpation of lymph nodes in the groin region, and inspection of the perianal area. Imaging techniques can help stage the disease and identify any potential metastasis. Biopsies may include high-resolution anoscopy with directed biopsy under local anesthesia, endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration cytology (EUS-FNAC), transrectal ultrasound (TRUS)-guided core needle biopsy, or surgical biopsy. Histologic features that suggest anal cancer include dyskeratosis, hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, mitotic activity, and invasion into the submucosa.

There is no evidence-based screening for anal cancer; however, some experts recommend that individuals with high risk of developing anal cancer should undergo regular anal cytology or biopsy . The most effective way to reduce your chances of getting anal cancer is by preventing HPV infection through vaccination. In addition, practicing safe sex (using condoms) can also help in reducing the chance of HPV transmission. Limiting sexual partners, avoiding tobacco smoking, limiting alcohol consumption, eating a healthy diet, and exercising regularly may also be beneficial in lowering the risk of anal cancer .

Diagnosis of adult central nervous system (CNS) tumors typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, neuroimaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and pathological examination of tissue samples obtained through biopsy or surgical resection. The specific diagnostic approach may vary depending on the location and type of suspected CNS tumor.

Childhood brain tumours are a group of central nervous system (CNS) cancers that occur in children under 15 years old . The most common childhood CNS tumour is astrocytoma, which accounts for about one-third of all paediatric brain tumours . Other types of childhood brain tumours include ependymomas, medulloblastomas, primitive neuroectodermal tumours (PNETs), atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumours (ATRTs), oligodendrogliomas, pilocytic astrocytomas, subependymomas, choroid plexus papillomas, craniopharyngiomas, gliomatosis cerebri, and diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG).

There have been several ongoing studies related to childhood brain tumors in recent years. The National Cancer Institute (NCI), which is part of the US Department of Health and Human Services, has conducted a number of pediatric preclinical testing programs (PPTPs). These PPTPs aim to identify new treatments for children with cancer by evaluating potential drugs in animal models that closely resemble human cancers .
The most common symptom in children with astrocytoma is headache. Other signs include vomiting, seizures, visual changes, weakness or numbness in one arm or leg, drowsiness, and difficulty walking.

The treatment of childhood astrocytoma depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, tumor location, grade, and other characteristics. For low-grade gliomas (LGGs), surgery is typically the first line of treatment. If possible, complete surgical resection can be curative in some cases . However, if the tumors cannot be completely removed or if they recur after surgery, chemotherapy may be recommended. Commonly used chemotherapeutic agents include carboplatin and vincristine . Radiation therapy may also be considered for LGGs that cannot be fully resected or have recurred after chemotherapy .

The prognosis of childhood central nervous system atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (AT/RT) is poor with an overall survival rate of less than 20% . AT/RTs are highly aggressive brain tumors that occur in infants and young children. They originate from undifferentiated embryonic cells called rhabdomyoblasts and often arise in the midline structures of the brain or spinal cord. Due to their location and rapid growth, these tumors can cause significant damage to surrounding tissues and organs, resulting in severe neurological deficits and high mortality rates. Despite advances in treatment, including surgical resection, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, the outcome for patients with AT/RT remains dismal due to the aggressive nature of this disease and its tendency to spread throughout the central nervous system.

The exact cause of childhood brain stem gliomas is unknown. However, several risk factors have been identified that may contribute to their development. These include exposure to ionizing radiation, genetic predisposition, certain environmental exposures such as pesticides or solvents, and family history of cancer .

The stages of childhood brain stem gliomas (BSGs) refer to the progression of these tumors over time. There is currently no standardized system for staging BSGs in children due to their rarity and heterogeneity. However, some studies have proposed classification systems that take into account various factors such as age at diagnosis, location within the brainstem, histology, and molecular features.

The most common symptom in children with central nervous system embryonal tumor is headache, which may be accompanied by vomiting or dizziness. Other possible signs include seizures, weakness or numbness in one side of the body, vision problems, difficulty walking, speech problems, and changes in behavior or personality. These symptoms can vary depending on the location and size of the tumor within the brain or spine. It is important for parents to seek immediate medical attention if their child experiences any of these symptoms.

Childhood central nervous system germ cell tumor refers to a group of rare malignant brain or spinal cord tumors that arise from cells with neural stem-cell properties in the developing fetus . These tumors can occur anywhere along the neuraxis but most commonly involve the pineal gland region, followed by the suprasellar area, basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum, and midbrain. The most common subtypes include medulloblastoma, ependymoma, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, and embryonal carcinoma.

The prognosis of childhood central nervous system germ cell tumors depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, location of the tumor within the CNS, histology, extent of metastasis, and treatment received . Overall survival rates have improved significantly over time due to advances in diagnostic techniques and treatments including chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation therapy .

Other symptoms include endocrine abnormalities (such as growth hormone deficiency), hypothalamic dysfunction (including obesity, developmental delay, behavior changes, and pubertal delay), hydrocephalus, and cerebral edema .

The treatment of childhood craniopharyngiomas typically involves a combination of surgery and radiation therapy. Surgery is usually performed to remove as much of the tumor as possible, while preserving important structures such as the pituitary gland and optic nerves. Radiation therapy may be used after surgery or in cases where complete removal of the tumor is not feasible. In some cases, chemotherapy may also be used before or during radiation therapy. It's worth noting that the specific treatment approach will depend on several factors, including the size and location of the tumor, its relationship with surrounding structures, and whether it has recurred after previous treatment.

The prognosis of childhood ependymomas depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, tumor location, histologic grade, and molecular features. Overall survival rates range from 60% to over 85%. Patients with younger age (less than 3 years old), low-grade tumors, or no evidence of metastasis have better outcomes.

Cholangiocarcinoma is diagnosed through a combination of imaging tests such as ultrasound, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), endoscopic retrograde cholangiography (ERCP), computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), and biopsy. The specific test used depends on the location of the tumor within the biliary system. For example, ERCP or MRCP may be used for tumors in the common bile duct, while CT scans may be more appropriate for tumors located outside of the common bile duct. Biopsies can also help confirm the diagnosis by identifying cancer cells from tissue samples taken during these procedures.

Childhood liver cancer refers to malignant tumors that arise in children aged 15 years or younger . The most common type of childhood liver cancer is hepatoblastoma, which accounts for approximately 60% of all cases . Other types of childhood liver cancers include hepatic blastoma, epithelial hemangioendothelioma, cholangiocarcinoma, and metastases from other primary sites such as neuroblastomas and rhabdomyosarcomas .

The stages of childhood liver cancer (also known as pediatric hepatoblastoma) are classified using the International Classification of Childhood Liver Tumors (ICCLT). This classification system is based on histology, tumor extent, vascular invasion, lymph node involvement, and metastasis .

The prognosis of patients with localized Ewing sarcoma has improved significantly over time due to advances in multimodal therapy . With current treatment regimens, approximately 70% of patients with localized disease can be cured . However, the overall survival rate remains poor at around 25%, mainly because of metastatic spread or recurrence after initial remission .

Osteosarcoma can occur in both children and adults but is more common in males between 10-25 years old . Risk factors include genetic predisposition (e.g., Li Fraumeni syndrome), prior radiation exposure, family history of osteosarcoma or other bone tumors, and rare inherited metabolic disorders such as Paget's disease, hypophosphatasia, hyperparathyroidism, McCune Albright syndrome, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, and neurofibromatosis type I .

The treatment options for osteosarcoma typically include surgery combined with chemotherapy. Surgery may involve limb amputation or limb-sparing resection depending on the location and severity of the tumor. Chemotherapy regimens often consist of high doses of methotrexate, cisplatin, doxorubicin, ifosfamide, and etoposide .

The diagnosis of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors typically involves a combination of clinical symptoms, endoscopic evaluation with biopsy, imaging studies such as CT or MRI, and laboratory tests such as serotonin levels in the blood. Endoscopy is often used to examine the digestive tract for signs of cancer, including ulcers, bleeding, and polyps. Biopsies can be taken during an endoscopy if any abnormalities are found. Imaging studies such as CT or MRI may also be ordered by your doctor to look for any signs of metastasis or other complications associated with cancer. Laboratory tests, such as measuring serotonin levels in the blood, can help confirm whether there is evidence of carcinoid syndrome. In addition, specialized tests such as somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (SRS) may be performed to locate small tumor deposits that cannot be detected by standard imaging techniques.

Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDSs) are a group of clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis resulting in cytopenia(s), dysplasia, and an increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). MDS can be further classified into lower-risk or higher-risk subtypes depending on various factors such as cytogenetics, bone marrow blast percentage, number of lineages with dysplasia, and transfusion requirement . The incidence rate for MDS increases significantly with age, affecting approximately 4 per 100,000 people under the age of 65 years and up to 23 per 100,000 people over the age of 70 years .

The treatment of chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) depends on several factors such as disease type, risk stratification, age, symptoms, and comorbidities . Low-risk patients with asymptomatic MPNs may be observed without any therapy or treated with low-dose aspirin to prevent thrombosis . High-risk patients with symptomatic MPNs can be treated with targeted therapies that inhibit JAK1/2 signaling pathways, including ruxolitinib, pegylated IFNα-2a, and hydroxyurea . Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is considered a curative option but has high morbidity and mortality rates due to graft versus host disease and other complications .

Primary myelofibrosis (PMF) is a type of chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN). It occurs when mutations in genes that regulate cell growth cause abnormal proliferation of blood stem cells . This leads to an overproduction of certain types of white blood cells, red blood cells, or platelets. The condition can result in bone marrow fibrosis, which interferes with normal hematopoiesis and causes organ damage .

The symptoms of essential thrombocythaemia (ET) typically include fatigue due to anaemia, headaches, dizziness or fainting caused by low red blood cell counts; easy bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, heavy menstrual periods, or purpura from low platelet counts; and weight loss, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and splenomegaly resulting from extramedullary haematopoiesis .

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL), also known as myeloid or idiopathic hypereosinophilia, is a rare chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by sustained peripheral blood eosinophilia of more than 10% of total white blood cells for at least six months . CEL can be further classified into two subtypes: CEL-2 and CEL-3.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified myeloid neoplasms into two categories: myelodysplastic syndromes (MDSs), which include refractory anemia with excess blasts in transformation (RAEB-T); and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs). MDS is characterized by cytopenias, dysplasia, and increased risk of acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), while MPN is characterized by hypercellular marrow, clonal proliferation, and increased risk for fibrotic progression .

The prognosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) varies depending on several factors such as age at diagnosis, white blood cell count, bone marrow blast percentage, chromosomal abnormalities, and mutational status . In general, CMML has an aggressive course with median survival time ranging from 1 to 5 years after diagnosis . Patients aged less than 60 years old have better overall survival compared to those over 60 years old .

The treatment of juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and supportive care. The specific treatment plan will depend on several factors, including the patient's age, genetic mutations associated with JMML, and other health-related characteristics.

MDS/MPN-U is a rare type of blood cancer that combines features of myeloid dysplasia with abnormal proliferation of one or more types of immature white blood cells in the bone marrow . It was first recognized as a distinct category of hematologic malignancies by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2016. The diagnosis of MDS/MPN-U requires evidence of both myelodysplasia and myeloproliferation, which can be detected through genetic testing such as karyotyping and next-generation sequencing .

The most common symptom of endometrial cancer is abnormal vaginal bleeding, which can occur during or between menstrual periods in postmenopausal women . Other symptoms include pelvic pain, discomfort during sexual intercourse, increased urinary urgency, dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse), weight loss, fatigue, anemia, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, vomiting, indigestion, gastritis, and gastrointestinal bleeding .

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials related to endometrial cancer that are listed in ClinicalTrials.gov . These include studies evaluating new treatment options such as targeted therapies or immunotherapies, as well as studies investigating ways to improve existing treatments. Some of these trials focus specifically on early-stage disease while others focus on advanced stages. It's important to note that some trials may have been suspended due to COVID-19 pandemic but most of them resumed with proper safety measures.

The prognosis of uterine sarcomas depends on several factors such as histologic subtype, tumor size, grade, stage, surgical margins, lymphovascular invasion, hormonal status, and adjuvant therapy . Overall survival rates range from 50% to 92%, with an average of approximately 70%. However, these figures vary widely depending on the specific type of uterine sarcoma. For example, endometrial stromal sarcomas have better outcomes than other types of uterine sarcomas .

Childhood extracranial germ cell tumors (EGCTs) are rare malignant neoplasms that arise from cells of embryonic origin outside of the central nervous system in children . These tumors can occur at any site in the body but most commonly involve the gonads, mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and anterior abdominal wall . EGCTs account for approximately 3% to 5% of all childhood solid tumors and have an annual incidence rate of about one per million individuals under the age of 14 years . The exact cause of these tumors remains unknown; however, they may be related to genetic factors or exposure to environmental carcinogens during fetal development or early life .

The prognosis of childhood extracranial germ cell tumours (EGCT) depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, primary site, histology, stage, and presence or absence of metastasis . Overall survival rates have improved significantly over time due to advances in diagnostic techniques, treatment strategies, and supportive care. In general, EGCTs have a better overall survival rate than intracranial GCTs, with 5-year survival rates ranging from 70% to 98%, depending on the specific type of tumour and its location .

Extragonadal germ cell tumors (EGCTs) can occur in both genders but are more common among males than females . The most commonly affected sites of EGCTs include retroperitoneum, mediastinum, testis, ovaries, endometrium, fallopian tube, urinary bladder, kidney, and central nervous system . Risk factors associated with EGCTs include family history of hereditary cancer syndromes such as familial retinoblastoma or Lynch syndrome, exposure to ionizing radiation during childhood, cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and undescended testicles .

The treatment of extragonadal germ cell tumors typically involves surgical resection followed by chemotherapy with cisplatin-based regimens . However, the specific treatment approach may vary depending on factors such as the location and stage of the tumor, age at diagnosis, and other individual characteristics .

Uveal melanoma is diagnosed through a combination of clinical examination, imaging tests such as ultrasound and optical coherence tomography, and genetic testing. The gold standard for diagnosis is histopathological evaluation of tissue biopsy samples obtained during enucleation or vitrectomy surgery.

Retinoblastomas are malignant tumors that arise from immature retinal cells in children aged 6 months to 4 years old . They can be unilateral or bilateral and usually present with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), strabismus, ocular pain, hyphema, proptosis, or vision loss . The most common presenting symptom is leukocoria, which occurs in approximately two-thirds of patients .

The prognosis of retinoblastoma depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, tumor size, extent of intraocular disease, presence or absence of metastasis, and genetic status (hereditary vs non-hereditary). With early detection and appropriate treatment, the cure rate for localized retinoblastoma can be up to 90%. However, if left untreated, it has an extremely poor prognosis with a survival rate of less than 15% .

Risk factors for ovarian epithelial cancer include increasing age, family history of breast or ovarian cancer, personal history of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), endometriosis, hormonal replacement therapy use, postmenopausal obesity, and infertility treatment with in vitro fertilization .

The prognosis of ovarian epithelial cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, histologic subtype, grade, age, surgical treatment, and response to chemotherapy . In general, patients with early-stage disease have better survival rates than those diagnosed with advanced-stage disease. However, most women present with advanced-stage disease due to nonspecific symptoms that can be attributed to other causes.

The most common symptom of ovarian germ cell tumor is irregular menstrual cycles or amenorrhea (no periods). Other possible signs include abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, urinary frequency, constipation, diarrhea, weight gain or loss, and fatigue. Some women may also experience pelvic pressure or pain, which can be felt as cramping in the lower right side of the abdomen.

The term "low malignant potential" is not commonly used in reference to ovarian tumors. It may be more accurate to use the terms "borderline tumor" or "tumor of low malignant potential." Borderline tumors are a group of epithelial ovarian neoplasms that have intermediate behavior between benign and malignant lesions. They do not metastasize but can recur locally and have the potential for progression .

Risk factors for ovarian cancer include increasing age, family history of breast or ovarian cancer, personal history of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), endometriosis, hormonal factors such as early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, infertility treatment using clomiphene citrate, and obesity .

Gallbladder cancer is diagnosed through a combination of imaging tests and tissue biopsy. Imaging tests such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) can help detect abnormalities in the gallbladder that may be suggestive of cancer. However, these tests cannot definitively diagnose cancer without further investigation.

Testicular cancer can affect men of any age but it most commonly occurs in young adult males between 20-49 years old . The exact cause of testicular cancer remains unknown, however certain factors have been identified that increase the risk of developing this disease such as cryptorchidism (undescended testicle), family history of testicular cancer, low sperm count or infertility, viral infection, exposure to pesticides, radiation therapy, and genetic syndromes like Down syndrome . It's important to note that these factors do not necessarily mean you will develop testicular cancer, but they may be worth discussing with your doctor if you have concerns about your health.

The outlook for testicular cancer depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, age of patient, presence or absence of metastasis, and type of treatment received. In general, if diagnosed early through regular self-examination and seeking prompt medical attention, testicular cancer has a high cure rate with treatments that include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination of these approaches . However, it's important to note that while rare, there is a possibility of recurrence in some cases, particularly when metastases have already spread beyond the regional lymph nodes. Regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare provider are recommended to monitor any signs of recurrence or new cancers.

The prognosis of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) depends on several factors such as the type of GTD, the size of the tumor at diagnosis, whether it has invaded other organs or spread to other parts of the body, and how well the patient responds to treatment . In general, with appropriate treatment, the cure rate for GTD is high, ranging from 95% to almost 100%. However, if left untreated, GTN can be fatal in up to half of all cases . It's important to note that early detection and prompt treatment are crucial for improving outcomes and preventing complications associated with GTD.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) can affect anyone of any age group but it most commonly affects children between 1 and 2 years old . It occurs more frequently in boys than girls. There is no known cause or genetic predisposition to developing LCH. However, there may be an association with viral infections such as human herpes virus type 6 (HHV-6).

The treatment of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation therapy depending on the severity and location of the disease. First-line systemic therapies include vinblastine monotherapy or vinblastine plus prednisone . If these regimens fail to achieve remission, second-line agents such as cladribine, denosumab, 6-mercaptopurine, cytarabine, doxorubicin, and busulfan may be considered . Surgery is often used in conjunction with systemic therapy to remove affected tissues and prevent complications . Radiation therapy may also be recommended in certain cases where surgical removal is not possible or effective enough .

Diagnosis of hypopharyngeal cancer typically involves a combination of clinical examination, imaging studies such as CT or MRI scans, and biopsy for histopathological evaluation. During the clinical exam, doctors will look for signs of swelling, redness, pain, difficulty swallowing, hoarseness, or any other abnormalities in the head and neck area. Imaging tests can help identify tumors, lymph node metastases, and other potential indicators of malignancy. Biopsies may be performed using endoscopic techniques such as transnasal endoscopy with brush cytology, forceps biopsy, or endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (EBUS-FNA). These procedures allow doctors to collect tissue samples from suspicious areas for further analysis under a microscope.

Oral cavity cancer refers to any type of malignant tumor that arises from the lips, tongue, salivary glands, oral mucosa, oropharynx, nasopharynx, tonsils, soft palate, uvula, and other areas within the mouth . The most common types of cancers in this area include squamous cell carcinoma, which accounts for approximately 90% of all cases, followed by undifferentiated carcinomas, lymphomas, adenocarcinomas, verrucous carcinomas, sarcomas, and melanomas .

The diagnosis of laryngeal cancer typically involves several steps, including a thorough physical examination of the head and neck region, as well as additional tests such as endoscopy with biopsy, imaging studies (such as CT scans or MRI), and other diagnostic procedures depending on the specific symptoms presented by the patient .

Lip and oral cavity cancer refers to malignant tumors that occur in the lips, tongue, salivary glands, or other parts of the mouth . These cancers are often caused by exposure to tobacco smoke, alcohol consumption, human papillomavirus infection, or betel quid chewing . Symptoms may include a lump or sore that does not heal, persistent pain or numbness, difficulty swallowing, or changes in speech . Diagnosis typically involves a physical examination, imaging tests such as CT scans or MRIs, and biopsy . Treatment options may include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapies, or immunotherapies . The prognosis for lip and oral cavity cancer depends on various factors including stage at diagnosis, location within the mouth, and overall health status . Early detection is crucial for successful treatment and improved survival rates .

The stages of lip and oral cavity cancer are as follows: Stage 0 (carcinoma in situ): This stage is characterized by confinement to the epithelium with no invasion into the stroma or other tissues.Stage I: At this stage, there is an extension beyond the confines of the epithelial layer but without involvement of any lymph nodes.Stage II: Involvement of one or more ipsilateral lymph nodes is present at this stage.Stage III: There is spread to multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes, including those above level II, as well as involvement of the maxillary sinuses, hard palate, pyriform fossa, pharyngeal walls, tongue base, mandible, and buccinator muscle.Stage IVA: Spread occurs to bilateral or contralateral nodal groups, including supraclavicular fossae, anterior mediastinal structures, prevertebral space, spinal cord, brain, skull base, masticator space, parapharyngeal spaces, skin of face, nasopharynx, middle ear, mastoid process, orbital contents, thyroid gland, hyoid bone, glottic larynx, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and parotid glands.

The diagnosis of metastatic squamous neck cancer with an occult primary site typically involves a combination of clinical examination, imaging studies such as CT or MRI scans, and biopsy of any suspicious lesions found during examination or imaging. In addition, other tests may be performed depending on the specific location of the suspected tumor. For example, if there is a suspicion of involvement in the oral cavity, endoscopic examinations using fiberoptic scopes can also be used.

Nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) is a type of head and neck cancer that originates from the nasopharynx, which is located in the upper part of the throat behind the nose and near the base of the skull . It can be divided into two main types: squamous cell carcinoma and undifferentiated carcinomas. The latter is more common in certain parts of Asia, particularly Southeast Asia and North Africa .

The stages of nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) are determined using the Tumor-Node-Metastasis (TNM) staging system, which is developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). This classification system takes into account three main factors: the size of the primary tumour (T), the extent of spread to local lymph nodes (N) and whether there has been any distant metastases (M).

The most common symptom of oropharyngeal cancer is a painless lump or sore that lasts for more than two weeks . Other symptoms include difficulty swallowing (dysphasia), hoarseness lasting longer than three weeks, persistent earache, sensation of something being stuck in your throat (known as dysgeusia), cough, bleeding from the mouth, trouble breathing, loose teeth, weight loss, and problems with speech .

There have been several ongoing studies related to oropharyngeal cancer in recent years. One such study is the phase II trial of pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy as first-line treatment for patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (NCT03741982). Another study is evaluating the efficacy and safety of nivolumab versus methotrexate, docetaxel, or cetuximab as second-line therapy for recurrent or metastatic disease (NCT03568216). Additionally, there is an open-label, single-arm phase Ib/II study investigating the combination of durvalumab and platinum-based chemotherapy in untreated advanced stage cancers including HNCs (NCT03121899).

The prognosis of paranasal sinus and nasal cavity cancer depends on several factors, including stage at diagnosis, tumor location, histologic type, grade, and patient characteristics such as age and overall health status . Surgery is often used to treat early-stage disease, while chemotherapy and radiation therapy may be recommended for more advanced stages or if surgery is not possible due to the extent of the cancer or its location . In general, patients with localized disease have better survival rates than those with regional or distant spread .

Salivary gland cancer can occur in any age group but is more common among adults aged 40 to 80 years old . The parotid glands (located near the jawline) are most commonly affected, followed by the submandibular glands (underneath the chin), and then minor salivary glands located throughout the oral cavity. Risk factors include exposure to radiation therapy or certain chemicals, smoking tobacco products, heavy alcohol consumption, family history of salivary gland tumors, genetic syndromes such as Muir-Torre syndrome and Fanconi anemia, and some viral infections including Epstein–Barr virus and human papillomavirus .

The treatment of salivary gland cancer typically involves a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or targeted therapies depending on the type and stage of the tumor. Surgery is often the first line of treatment and may involve partial or complete removal of one or more salivary glands, as well as surrounding tissue and lymph nodes if necessary. Radiation therapy uses high-energy X-rays or particles to kill cancer cells and can be used before, after, or in place of surgery. Chemotherapy uses drugs that target rapidly dividing cells and can be given alone or in conjunction with other treatments. Targeted therapies use medications that specifically target molecules involved in cell growth and division, such as tyrosine kinases and epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFR). These therapies can be used alone or in combination with other treatments.

Pancreatic cancer can affect anyone; however, certain factors increase the likelihood of developing this disease. The main risk factor for pancreatic cancer is smoking, which doubles the risk compared to non-smokers . Other major risk factors include age (with higher incidence in people over 60 years old), family history of pancreatic or other types of cancer, chronic pancreatitis, diabetes mellitus, obesity, alcohol consumption, heavy occupational exposure to chemicals such as chlorinated hydrocarbons, acrylamides, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and genetic syndromes like Peutz–Jeghers syndrome and familial atypical multiple mole melanoma .

The standard treatment for pancreatic cancer is surgical resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with gemcitabine or FOLFIRINOX (a combination of 5-fluorouracil, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin). For patients who are not candidates for surgery, chemotherapies such as gemcitabine monotherapy or FOLFIRINOX can be used to prolong survival and improve quality of life. Targeted therapies and immunotherapies are also being investigated in clinical trials.

The prognosis of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pNET) depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, grade, Ki-67 index, and location within the pancreas . Generally, patients with well-differentiated pNETs have a better prognosis than those with poorly differentiated or undifferentiated tumors . Surgery remains the mainstay treatment option for resectable localized disease, while systemic chemotherapy plays an important role in metastatic or unresectable cases .

The stages of renal cell cancer (RCC) are determined using the Tumor-Node-Metastasis (TNM) classification system developed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). This staging system takes into account three factors: the size of the tumor (T), whether it has spread to other parts of the kidney or surrounding tissues (N), and whether it has metastasized to distant organs (M).

Diagnosis of transitional cell cancer (TCC) of the renal pelvis or ureter typically involves a combination of clinical symptoms, physical examination findings, imaging studies such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), cystoscopy with biopsy, urine analysis, and tumor markers .
Wilms tumour is a type of kidney cancer that usually occurs in children under 5 years old. It can be treated with surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy.

The most common pediatric kidney tumor is Wilms tumor (WT), which accounts for approximately 6% of all childhood cancers . WT typically presents as an abdominal mass in children aged between 2 and 4 years old. It originates from blastemal cells that fail to differentiate into mature nephrons during embryonic development .

There is no guaranteed way to completely prevent breast cancer as it can be caused by many factors such as genetics, lifestyle, and environmental exposures. However, there are several steps that women can take to reduce their risk of developing breast cancer or detecting it early when treatment is more effective. These include maintaining a healthy body weight throughout life, limiting alcohol consumption, not smoking cigarettes, eating a diet rich in fruits and vegetables, exercising regularly, taking oral contraceptives, having children at an earlier age, and undergoing regular mammograms starting at age 40 . Additionally, women with certain genetic mutations may benefit from receiving prophylactic surgery to remove their breasts or ovaries .

The stages of breast cancer refer to how far the cancer has spread within the breast or outside of the breast into other organs in the body. There are four main stages of breast cancer: stage 0 (noninvasive), stage I, II, III, and IV.

No, male breast cancer is not thought to be inherited in the same way as female breast cancer. While there may be some genetic factors that contribute to an increased risk of developing the disease, they have not yet been identified. However, certain genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, which increase the risk of hereditary breast cancer, can also cause other types of cancers including ovarian, prostate, pancreatic, and colon cancer .

The treatment of male breast cancer typically involves a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and hormone therapy. Surgery is usually the first line of treatment and may involve mastectomy or lumpectomy depending on the stage and size of the tumor. Radiation therapy is often recommended after surgery to help prevent recurrence. Chemotherapy is also commonly used as an adjuvant treatment in patients with advanced disease. Hormonal therapies such as tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors can be effective in treating estrogen receptor-positive tumors. Targeted therapies such as trastuzumab (Herceptin) and lapatinib may be considered for patients with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive tumors.

The three main types of skin cancer are basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and melanoma. BCC is the most common type of skin cancer, accounting for about 80% of all cases. It usually appears as small, flesh-colored or red bumps or lesions on the face, ears, neck, or other sun-exposed areas of the body. SCC accounts for about 20% of all skin cancers and typically presents as scaly, thickened patches or nodules that may be pink, brown, gray or blue in color. Melanoma is less common than BCC and SCC but it is more dangerous because it can spread quickly to other parts of the body if left untreated. Melanomas often appear as dark spots or moles that are irregularly shaped with varied colors.

The most common symptom of melanoma is an abnormal skin lesion that appears suddenly and looks different from existing moles or blemishes. Other signs include changes in the size, shape, color, or texture of an existing mole; a new dark spot on the skin; a sore that does not heal; a wart-like growth; a thickened patch of skin; and unusual pigmentation of the palms of hands, soles of feet, mouth, genitals, or toenails.

There have been several ongoing studies to investigate new treatments for melanoma. One such study is the KEYNOTE-054 trial, which evaluated pembrolizumab as monotherapy in patients with previously untreated advanced melanoma. The results of this trial showed that pembrolizumab was effective in treating these patients, with an overall response rate of 32% . Another ongoing study is the CheckMate-675 trial, which compares nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus nivolumab alone in patients with previously untreated advanced melanoma. Preliminary data from this trial suggests that combination therapy may be more effective than monotherapy, with an objective response rate of 58% for the combination group compared to 49% for the nivolumab only group .

The prognosis of Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor location, size, grade, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis . MCC has a high tendency to spread to regional lymph nodes and distant organs, particularly the lung, liver, bone marrow, brain, and skin .

Plasma cell neoplasm refers to any malignant tumor that arises from plasma cells or B lymphocytes in their differentiated state . The most common type of plasma cell neoplasm is multiple myeloma, which accounts for approximately 1% of all cancers worldwide .

The treatment of plasma cell neoplasms depends on several factors, including the type and stage of disease, age, overall health status, and personal preferences. For multiple myeloma, which is the most common type of plasma cell neoplasm, standard first-line therapy typically involves combination chemotherapy with an immunomodulatory drug such as lenalidomide or pomalidomide plus dexamethasone . Other options include autologous stem cell transplantation after induction therapy and monoclonal antibody therapies targeting CD38, such as daratumumab, and those targeting B cell maturation antigen, such as elotuzumab.

Neuroblastoma is diagnosed through a combination of clinical symptoms, physical examination findings, imaging studies such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and bone scintigraphy, laboratory tests including urine vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA) levels, and histopathological evaluation of tumor tissue obtained by biopsy or surgery .

Neuroblastoma (NB) is a pediatric tumor that arises from neural crest cells of the adrenal medulla or along sympathetic ganglia in the abdomen . It occurs most frequently in children under 5 years old, with an incidence peak between 12–18 months of age . NB accounts for approximately 7% of all childhood cancers and 15% of all pediatric solid tumors . The disease has no gender predilection, although males have slightly higher rates than females .

The prognosis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, age, performance status, histology, and other comorbidities . According to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines, patients with early-stage NSCLC have a 5-year survival rate of up to 80–92%, while those with advanced-stage disease have a 5-year survival rate of only 4% . However, recent advancements in treatment options such as targeted therapies and immunotherapies have improved outcomes for some subgroups of patients with metastatic or recurrent NSCLC .

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a type of aggressive neuroendocrine tumor that develops in the lungs. It accounts for about 15% of all lung cancers diagnosed each year . SCLC most commonly affects men over the age of 60 who have a history of smoking tobacco cigarettes or other forms of tobacco products such as pipes or cigars. Smoking remains to be one of the main risk factors associated with SCLC development. The more pack-years smoked increases the likelihood of developing this disease. In addition, exposure to secondhand smoke also contributes to an increased risk of SCLC. Other risk factors include occupational exposures to certain chemicals and radiation therapy.

There have been several ongoing studies related to small cell lung cancer (SCLC). One such study is the CheckMate 738 trial, which is evaluating nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus chemotherapy in patients with SCLC who have not received prior treatment or who have relapsed after first-line therapy . Another study, JAVELIN Solid Tumors, is investigating avelumab as maintenance therapy in patients with advanced solid tumours, including SCLC, who have responded to platinum-based chemotherapy . The KEYNOTE-604 trial is examining pembrolizumab plus etoposide and either carboplatin or cisplatin versus placebo plus etoposide and either carboplatin or cisplatin in patients with extensive stage SCLC who are naive to treatment or whose disease has progressed within six months of starting first-line chemotherapy .

Parathyroid cancer (PC) is an extremely rare endocrine malignancy that accounts for less than 1% of all thyroid cancers . The incidence rate of PC in the general population has been estimated to be between 0.5 and 2 cases per million people annually , with no significant difference observed among men and women.

The treatment of parathyroid cancer typically involves surgical removal of the tumor or tumors along with any affected parathyroid glands. Depending on the size and location of the tumor(s), this may involve either a focused resection to remove only the diseased tissue (parathyroidectomy) or more extensive surgery such as total thyroidectomy plus bilateral central neck dissection or even partial or complete laryngectomy in rare cases . In some cases, chemotherapy or radiation therapy may also be used before or after surgery depending on the specific type of cancer involved.

The diagnosis of penile cancer typically involves a combination of physical examination, patient history, imaging tests such as ultrasound or MRI, and biopsy for histopathological evaluation. During a physical exam, the doctor will look for any abnormalities in the appearance, texture, color, or feel of the skin on the penis. They may also ask about symptoms such as discharge from the meatus (the opening at the tip of the penis), pain or difficulty urinating, or bleeding.

A pituitary tumor refers to any type of growth that occurs within or around the pituitary gland. The pituitary gland is a small pea-sized endocrine gland located at the base of the brain behind the nose and sphenoid sinus . It produces several hormones including adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), prolactin, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), and growth hormone (GH).

The diagnosis of prostate cancer typically involves several steps, including a digital rectal examination (DRE), blood tests for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, transrectal ultrasound (TRUS), multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI), and biopsy of the prostate gland.

Prostate cancer can affect any man regardless of age or race; however, it is more common in men over 50 years old and those of African American descent. Other factors that may increase the risk include having a family history of prostate cancer, particularly in first-degree relatives such as fathers and brothers, consuming a diet high in fat and low in fruits and vegetables, being overweight or obese, smoking tobacco products, and exposure to certain chemicals or radiation. It is important for all men to be aware of these risk factors and to discuss them with their healthcare provider during regular checkups.
