It originates from the cells of the retina and usually affects one eye at an early age (between 6 months to 3 years). However, it may also occur in both eyes simultaneously or successively. The symptoms include leukocoria (white spots inside the eye), strabismus (crossed eyes), ocular inflammation, and vision loss. If left untreated, this disease can spread into the brain and cause death.

The prognosis of pediatric soft tissue sarcomas depends on several factors including histologic subtype, tumor grade, size, location, stage at diagnosis, age, presence or absence of metastasis, and patient’s overall health status . Overall survival rates range from 40% to over 85%, with lower survival associated with older children (teenagers) and higher-grade tumors.

The types of cancer that occur more frequently in women within the female reproductive system include breast cancer, cervical cancer, endometrial cancer (cancer of the uterus), ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer, vaginal cancer, vulvar cancer, choriocarcinoma (a rare form of trophoblastic cancer), and placental site trophoblastic tumors.

The prognosis of patients with uterine cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, histologic type, grade, lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), myometrial invasion (MI) depth of MI, lymph node involvement, and receptor status . In general, early-stage endometrioid carcinoma has an excellent prognosis, while advanced disease or nonendometrioid subtypes have poor outcomes.

Testicular cancer is one type of cancer that can cause nausea and vomiting in young men. Other types of cancer such as stomach or pancreatic cancer may also present with these symptoms. It's important to consult a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.

There is an ongoing phase I trial (NCT04198765) that aims to evaluate the safety of combining niraparib with cediranib in patients with recurrent solid tumors, including ovarian cancer. The primary objective of this study is to determine the maximum tolerated dose of the combination therapy.

Borderline low malignant potential (LMP) tumors are rare ovarian neoplasms that have been recently reclassified as epithelial ovarian cancers with low malignant potential by the World Health Organization . They typically occur in young women and are often unilateral or bilateral cystic masses with no solid components. The histologic features of these tumors include papillary structures lined by cuboidal to columnar cells with microvilli, hobnail changes, and pseudostratification.

Cancer is a complex disease that can occur in people of any age group or gender. However, certain types of cancer appear to be more common among specific demographics than others. For example, breast cancer affects women more often than men, while prostate cancer tends to affect men more frequently than women. Lung cancer is most commonly diagnosed in older adults over 50 years old, but it can also occur in younger individuals who smoke cigarettes. Skin cancer is more prevalent in fair-skinned populations due to increased sun exposure and susceptibility to ultraviolet radiation damage. Colorectal cancer is more common in older adults, with rates increasing after the age of 40. Rates of colorectal cancer are lower for those under 40, but they do occur in this population as well.

The most common diagnostic test for pancreatic cancer is an abdominal ultrasound (USG) followed by computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS), positron emission tomography (PET), or biopsy of the tumor tissue .

Yes, there is an increased risk of prostate cancer in men who have had sex with other men (MSM). A study published in JAMA Oncology found that MSM were 83% more likely to develop prostate cancer than non-gay or bisexual men . This may be due to several factors such as higher rates of human papillomavirus infection, chronic inflammation, and hormonal differences between MSM and heterosexual men. It's important for MSM to get screened regularly for prostate cancer to catch it early when treatment is most effective.

The overall 5-year survival rate for anal cancer is approximately 80%. However, it varies depending on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor size, lymph node involvement, histologic grade, and patient age. Patients with early-stage localized disease have an excellent prognosis, while those diagnosed with advanced metastatic disease have poorer outcomes. Regular follow-up examinations including physical examination, blood tests, imaging scans (such as CT or MRI), and endoscopy can help detect recurrence or new primary lesions in patients who have completed treatment to improve their chances of survival.

The prognosis depends on the underlying cause of fetal growth restriction (FGR). If FGR is due to maternal factors such as hypertensive disorders or diabetes mellitus, the prognosis may be better than if it is caused by placental insufficiency or chromosomal abnormalities. Treatment options include close monitoring with serial ultrasounds, bed rest, dietary modifications, and medications such as calcium supplementation and low-dose aspirin. In severe cases where there is significant risk of adverse perinatal outcomes despite medical management, early delivery via induction of labor or cesarean section may be necessary. However, even after successful intervention, infants born from pregnancies complicated by FGR have an increased risk of neonatal morbidity and mortality compared to those born at term without complications.

The exact cause of ALS is unknown; however, several factors have been identified that may increase an individual's risk for developing the disease. These include family history of ALS or frontotemporal dementia (FTD), age over 65 years old, military service in the Gulf War, exposure to heavy metals such as aluminum, lead, mercury, and manganese, smoking tobacco products, prior head trauma, and certain genetic mutations.

Treatment of HLH is typically divided into two phases: induction therapy to quickly control symptoms during acute episodes and long-term maintenance therapy to prevent relapses . The first line treatment regimen consists of dexamethasone plus etoposide or cyclosporine A plus vinblastine. In addition, intravenous immunoglobulin may be used in combination with these therapies. Second line treatment includes alemtuzumab, anti-interferon gamma monoclonal antibody emapalumab, and allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation .
Laryngeal SCC is diagnosed by biopsy of suspicious lesions with endoscopy as well as imaging such as CT or MRI scans to determine if it has spread (metastasized) to other parts of the body.
Oral Cancer

There are several symptoms which can suggest cancer of the throat including persistent coughing or difficulty swallowing, pain when swallowing food or liquids, hoarseness lasting more than two weeks, soreness or irritation inside your mouth, trouble breathing through your nose, among others. It is important to note that these symptoms could also be related to other conditions not associated with cancer; therefore it's recommended to see an Ear Nose Throat specialist for proper diagnosis.
The patient has oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

The different stages of oral cavity cancer refer to how far the cancer has spread in terms of depth into the tissue layers (T stage) and whether it has spread to nearby lymph nodes or other parts of the body (N and M stage). These stages are used by doctors to determine what type of treatment is best for each patient.

In cases where the primary site of cancer is unknown or difficult to determine, doctors may use various imaging techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, ultrasound, and bone scans to help locate the primary tumor. Once the primary tumor has been identified, additional tests including biopsies and immunohistochemical staining can then be performed to confirm the diagnosis and determine whether it has spread to other organs or tissues.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a rare form of head and neck cancer that originates from the epithelial cells lining the inner surface of the nasopharynx. It accounts for approximately 1% of all cancers worldwide . The incidence rate varies significantly depending on geographic location, with higher rates observed among individuals living in North Africa, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Alaska compared to those residing in Europe or North America .

The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) has developed a staging system for head and neck cancers that is used worldwide. This system classifies NPC into eight stages ranging from stage 0 to IVB, with higher numbers indicating more advanced disease.

The most common signs and symptoms of infection or malignancies in the head and neck area include pain (early), redness, swelling, fever, chills, difficulty swallowing, bleeding, cough, odynophagia, dysphonia, otalgia, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, sore throat, halitosis, dysgeusia, weight loss, hoarseness, lymphadenopathy, skin changes, ulceration, induration, mass, and discharge .

There are several new therapies being investigated in clinical trials for HNSCC treatment including targeted therapy with EGFR inhibitors such as cetuximab or panitumumab, PARP inhibitor olaparib, immunotherapy with nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, ipilimumab, and combination of anti-PD1 antibodies with chemotherapeutic agents like cisplatin or 5FU, radiation sensitizers such as palbociclib, and other novel therapeutics .

The prognosis for patients with malignant tumors originating from the sinonasal cavity depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, histologic type, treatment received, and patient characteristics (age, comorbidities). In general, early-stage cancers have better outcomes than advanced-stage ones. For example, 5-year survival rates range between 80% to 90% for Stage I disease compared to less than 20% for Stage IV disease . However, it should be noted that these statistics vary widely depending on the specific subtype of cancer involved.

Salivary gland tumor development is associated with genetic mutations (e.g., BRCA1), exposure to radiation or certain chemicals such as tobacco smoke, alcohol consumption, and family history of salivary gland cancer .

Treatment options for head and neck cancer with distant metastasis include chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiation therapy, surgical resection, or palliative care depending on the location and number of metastases, patient's overall health status, and preference.

There are several risk factors that have been identified to increase the chance of developing pancreatic cancer including smoking, age (older than 60 years), family history of pancreas or other cancers, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, diabetes mellitus, heavy alcohol consumption, occupational exposure to chemicals such as chlorinated hydrocarbons, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and trichloroethylene, and certain dietary habits like high intake of red meat .

For patients with advanced gastric cancer that is not amenable to surgical resection, chemotherapy remains the mainstay of treatment. The current standard first-line therapy involves combination regimens consisting of fluoropyrimidine (either 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine) plus cisplatin. Other agents such as irinotecan, oxaliplatin, ramucirumab, trastuzumab, and docetaxel may be added depending upon the specific molecular profile of the tumor.

The typical prognosis of patients with an insulinoma depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, size of the tumour, location within the pancreas, and whether it has been resected completely or not. If left untreated, insulinomas can lead to hypoglycemia-related complications including seizures, coma, brain damage, permanent disability, and even death . However, if diagnosed early and treated appropriately through surgery, most patients experience complete resolution of symptoms and return to normal life activities .

Kidney cancers are classified into renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and non-renal cell carcinomas (NRCC). RCC accounts for about 90% of all cases while NRCCs account for less than 10%. The most common type of RCC is clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), which arises from proximal tubular cells .

A doctor may order additional tests to confirm or rule out kidney cancer if there is blood in your urine. These include imaging tests such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET) scans, and biopsies of suspicious areas. The type of test used depends on various factors, including age, family history, risk factors for other diseases that can cause hematuria, and personal preferences. It's important to note that while these tests can help diagnose kidney cancer, they cannot definitively confirm it without a tissue sample obtained through a biopsy.

Wilms’ tumor is a pediatric renal neoplasm that arises from immature mesodermal cells in the metanephros during embryogenesis. It belongs to the category of germ cell tumors (GCTs), which originate from primordial germ cells or their precursors . GCTs account for approximately 3% of all childhood malignancies and occur most frequently between ages 4–10 years old with an average age at diagnosis of 5 years old .

Childhood cancers are classified into two main groups: leukemia (which affects blood cells) and solid tumors (which affect tissues). The most common types of childhood cancers include acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), neuroblastoma, Wilms’ tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, retinoblastoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and brain tumors such as medulloblastomas and primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNETs).

There is no absolute way to guarantee prevention of cancer but there are several steps you can take that may help reduce your risk. Firstly, maintain a healthy body weight throughout life as obesity increases the risk for many types of cancer . Secondly, eat plenty of fruits and vegetables which contain antioxidants and other compounds with anti-cancer properties . Thirdly, exercise regularly because it helps control body fat and strengthens the immune system . Fourthly, limit alcohol consumption since chronic heavy drinking has been associated with an increased risk of certain types of cancer such as liver, esophageal, head and neck cancers . Fifthly, avoid tobacco products because they increase the risk of almost all types of cancer . Finally, protect yourself from the sun by seeking shade, wearing protective clothing, using a broad spectrum sunscreen, and avoiding tanning beds .

The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) has defined four stages for breast cancer based on the TNM staging system. Stage 0 is considered as carcinoma in situ or non-invasive breast cancer where cells have not spread beyond the inner lining of the milk ducts. This stage is further divided into two categories: DCIS (ductal cell carcinoma in situ), which involves abnormal cells confined to the lobules or ducts of the breast tissue; and LCIS (lobular cell carcinoma in situ), which occurs when abnormal cells accumulate within the lobules of the breast but do not form a mass or invade nearby tissues.

Yes, there is an increased risk of developing breast cancer in women with a positive family history of the disease. The risk increases if more than one first-degree relative has been diagnosed with breast cancer.

The most common type of breast cancer in men is invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC). Other types include lobular carcinoma, mucinous adenocarcinoma, papillary carcinomas, medullary carcinomas, metastatic tumors from other organs, and phylloides tumor.

The different stages of psoriasis include: 1) pre-lesional stage (before visible changes in the skin), 2) acute phase (visible red patches with silvery scales), 3) subacute phase (spreading of scaly plaques), 4) chronic phase (long-term persistence of symptoms).

Melanomas arising from pre-existing moles can present with changes to the appearance of the mole such as asymmetry, increased diameter (greater than 6 mm), change in color or texture, bleeding, itching, soreness, or pain. However, most concerning features include rapid growth or spreading of pigmentation beyond the borders of the original lesion .

As of August 2021, there are several ongoing phase III clinical trials evaluating new treatments for patients with metastatic or unresectable melanoma (NCT03584796, NCT03429619, NCT03519971, NCT03608631). These include studies investigating combination immunotherapy regimens such as nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus nivolumab monotherapy (CheckMate-238), pembrolizumab plus axitinib versus pembrolizumab alone (KEYNOTE-764) and dabrafenib plus trametinib versus dabrafenib alone (NCT03608631). Other studies are assessing novel therapies including targeted therapy with encorafenib plus binimetinib plus cetuximab (NCT04170313) and anti-PD-L1 antibody durvalumab in combination with tremelimumab and platinum chemotherapy (NCT03298451).

The most common types of aggressive skin cancer include melanoma (which originates from pigment cells in the skin), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC; which arises from keratinocytes in the epidermis), and basal cell carcinoma (BCC; which also develops from keratinocytes but is less aggressive than SCC).

Multiple Myeloma (MM) is a malignant plasma cell disorder characterized by clonal proliferation of bone marrow plasma cells that produce an excess of light chains or immunoglobulin in the bloodstream . It accounts for 1% of all cancers worldwide with an estimated incidence rate of 4-5 cases per 100,000 people annually . The median age at diagnosis is around 69 years old and men are more likely to develop MM than women .

Multiple myeloma is treated with chemotherapeutic agents such as melphalan, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, carmustine, vincristine, vinblastine, cisplatin, etoposide, ifosfamide, idarubicin, and prednisone . The choice of treatment depends on several factors, including age, overall health, previous treatments, and stage of cancer. Other drugs that may be used to treat multiple myeloma include thalidomide (Thalomid), lenalidomide (Revlimid) , bortezomib (Velcade), daratumumab (Darzalex), elotuzumab (Empliciti), ixazomib (Ninlaro), obinitizumab (Gazyva), panobinsitumab (Lyramid), and pomalidomide (Pomalyst).

Neuroblastoma is usually diagnosed by ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen when there is an enlargement of the adrenal gland or other symptoms such as fever, pain, swelling, weakness, weight loss, paleness, jaundice, constipation, vomiting, diarrhea, difficulty urinating, or bone pain. A biopsy may be performed to confirm the diagnosis. The tumor can also spread to lymph nodes, liver, bones, skin, and brain.

Neuroblastoma is more common in infants under one year old than in older children. It occurs slightly more often in boys than girls. The disease can also be inherited but this is very rare. Children with certain genetic conditions such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), Hirschsprung's disease, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) and some other syndromes have an increased risk for developing neuroblastoma.

The overall 5-year relative survival rate for NSCLC patients diagnosed from 2014 to 2018 was about 26%. However, it varies depending on different stages at diagnosis. For example, the 5-year survival rates were 9% for stage IA, 37% for stage IIB, 45% for stage IIIA, and 16% for stage IIIB .

Small cell lung cancer is often linked to smoking history. However, it can also be caused by exposure to radiation, asbestos, uranium, nickel chromate, arsenic, coal dust, and other chemicals. Additionally, genetic syndromes such as Li-Fraumeni syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, and certain mutations in BRCA1 may increase the likelihood of developing SCLC.

There is currently an ongoing phase II study evaluating the efficacy of pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy as first line treatment for patients with advanced NSCLC who have high PD-L1 expression levels (≥50%) . The results from this trial showed that the combination therapy was well tolerated and had promising antitumor activity compared to standard chemotherapy alone. Another phase III trial comparing atezolizumab plus carboplatin and paclitaxel versus placebo plus carboplatin and paclitaxel is also underway for patients with untreated metastatic or recurrent squamous NSCLC regardless of their PD-L1 status .

There are several factors that can increase the risk of developing thyroid nodules including age (older than 50 years), female gender, radiation exposure, family history of thyroid cancer, iodine deficiency or excess intake, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, certain hormonal treatments such as oral contraceptives, and genetic predisposition to specific types of thyroid cancer .

Treatment options for parathyroid cancer include surgery (parathyroidectomy), radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapies such as everolimus or sirolimus, and clinical trials of new agents . The type of treatment depends on several factors, including the size and location of the tumor, whether it has spread to other parts of the body, and the patient's overall health status. Surgery is typically recommended for most patients with parathyroid cancer, but may not be possible in all cases due to the extent of the disease or the risk associated with anesthesia. Radiation therapy can also be used alone or after surgery if complete removal of the tumor cannot be achieved during parathyroidectomy. Chemotherapy and targeted therapies have shown limited effectiveness in treating parathyroid cancer, although some studies suggest they may help slow down its progression. Clinical trials of new agents are ongoing and may offer additional treatment options in the future.

Doctors may perform physical examinations such as palpation (examination through touch) and visual inspection using magnifying glasses like colposcopes to diagnose a lump in the genitals. They can also order biopsies for further examination under a microscope.

I'm sorry to hear that you have noticed some lesions in your brain. Brain lesions can be caused by various factors such as tumors, strokes, infections, or degenerative diseases like multiple sclerosis (MS). It is important to consult with a neurologist who will be able to perform further tests and imaging scans to determine the exact cause of the lesion(s) and provide appropriate treatment options. In the meantime, it would be helpful if you could share any additional symptoms you may be experiencing along with any previous medical history related to this condition so that the physician can better assess your situation.

Glomus tumor (GT) is an extremely rare neuroepithelial neoplasm that originates from the capillary bed of the brain or spinal cord . GTs can occur at any age but most commonly present between 20–40 years old with no gender predilection . The majority of these lesions arise from the cerebellum, followed by the basal ganglia, thalamus, midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata, and rarely from the spinal cord .

A doctor can use several methods to diagnose prostate cancer in men. The initial diagnosis is usually made from blood tests that measure prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels and digital rectal examination (DRE). If PSA or DRE results are abnormal, then further testing may be required such as transrectal ultrasound (TRUS), biopsy of the prostate tissue, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or positron emission tomography (PET) scan. It's important for doctors to combine all these diagnostic tools when making a final decision about whether a patient has prostate cancer.

There are several known risk factors for developing prostate cancer including age (the average age at diagnosis is 68 years), family history of prostate or other cancers in first degree relatives, African American race, high fat diet, smoking tobacco products, obesity, low physical activity level, hormonal factors such as testosterone levels, exposure to radiation from sources like X-rays and radon gas, and certain genetic syndromes.

There is no single test that can definitively diagnose a serious condition in the abdomen or gastrointestinal (GI) tract. A variety of diagnostic tools may be used to evaluate GI conditions depending on the presenting symptoms and clinical suspicion for a particular disease process. These include blood work, imaging studies such as X-ray, CT scan, MRI, ultrasound, endoscopy with biopsy, stool sample analysis, etc. The choice of testing depends on various factors including patient age, family history, physical examination findings, and other laboratory results. It's important to consult a healthcare professional if you have concerns about your health.

Colon cancer is an abnormal growth of cells that occurs in the inner walls of the large intestine or colon. It can also be referred to as colorectal cancer (CRC). The term “colon cancer” refers to tumors found in either the ascending or descending parts of the colon, whereas “colorectal cancer” encompasses both the colon and rectum.

The different stages of worsening in patients with lower gastrointestinal tract malignancies include: 1) Diarrhea or constipation; 2) Abdominal pain; 3) Weight loss; 4) Anemia; 5) Rectal bleeding; 6) Jaundice; 7) Ascites; 8) Bowel obstruction; 9) Peritonitis. These symptoms can be used to assess disease progression and prognosis in these patients.

There are several risk factors that can increase the chance of developing colorectal cancer (CRC). These include age, family history of CRC or polyps, personal history of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), lifestyle choices such as smoking tobacco products, excessive alcohol consumption, physical inactivity, high-fat diet, obesity, diabetes mellitus, and certain genetic syndromes like familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC).

There are several diagnostic tests that can be used to diagnose malignant growths in the GI tract including endoscopy with biopsy, CT colonography, capsule endoscopy, barium enema, MRI enterography, ultrasound, positron emission tomography (PET), and laparoscopic exploration. The choice of test depends on various factors such as patient symptoms, risk factors for cancer, previous history of cancer, and availability of testing modalities. It is important to note that different tests have varying levels of sensitivity and specificity for detecting GI cancers, so multiple tests may sometimes be necessary to make an accurate diagnosis.

Thymic carcinoma is an uncommon malignant tumor that arises from epithelial cells of the thymus gland . The most common presenting symptom in patients with thymic carcinomas is dyspnea due to local invasion or distant metastasis. Other symptoms include coughing, chest pain, weight loss, fatigue, myalgia, weakness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, back pain, headache, blurred vision, facial paralysis, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, palpitations, and shortness of breath.

Treatment options include surgery to remove the tumor, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted drug therapy, hormone therapy, and immunotherapy. The specific treatment plan will depend on several factors such as the size of the tumor, whether it has spread to other parts of the body, and the type of breast cancer. It is recommended that patients receive care from a multidisciplinary team of healthcare professionals who can work together to develop an individualized treatment plan.

Prostate cancer can be classified into four stages (I-IV) according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). Stage I refers to noninvasive tumors that have not spread outside the prostate gland. In contrast, stage II indicates invasive tumors that may have spread beyond the prostate capsule but remain localized within the pelvis. Stages III and IV represent locally advanced and metastatic disease, respectively.

Doctors typically perform a physical examination of the genitals followed by biopsy for histopathological evaluation. Imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT scans, MRI, PET-CT, and cystoscopy can also be used depending on the location and type of lesion.

Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) is characterized by chest pain that lasts more than 30 minutes and can be accompanied by shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, sweating, palpitations, dizziness, fatigue, and other symptoms . The most common symptom is persistent retrosternal chest discomfort or pressure that may radiate to the jaw, neck, arms, shoulders, back, or abdomen . It typically occurs during rest or at night while sleeping .

Certainly! Fat malabsorption is also known as steatorrhea or lipid maldigestion. It can be caused by various conditions such as pancreatic insufficiency, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), cystic fibrosis, bariatric surgery, celiac disease, and medications that affect digestive enzymes. The most common symptom of fat malabsorption is oily stools, which may appear yellowish due to excess fat content. Other possible symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, flatulence, weight loss, and decreased absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

Malabsorption syndromes can be treated by replacing the missing nutrients through dietary supplements such as vitamins or pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT). PERT is used to treat exocrine pancreas insufficiency in patients with cystic fibrosis and chronic pancreatitis. It consists of capsules that contain lipase, protease, and amylase to aid digestion. The dosage depends on fat content of meals but should be taken 10-20 minutes before eating.

Congenital patellar dislocation syndrome is characterized by recurrent subluxation or complete dislocation of the patella during knee flexion and extension. The most common symptom of this condition is pain around the knee joint that can be present at birth or develop within the first few years of life. Other symptoms include claudication, limping, and restricted range of motion. In some cases, there may also be an audible “pop” sound when the patella dislocates.

The symptoms that occur with additional peripheral neuropathy affecting the lower limbs include tingling, numbness, discomfort, weakness, muscle atrophy, gait disturbance, balance impairment, pain in feet or legs, burning sensation, sensitivity to touch, loss of reflexes, and difficulty lifting the forefoot or toes.

The condition you are referring to is called porphyria. It is not typically considered a genetic disease but rather an inherited predisposition. Porphyrias are disorders that occur when certain chemicals involved in heme synthesis (a component of hemoglobin) are deficient or absent due to enzyme defects. There are several types of porphyrias, including acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), hereditary coproporphyria (HCP), variegate porphyria (VP), and aminolevulinic acid dehydratase deficiency (ALAD). AIP is the most common type of porphyria, affecting approximately 5-10 people per million worldwide .

Food getting stuck in the throat during swallowing is called dysphagia or difficulty in swallowing. There can be many reasons for this problem such as neurological disorders like stroke, Parkinson’s disease, cerebral palsy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), head trauma, brain tumors; anatomical abnormalities including esophageal strictures, cleft palate, vocal cord paralysis, and congenital anomalies of the airway; muscular diseases like myasthenia gravis; oral problems like ill-fitting dentures, poor oral health causing pain while chewing, mouth ulcers, tongue swelling, dry mouth due to medications or Sjogren's syndrome; psychological issues like anxiety, depression, panic attacks; gastrointestinal reflux disease; medication side effects; alcohol abuse; and cancer of the head and neck region.

Congenital hypochondroplasia (CH) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by short stature with disproportionate rhizomelia or mesomelia affecting mainly the limbs. Infant CH presents with bowing deformity of the long bones, most commonly the humerus and femur. The characteristic appearance of CH is described as “elbow-knee” or "poker stick" limb shape due to underdevelopment of the middle portion of the bone. Other symptoms include restricted joint mobility, particularly at the elbows and knees, and facial dysmorphism such as microcephaly, midface flattening, depressed nasal bridge, hypertelorism, and ptosis. Diagnosis can be confirmed through radiographic imaging showing metaphyseal dysostosis and epiphyseal stippling. Treatment typically involves physical therapy and surgical interventions for corrective purposes.

The main clinical feature of LWD is short stature due to disproportionate growth failure of the lower limbs. Infants with this condition may also have other symptoms such as delayed bone age, asymmetric overgrowth of the upper limb bones, flared iliac wings, coxa vara deformity, genu valgum or recurvatum, and thoracic cage abnormalities including pectus carinatum and rib crowding .

There is no single cause of all types of dwarfism. Dwarfism can be caused by more than 400 different gene mutations that affect various signaling pathways involved in cellular proliferation, growth hormone production or action, and insulin-like growth factor (IGF) synthesis or action . The most common type of dwarfism is achondroplasia, which results from a mutation in the FGFR3 gene, leading to impaired chondrogenesis during endochondral ossification . Other forms of dwarfism include hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalcemia, multiple epiphyseal dysplasias, and skeletal dysplasias such as Morquio syndrome, McKusick-Kaufman syndrome, and Turner syndrome.

Patients with severe birth defects involving short stature and an immunodeficiency may present with various signs and symptoms including growth retardation, failure to thrive, recurrent respiratory tract infections such as pneumonia or bronchitis, otitis media, sinusitis, ear discharge, hearing loss, chronic diarrhea, poor appetite, malnutrition, delayed puberty, skin rashes, eczema, allergies, frequent mouth ulcers, swollen gums, bleeding from the nose or gastrointestinal tract, easy bruising, joint pain, arthritis, muscle weakness, fatigue, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and abnormal laboratory findings such as low levels of white blood cells (leukopenia), low counts of specific types of immune cells (lymphocytopenia) and decreased antibody responses.

Anemia is defined as a condition in which there is a decrease in red blood cells or hemoglobin levels in the body . This can result from blood loss due to injury, surgery, menstruation, or internal bleeding; decreased production of new red blood cells by bone marrow; or increased destruction of red blood cells. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, dizziness, palpitations, headaches, chest pain, impaired immune function, and poor exercise tolerance. If left untreated, it may lead to severe complications such as heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, and even death.

In addition to diarrhea, perioral dermatitis, and alopecia, other possible symptoms of severe zinc deficiency include anemia, impaired immune function, delayed wound healing, appetite loss, hypogeusia or ageusia (loss of taste), hyposmia or anosmia (loss of smell), pneumonia, osteopenia, testicular dysfunction, and psychiatric disorders such as depression, anxiety, irritability, and manic behavior .

Acanthosis nigricans is characterized by velvety-appearing areas of hyperkeratotic thickened skin that most commonly affect the neck, axillae, groin, and perianal region. It can also occur on other sites such as the scalp, lips, oral mucosa, umbilicus, and gluteal folds. The lesions may be tan to brown in color and range from small macules to large plaques up to several centimeters in diameter. They usually do not cause itching or discomfort but may feel rough to the touch.

Certainly! The term “dysplasia” refers to an abnormal development of bone tissue during growth, resulting in short stature or skeletal malformation. It can also refer to any type of abnormality in the development of organs such as the heart, kidney, liver, brain, etc. Dysplastic disorders are classified into two categories depending on their mode of inheritance: (1) hereditary dysplasias that follow Mendelian patterns of inheritance; and (2) non-hereditary dysplasias caused by environmental factors or unknown causes.

Patients with large cortisol-secreting adenomas may experience various signs and symptoms due to hypercortisolemia, including weight gain, moon face (facial plethora), facial hirsutism, easy bruising, skin atrophy, hypertension, glucose intolerance, osteoporosis, menstrual irregularities, muscle weakness, and psychiatric disturbances such as depression, anxiety, and memory loss .

Viral exanthems are skin rashes that occur as a result of an immune response to a viral infection. They can be caused by a variety of different viruses including herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella zoster virus (VZV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and adenovirus. The appearance of these rashes varies depending on the specific virus involved but they generally appear as small red spots or blisters that develop into scaly patches. These rashes typically last for 7–10 days and may be accompanied by other symptoms such as fever, sore throat, coughing and fatigue. In most cases, viral exanthems are not serious and will resolve without treatment; however, in some instances, particularly if there is underlying immunosuppression, more severe complications can arise. If you experience a viral exanthem, it is important to seek medical attention so that appropriate management can be provided.

Abdominal pain and neurologic symptoms can be caused by several rare genetic disorders that affect metabolic pathways. These include disorders of amino acid metabolism (e.g., phenylketonuria), lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Fabry disease), mitochondrial disorders (e.g., Leigh syndrome), peroxisome biogenesis defects (e.g., Zellweger spectrum disorder), organic acid disorders (e.g., maple syrup urine disease), urea cycle disorders (e.g., ornithine transcarbamoylase deficiency), fatty acid oxidation disorders (e.g., medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency), congenital disorders of glycosylation (e.g., McLeod syndrome) and others. The specific cause depends on the underlying genetic mutations involved.

There is no single treatment for all types of severe respiratory diseases leading to hypoxemia or low blood oxygen levels. The main goal in treating patients with acute respiratory failure is to improve gas exchange (oxygenation) and alveolar ventilation while minimizing complications associated with mechanical ventilation such as lung injury from positive pressure ventilation. Treatment options include non-invasive ventilation (NIV), high flow nasal cannula (HFNC), continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP), endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV). NIV is often tried first if there is concern about the patient's ability to protect their airways and maintain an open upper airway during breathing. If the patient cannot tolerate NIV, HFNC may be attempted. CPAP and BiPAP may also be considered before IMV depending on the severity of symptoms and other factors. Endotracheal intubation and IMV are typically reserved for when these measures fail to correct hypoxemia and hypercarbia.

Abnormally rapid jaw growth can be caused by several factors including hormonal imbalances such as acromegaly or gigantism due to pituitary gland disorders; FAP (familial adenomatous polyposis), which is an inherited disorder that leads to cancer in the colon; McCune-Albright syndrome, which is a rare genetic condition characterized by overgrowth of bones and soft tissues; hyperparathyroidism, which results from too much parathyroid hormone being produced by one or more of the four small glands located behind the thyroid gland; and Paget disease, which affects bones and joints throughout the body.

Salivary Gland Cancer (SGC) is a rare type of head and neck cancer that begins in one of the major salivary glands located inside the cheeks, jawline, or palate. SGCs may also occur in minor salivary glands found throughout the lips, tongue, and lining of the oral cavity .

Congenital Hyperphenylalaninemia (CHH) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme resulting in elevated levels of blood phenylalanine . The most common type of CHH is due to mutations in the gene encoding phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which is located on chromosome 12q24.31 .

Lipedema is diagnosed clinically by assessing physical symptoms such as disproportionate fat accumulation in the arms or legs with skin changes including dermatosclerosis (skin thickening), papules, edema, and adiposity of the neck, trunk, and face. The diagnosis can be confirmed through imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or lymphoscintigraphy to show impaired lymphatic drainage. There are no specific blood tests for lipedema.

Typical symptoms of scoliosis include back pain, uneven shoulders or hips, unequal leg lengths, difficulty breathing due to lung compression, and spine deformity that appears as a C-shaped curve, S-shaped curve, or an "S" shaped curve with a hump on one side .

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is an irreversible neurodegenerative disorder that affects memory, thinking, and behavior. It is the most common cause of dementia in older adults. The pathological hallmarks of AD include extracellular amyloid plaques composed of aggregated β-amyloid peptides and intraneuronal tangles containing hyperphosphorylated tau protein. Other features include neuron loss, synaptic dysfunction, inflammation, oxidative stress, and cerebrovascular changes.

Acute illnesses characterized by fever, joint pain, and rash in adults can be caused by viral or bacterial infections such as influenza virus infection, dengue fever, Zika virus infection, chikungunya virus infection, leptospirosis, and streptococcal pharyngitis with streptococcus pyogenes (strep throat).

The condition you described may be macular degeneration (MD), which can affect both eyes or one eye only. It is important to see your doctor immediately as MD can lead to blindness without proper intervention. There is no cure for MD but early detection and monitoring with regular follow-ups can help slow down its progression. Treatment options include anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy such as intravitreal injection of ranibizumab, aflibercept, or bevacizumab. If left untreated, MD will continue to damage the retina leading to irreversible blindness.

Patients with bleeding disorders due to platelet dysfunction may be treated using aspirin avoidance or low-dose aspirin therapy depending upon their specific diagnosis. Aspirin should not be used in patients with thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100 × 109/L), as it can increase the risk of bleeding . However, some studies suggest that low doses of aspirin (25–325 mg) do not affect platelet counts nor increase the risk of bleeding in patients with immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Therefore, low-dose aspirin is sometimes prescribed to ITP patients to prevent thromboembolism .

Congenital malformations of the abdominal organs can be caused by genetic factors or environmental exposures that affect organogenesis during embryonic development. Genetic mutations may result from chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 13 or 18, while environmental exposures include maternal medications (e.g., thalidomide), alcohol consumption, smoking, and certain chemicals or toxins. Additionally, some conditions such as cystic fibrosis or diabetes mellitus may also increase the risk for these types of birth defects.

In children with type 2 HLH, common symptoms include fever, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, pancytopenia, skin rash, neurological manifestations such as seizures or cerebral edema, and hemophagocytosis in bone marrow or spleen .

Aicardi-Goutieres Syndrome (AGS) is an autosomal recessive disorder that causes severe encephalopathy with early onset microcephaly, spasticity, intracranial calcifications, basal ganglia abnormalities, leukodystrophy, and elevated levels of interferon in cerebrospinal fluid . It can be caused by mutations in genes involved in nucleotides metabolism or transport such as RNASEH2A, RNASEH2B, RNASEH2C, TREX1, SAMHD1, ADAR1, and MDA5. The diagnosis of AGS requires clinical features along with genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment involves management of symptoms including anti-inflammatory drugs, antioxidants, and physical therapy.

Amyloidosis refers to a group of rare diseases characterized by abnormal deposition of insoluble fibrillar proteins in various organs such as heart, kidneys, liver, nerves, gastrointestinal tract, and skin . These deposits interfere with normal organ function leading to tissue damage and organ failure. The most common types of amyloid protein found in patients with systemic disease include immunoglobulin light chains (AL), serum amyloid A protein (AA) or transthyretin (ATTR). AL amyloidosis occurs when there is an overproduction of monoclonal antibodies produced by plasma cells, while AA amyloidosis develops due to chronic inflammation resulting in increased production of acute-phase reactant SAA . ATTR amyloidosis may be hereditary or wild type. Hereditary forms occur due to mutations in TTR gene which encodes for transthyretin protein. Wild type form of ATTR amyloidosis usually affects elderly people above 80 years of age and results in progressive cardiomyopathy .

Patients presenting with abnormal growth patterns and skeletal deformities may be diagnosed with either a genetic mutation or an endocrine disorder. Genetic mutations can include conditions such as Turner syndrome (a complete or partial loss of one X chromosome), Marfan syndrome (an autosomal dominant disorder affecting connective tissue), Noonan syndrome (a rare inherited disease that affects multiple organ systems) and many others. Endocrine disorders can include conditions such as hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, acromegaly, and many more. It is important for healthcare providers to consider both genetic and endocrine factors when evaluating these types of patients in order to provide appropriate treatment and management plans.

The condition that causes patchy hair loss without an apparent reason is called alopecia areata (AA). It is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the appearance of smooth, round or oval patches where hair has stopped growing on the scalp, body, or beard. Although it can occur at any age, AA most commonly affects children under 15 years old and adults between 30 to 40 years old.

Alopecia universalis (ALO) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by complete loss of scalp hair and body hair, including eyebrows and eyelashes . It can be further classified into two types: congenital or acquired. Congenital ALO presents at birth or within the first few months of life, while acquired ALO develops after one year of age. The exact cause of ALO remains unknown; however, it has been associated with certain genetic mutations in genes involved in immune regulation such as IL2RA, CD180, TYK2, and STAT3 .

Hair loss can be hereditary but not always. It is important to note that there may be other factors contributing to hair loss such as stress, hormonal changes, certain medications, or underlying health conditions. If someone has a family member with baldness, they may also have an increased risk for developing baldness themselves. However, just because someone has no family members who experience baldness doesn’t mean they won’t develop baldness later in life.

The condition you are referring to is called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD). It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene that results in decreased or absent levels of circulating AAT protein. This can lead to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) due to unchecked proteolytic activity within the lungs as well as other complications such as liver dysfunction and increased risk for hepatocellular carcinoma.

Alpha-ketoglutaric aciduria (AKGA) is a rare genetic disorder that affects amino acid catabolism and energy production in cells. It can cause severe developmental delay, seizures, coma, and death during infancy or early childhood. The most common symptom of AKGA is hypotonia, which refers to low muscle tone. Other symptoms include poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, weak cry, apnea, hyperammonemia, encephalopathy, cerebral edema, and brainstem dysfunction.

Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by defects in erythrocyte membrane proteins that result in osmotic fragility of red blood cells . The mainstay of therapy for patients with symptomatic HS consists of lifelong avoidance of dehydration and transfusion as needed to correct severe anemia or acute exacerbations . Patients should be educated about avoiding strenuous exercise and maintaining adequate hydration status. Splenectomy may improve hemolysis but increases risk of thromboembolism; therefore, it is recommended only for those who have significant chronic hemolysis despite conservative management .

The most common symptoms of ADPKD include abdominal or epigastric pain, hematuria, progressive fatigue, and decreased appetite. Other less frequent symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, fever, chills, weight loss, flank or back pain, and weakness. Urinary tract infections, hypertension, and vision impairment are also commonly observed in patients with ADPKD.

Dementia is a condition that can cause frequent confusion and forgetfulness in older individuals who may also exhibit other symptoms such as difficulty with language, disorientation to time or place, impaired judgment, and changes in mood or personality .

Hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta is an autosomal dominant disorder that affects enamel development during tooth mineralization. It can present with various clinical features depending on the severity of the condition. In general, affected individuals may experience delayed tooth eruption, discolored teeth, abnormal tooth shape, and increased susceptibility to dental caries. Adults with this condition typically have irregularly shaped teeth with short crowns, which may be yellow or brownish-black in color due to dentin exposure. They may also complain of painless chewing difficulties and sensitivity to cold temperatures. Dental treatment for these patients should focus on improving oral function and aesthetics through restorative procedures such as composite bonding, porcelain veneers, and crown lengthening surgery.

The typical appearance of teeth affected by dental erosion is characterized by loss of tooth structure without cavitation or caries. It can appear as smooth, glossy surfaces with sharp margins, or it may be more diffuse in nature. In some cases, there may also be signs of wear facets that resemble those seen in patients who grind their teeth at night (bruxism).

The typical symptoms of Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy Lactic Acidosis Stroke-like episodes (MELAS) syndrome include developmental delay or regression, seizures, stroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis, myopathy, cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus, retinal degeneration, gastrointestinal dysfunction, vomiting, diarrhea, failure to thrive, hypotonia, hypertonia, ataxia, dystonia, choreoathetosis, and dementia . It is important to note that these symptoms may also be present in other conditions such as mitochondrial disease, metabolic disorders, genetic syndromes, and infectious diseases. Therefore, it is crucial for healthcare professionals to consider MELAS syndrome when evaluating an infant with unexplained neurological symptoms and perform further testing to confirm the diagnosis.

An ultrasound can be used to identify certain chromosome abnormalities by examining the physical features of the fetus for signs of genetic disorders. These include structural anomalies such as heart defects or other organ malformations that may indicate Down syndrome (DS) or Edwards syndrome (ES). In addition, ultrasounds can also measure the nuchal translucency (NT), which is the amount of fluid under the skin at the back of the baby’s neck. A thickened NT is associated with DS, trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome), and other chromosomal conditions .

Doctors can perform several diagnostic tests to detect protein deposits in the eye that may cause cloudiness of the cornea. These include slit-lamp biomicroscopy, optical coherence tomography (OCT), fluorescein staining, and ultrasonography. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy is commonly used by ophthalmologists as it allows for detailed examination of the anterior segment structures such as the iris, lens, and cornea. OCT provides high-resolution images of the retina and optic nerve head, allowing for early detection of macular edema associated with various diseases. Fluorescein staining involves placing drops of dye onto the surface of the eye, which will stain areas where there are defects or damage to the epithelial cells lining the corneal surface. Ultrasonography uses sound waves to produce an image of the internal structure of the eye, including the cornea. This test is often performed if other imaging modalities cannot be used due to opacity of the media obscuring visualization of the posterior pole.

The condition you are referring to is called amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). It is characterized by degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons that control voluntary muscles such as those used for speaking, walking, swallowing, and breathing. This can lead to muscle atrophy, weakness, fasciculations, spasticity, and paralysis over time.

The cause of your symptoms could be due to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease. ALS is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord, leading to muscle atrophy and weakness throughout the body. There is currently no cure for ALS, but there are treatments available to help manage symptoms and prolong survival. These include medications such as riluzole and edaravone, which can slow down the progression of the disease; non-invasive ventilation to help with breathing difficulties; physical therapy to maintain strength and mobility; and other supportive care measures. It is important to consult with a neurologist or other healthcare professional who has experience treating ALS patients to determine the best course of action for you.

Yes, certain genetic mutations can increase the risk of developing aggressive brain tumors such as glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). For example, people with neurofibromatosis type 1 have an increased risk of developing GBM due to a mutation in the NF1 gene that leads to overactivation of the RAS-MAPK pathway . Similarly, people with Li Fraumeni syndrome or germline mutations in TP53 also have an increased risk of developing GBM .

Myopathies can present with various symptoms such as muscle weakness, fatigue, pain, difficulty breathing due to weak respiratory muscles, or even cardiac arrhythmias in severe cases. The specific symptoms depend on which type of myopathy is being referred to.

Hypogonadism is characterized by low levels of testosterone due to damage or dysfunction of the gonads (testes) or accessory sex organs such as the pituitary gland. In males, this condition can result in decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility, loss of body hair, reduced muscle mass and strength, osteoporosis, fatigue, depression, irritability, lack of concentration, and breast enlargement .

Congenital malformation of fetal brain development is caused by genetic factors (chromosomal abnormalities), environmental factors such as maternal exposure to teratogens or infections, and complex interactions between genes and environment.

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children presents with symptoms of age-inappropriate levels of inattentiveness, impulsivity, or hyperactivity that cause functional impairment . The diagnostic criteria for ADHD include developmentally inappropriate levels of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that occur before 12 years old and persist over at least six months . Symptoms must be present in two different settings such as home and school to confirm diagnosis. Children may also have comorbid conditions including learning disabilities, oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorders, mood disorders, anxiety disorders, substance abuse, and other externalizing behavioral problems .
The name of congenital ocular anomaly affecting pigmentation in the eye is iris coloboma.

The condition you may be referring to is called degenerative disc disease (DDD). It occurs when there is damage or changes in the structure of one or more intervertebral discs in your spine. This can lead to pain, stiffness, and limited movement in the affected area. Over time, this can result in spinal fusion, which involves the joining of two or more vertebrae together through bone growth. While DDD is common among older adults, it can also occur at any age. There are several factors that contribute to DDD, including genetics, lifestyle choices such as smoking and lack of exercise, and occupation. If you have concerns about your back health, it's important to talk with your healthcare provider who can help determine if further evaluation or treatment is needed.

The most common causes for your symptoms could be insect bites or contact dermatitis. Other possible causes include allergic reactions to food or medications, viral infections such as chickenpox, or fungal infections. It would be helpful if you can provide more details about when these rashes started appearing, any recent exposure to animals or insects, any new medication use, or any other relevant information that may help diagnose the problem.

Nail dystrophy is one of the most common manifestations of congenital disorders affecting nails. It can be seen as thickened or brittle nails with longitudinal ridges, pitting, splitting, and flaking. Other associated features include ectodermal abnormalities such as hair loss (hypotrichosis), dental anomalies, and ocular defects. The differential diagnosis includes trichothiodystrophy, Meckel-Gruber syndrome, and Rothmund-Thomson syndrome .

The condition you are referring to is called "Crow's feet." They are fine lines that form around the corners of your eyes when you squint or smile. While they can be hereditary, prolonged sun exposure and repeated facial expressions also contribute to their development.

The patient's symptoms of coughing up blood, shortness of breath, chest pain, and wheezing could indicate several conditions involving an immune response against the lungs such as pulmonary fibrosis or bronchiectasis. However, without further information, it is difficult to determine if these conditions involve any specific autoantibodies.

The condition you are referring to is called scoliosis. Scoliosis can occur as a congenital (birth) defect when there is an abnormality in bone development during fetal growth. It may also be caused by hormonal problems such as hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism. While some cases of scoliosis have been associated with genital anomalies, this is not always the case.

Congenital syndromes can be diagnosed using various genetic testing methods such as chromosomal analysis (karyotyping), microarray-based comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) analysis, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based sequencing, whole exome or whole genome sequencing, and array-comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH). Imaging studies like ultrasound, X-ray, CT scan, and MRI may also help identify physical abnormalities associated with certain syndromes.

Newborns with a small area of missing skin or an open wound at birth can be treated using topical antibiotics to prevent infection. If there is bleeding from the wound, pressure should be applied until the bleeding stops. The baby's temperature should also be monitored closely during this time. In some cases, surgery may be required if the injury is severe enough.

Certainly! Based on your description, it sounds like you may be experiencing some common symptoms associated with allergic rhinitis (also known as hay fever). These include sneezing, runny or stuffy nose, nasal congestion, postnasal drip, itchy eyes, watery eyes, coughing, wheezing, sore throat, fatigue, and headache. Allergic rhinitis is an immune system reaction to airborne substances such as pollen, dust mites, pet dander, mold spores, and cockroaches. It is caused by the release of histamine from mast cells that results in inflammation and swelling of the lining of the nose. Symptoms typically worsen during the spring and fall seasons when there is increased exposure to these triggers.

Individuals with Marfan syndrome may experience various skeletal abnormalities such as tall stature, long fingers or arms, flat feet, chest deformity, scoliosis, and bone fractures. They can also have cardiovascular complications including mitral valve prolapse, aortic root dilation, and dissection of the ascending aorta. Additionally, they might develop eye problems like ectopia lentis (dislocation of the lens) and myopia. Other common features include pulmonary function impairment, striae atrophicae (stretch marks), and benign skin tumors.
reference_answers: Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. The prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options depend on the following: - The age of the patient. - Whether the cancer has spread to the brain or spinal cord. - Whether there are certain changes in the genes, including the Philadelphia chromosome. - Whether the cancer has been treated before or has recurred (come back).

Smoking, previous chemotherapy treatment, and exposure to radiation may affect the risk of adult AML. Anything that increases your risk of getting a disease is called a risk factor. Having a risk factor does not mean that you will get cancer; not having risk factors doesnt mean that you will not get cancer. Talk with your doctor if you think you may be at risk. Possible risk factors for AML include the following: - Being male. - Smoking, especially after age 60. - Having had treatment with chemotherapy or radiation therapy in the past. - Having had treatment for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in the past. - Being exposed to radiation from an atomic bomb or to the chemical benzene. - Having a history of a blood disorder such as myelodysplastic syndrome.

Key Points - There are different types of treatment for patients with adult acute myeloid leukemia. - The treatment of adult AML usually has 2 phases. - Four types of standard treatment are used: - Chemotherapy - Radiation therapy - Stem cell transplant - Other drug therapy - New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials. - Targeted therapy - Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. - Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. - Follow-up tests may be needed. There are different types of treatment for patients with adult acute myeloid leukemia. Different types of treatment are available for patients with adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Some treatments are standard (the currently used treatment), and some are being tested in clinical trials. A treatment clinical trial is a research study meant to help improve current treatments or obtain information on new treatments for patients with cancer. When clinical trials show that a new treatment is better than the standard treatment, the new treatment may become the standard treatment. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. Some clinical trials are open only to patients who have not started treatment. The treatment of adult AML usually has 2 phases. The 2 treatment phases of adult AML are: - Remission induction therapy: This is the first phase of treatment. The goal is to kill the leukemia cells in the blood and bone marrow. This puts the leukemia into remission. - Post-remission therapy: This is the second phase of treatment. It begins after the leukemia is in remission. The goal of post-remission therapy is to kill any remaining leukemia cells that may not be active but could begin to regrow and cause a relapse. This phase is also called remission continuation therapy. Four types of standard treatment are used: Chemotherapy Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells or by stopping them from dividing. When chemotherapy is taken by mouth or injected into a vein or muscle, the drugs enter the bloodstream and can reach cancer cells throughout the body (systemic chemotherapy). When chemotherapy is placed directly into the cerebrospinal fluid (intrathecal chemotherapy), an organ, or a body cavity such as the abdomen, the drugs mainly affect cancer cells in those areas (regional chemotherapy). Intrathecal chemotherapy may be used to treat adult AML that has spread to the brain and spinal cord. Combination chemotherapy is treatment using more than one anticancer drug. The way the chemotherapy is given depends on the subtype of AML being treated and whether leukemia cells have spread to the brain and spinal cord. See Drugs Approved for Acute Myeloid Leukemia for more information. Radiation therapy Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment that uses high-energy x-rays or other types of radiation to kill cancer cells or keep them from growing. There are two types of radiation therapy: - External radiation therapy uses a machine outside the body to send radiation toward the cancer. - Internal radiation therapy uses a radioactive substance sealed in needles, seeds, wires, or catheters that are placed directly into or near the cancer. The way the radiation therapy is given depends on the type of cancer being treated and whether leukemia cells have spread to the brain and spinal cord. External radiation therapy is used to treat adult AML. Stem cell transplant Stem cell transplant is a method of giving chemotherapy and replacing blood -forming cells that are abnormal or destroyed by the cancer treatment. Stem cells (immature blood cells) are removed from the blood or bone marrow of the patient or a donor and are frozen and stored. After the chemotherapy is completed, the stored stem cells are thawed and given back to the patient through an infusion. These reinfused stem cells grow into (and restore) the body's blood cells. Other drug therapy Arsenic trioxide and all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) are anticancer drugs that kill leukemia cells, stop the leukemia cells from dividing, or help the leukemia cells mature into white blood cells. These drugs are used in the treatment of a subtype of AML called acute promyelocytic leukemia. See Drugs Approved for Acute Myeloid Leukemia for more information. New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials. This summary section describes treatments that are being studied in clinical trials. It may not mention every new treatment being studied. Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website. Targeted therapy Targeted therapy is a type of treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells without harming normal cells. Monoclonal antibody therapy is one type of targeted therapy being studied in the treatment of adult AML. Monoclonal antibody therapy is a cancer treatment that uses antibodies made in the laboratory from a single type of immune system cell. These antibodies can identify substances on cancer cells or normal substances that may help cancer cells grow. The antibodies attach to the substances and kill the cancer cells, block their growth, or keep them from spreading. Monoclonal antibodies are given by infusion. They may be used alone or to carry drugs, toxins, or radioactive material directly to cancer cells. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Clinical trials are part of the cancer research process. Clinical trials are done to find out if new cancer treatments are safe and effective or better than the standard treatment. Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment. Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward. Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment. Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials. Follow-up tests may be needed. Some of the tests that were done to diagnose the cancer or to find out the stage of the cancer may be repeated. Some tests will be repeated in order to see how well the treatment is working. Decisions about whether to continue, change, or stop treatment may be based on the results of these tests. Some of the tests will continue to be done from time to time after treatment has ended. The results of these tests can show if your condition has changed or if the cancer has recurred (come back). These tests are sometimes called follow-up tests or check-ups. Treatment Options for Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia Untreated Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia Standard treatment of untreated adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) during the remission induction phase depends on the subtype of AML and may include the following: - Combination chemotherapy. - High-dose combination chemotherapy. - Low-dose chemotherapy. - Intrathecal chemotherapy. - All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) plus arsenic trioxide for the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). - ATRA plus combination chemotherapy followed by arsenic trioxide for the treatment of APL. Check the list of NCI-supported cancer clinical trials that are now accepting patients with untreated adult acute myeloid leukemia. For more specific results, refine the search by using other search features, such as the location of the trial, the type of treatment, or the name of the drug. Talk with your doctor about clinical trials that may be right for you. General information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website. Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia in Remission Treatment of adult AML during the remission phase depends on the subtype of AML and may include the following: - Combination chemotherapy. - High-dose chemotherapy, with or without radiation therapy, and stem cell transplant using the patient's stem cells. - High-dose chemotherapy and stem cell transplant using donor stem cells. - A clinical trial of arsenic trioxide. Check the list of NCI-supported cancer clinical trials that are now accepting patients with adult acute myeloid leukemia in remission. For more specific results, refine the search by using other search features, such as the location of the trial, the type of treatment, or the name of the drug. Talk with your doctor about clinical trials that may be right for you. General information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website. Recurrent Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia There is no standard treatment for recurrent adult AML. Treatment depends on the subtype of AML and may include the following: - Combination chemotherapy. - Targeted therapy with monoclonal antibodies. - Stem cell transplant. - Arsenic trioxide therapy. - A clinical trial of arsenic trioxide therapy followed by stem cell transplant. Check the list of NCI-supported cancer clinical trials that are now accepting patients with recurrent adult acute myeloid leukemia. For more specific results, refine the search by using other search features, such as the location of the trial, the type of treatment, or the name of the drug. Talk with your doctor about clinical trials that may be right for you. General information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website.

Tests that examine the blood, bone marrow, and lymph nodes are used to detect (find) and diagnose chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The following tests and procedures may be used: - Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as lumps or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patients health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken. - Complete blood count (CBC) with differential : A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following: - The number of red blood cells and platelets. - The number and type of white blood cells. - The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells. - The portion of the blood sample made up of red blood cells. - Immunophenotyping : A laboratory test in which the antigens or markers on the surface of a blood or bone marrow cell are checked to see if they are lymphocytes or myeloid cells. If the cells are malignant lymphocytes (cancer), they are checked to see if they are B lymphocytes or T lymphocytes. - FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization): A laboratory technique used to look at genes or chromosomes in cells and tissues. Pieces of DNA that contain a fluorescent dye are made in the laboratory and added to cells or tissues on a glass slide. When these pieces of DNA bind to specific genes or areas of chromosomes on the slide, they light up when viewed under a microscope with a special light. - Flow cytometry : A laboratory test that measures the number of cells in a sample, the percentage of live cells in a sample, and certain characteristics of cells, such as size, shape, and the presence of tumor markers on the cell surface. The cells are stained with a light-sensitive dye, placed in a fluid, and passed in a stream before a laser or other type of light. The measurements are based on how the light-sensitive dye reacts to the light. - IgVH gene mutation test: A laboratory test done on a bone marrow or blood sample to check for an IgVH gene mutation. Patients with an IgVH gene mutation have a better prognosis. - Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy : The removal of bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone or breastbone. A pathologist views the bone marrow, blood, and bone under a microscope to look for abnormal cells.

Signs and symptoms of chronic myelogenous leukemia include fever, night sweats, and tiredness. These and other signs and symptoms may be caused by CML or by other conditions. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following: - Feeling very tired. - Weight loss for no known reason. - Night sweats. - Fever. - Pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs on the left side. Sometimes CML does not cause any symptoms at all.

Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment. Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials.

Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose hairy cell leukemia. The following tests and procedures may be used: - Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as a swollen spleen, lumps, or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patients health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken. - Complete blood count (CBC): A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following: - The number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells. - The portion of the sample made up of red blood cells. - Peripheral blood smear : A procedure in which a sample of blood is checked for cells that look "hairy," the number and kinds of white blood cells, the number of platelets, and changes in the shape of blood cells. - Blood chemistry studies : A procedure in which a blood sample is checked to measure the amounts of certain substances released into the blood by organs and tissues in the body. An unusual (higher or lower than normal) amount of a substance can be a sign of disease. - Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy : The removal of bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone or breastbone. A pathologist views the bone marrow, blood, and bone under a microscope to look for signs of cancer. - Immunophenotyping : A laboratory test in which the antigens or markers on the surface of a blood or bone marrow cell are checked to see what type of cell it is. This test is done to diagnose the specific type of leukemia by comparing the cancer cells to normal cells of the immune system. - Flow cytometry : A laboratory test that measures the number of cells in a sample, the percentage of live cells in a sample, and certain characteristics of cells, such as size, shape, and the presence of tumor markers on the cell surface. The cells are stained with a light-sensitive dye, placed in a fluid, and passed in a stream before a laser or other type of light. The measurements are based on how the light-sensitive dye reacts to the light. - Cytogenetic analysis : A laboratory test in which cells in a sample of tissue are viewed under a microscope to look for certain changes in the chromosomes. - Gene mutation test: A laboratory test done on a bone marrow or blood sample to check for mutations in the BRAF gene. A BRAF gene mutation is often found in patients with hairy cell leukemia. - CT scan (CAT scan): A procedure that makes a series of detailed pictures of areas inside the body, taken from different angles. The pictures are made by a computer linked to an x-ray machine. A dye may be injected into a vein or swallowed to help the organs or tissues show up more clearly.
