Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of chronic, inflammatory arthritis that mainly affects the spine. It usually begins with inflammation of the joints between the pelvic bones and spine, gradually spreading to the joints between the vertebrae. Signs and symptoms usually begin in adolescence or early adulthood and may include back pain and stiffness. Back movement gradually becomes more limited as the vertebrae fuse together. The condition may also affect the shoulders; ribs; hips; knees; and feet; as well as the eyes; bowel; and very rarely, the heart and lungs. AS is likely caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors; variations in several genes are thought to affect the risk to develop AS. In most cases, treatment involves exercise and medications to relieve pain and inflammation.

Annular atrophic lichen planus (LP) is a rare form of lichen planus, which is a condition that affects the skin and/or mouth. In annular atrophic LP, specifically, affected people develop skin lesions with features of both annular LP and atrophic LP - ring-shaped, slightly raised, purple lesions with central atrophy (tissue breakdown). Although these lesions can be found anywhere on the body, they most commonly affect the trunk and legs. The exact underlying cause of annular atrophic LP is unknown. Treatment is not always necessary as some cases of annular atrophic LP resolve on their own. Mild cases that are diagnosed early can often be managed with topical steroids, while more intensive therapies may be required for severe cases.

Antecubital pterygium is characterized by and antecubital webbing, posterior subluxation (dislocation) of radial head, maldevelopment of radioulnar joint, and limited elbow extension with unimpeded elbow flexion. Most reported cases come from the island of Mauritius or nearby islands. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. This condition is sometimes found as a symptom of nail-patella syndrome.

Antisynthetase syndrome is a chronic autoimmune condition that affects the muscles and various other parts of the body. The signs and symptoms can vary but may include muscle inflammation (myositis), polyarthritis (inflammation of many joints), interstitial lung disease and Raynaud phenomenon. The exact underlying cause is unknown; however, the production of autoantibodies (antibodies that attack normal cells instead of disease-causing agents) that recognize and attack certain enzymes in the body called 'aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases' appears to be linked to the cause of the syndrome. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person but may include corticosteroids, immunosuppressive medications, and/or physical therapy.

Antley Bixler syndrome is a rare condition that is primarily characterized by craniofacial abnormalities and other skeletal problems. The signs and symptoms vary significantly from person to person but may include craniosynostosis; midface hypoplasia (underdeveloped middle region of the face); frontal bossing; protruding eyes; low-set, unusually-formed ears; choanal atresia or stenosis (narrowing); fusion of adjacent arm bones (synostosis); joint contractures; arachnodactyly; bowing of the thigh bones; and/or urogenital (urinary tract and genital) abnormalities. The exact underlying cause of Antley Bixler syndrome is unknown in many cases; however, some are due to changes (mutations) in the FGFR2 gene or the POR gene. There appear to be autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms of the condition. Treatment is based on the signs and symptoms present in each person.

How is Apert syndrome diagnosed? Is genetic testing needed to confirm the diagnosis? Apert syndrome and the other conditions associated with FGFR-related craniosynostosis were clinically defined long before the molecular basis of this group of disorders was discovered. Apert syndrome can be diagnosed primarily based on the following clinical findings: Turribrachycephalic skull shape (cone-shaped or towering skull) which is observable clinically and can be confirmed by skull radiograph or head CT examination; Characteristic facial features including moderate-to-severe underdevelopment of the midface, bulging and wide-set eyes, beaked nose, underdeveloped jaw and shallow eye sockets; Variable hand and foot findings such as syndactyly of the fingers and toes and polydactyly. While clinical findings are suggestive of Apert syndrome, molecular genetic testing can help to confirm the diagnosis. Fibroblast growth factor receptor type 2 (FGFR2) sequence analysis is highly sensitive for Apert syndrome. More than 98% of cases are caused by a specific mutation in the 7th exon of the gene encoding FGFR2. The remaining cases are due to another specific mutation in or near exon 9 of FGFR2. GeneTests lists laboratories offering clinical genetic testing for this condition. Clinical genetic tests are ordered to help diagnose a person or family and to aid in decisions regarding medical care or reproductive issues. Talk to your health care provider or a genetic professional to learn more about your testing options.

How might aplasia cutis congenita be treated? The management of aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp is controversial.; both surgical and conservative treatment modalities have their proponents and opponents. The decision to use medical, surgical, or both forms of therapy in aplasia cutis congenita depends primarily on the size, depth, and location of the skin defect. Local therapy includes gentle cleansing and the application of bland ointment or silver sulfadiazine ointment to keep the area moist. Antibiotics may be utilized if overt signs of infection are noted. In many cases, other treatment is not necessary because the erosions and the ulcerations almost always heal on their own. Recently, a variety of specialized dressing materials have been developed and used. Surgical repair is not usually indicated if the defect is small. Recovery is generally uneventful, with gradual epithelialization and formation of a hairless, atrophic scar over several weeks. Small underlying bony defects usually close spontaneously during the first year of life. Surgical repair of large or multiple scalp defects may require excision with primary closure, if feasible, or the use of tissue expanders and rotation of a flap to fill the defect. On occasion, skin and bone grafts may also be required.

Aquagenic pruritus is a condition in which contact with water of any temperature causes intense itching without any visible skin changes. The symptoms may begin immediately after contact with water and can last for an hour or more. The cause of aquagenic pruritus is unknown; however, familial cases have been described. The symptoms of the condition are similar to those seen in patients with other conditions; therefore, a thorough evaluation should be performed to rule out other more serious conditions. Overall, treatment is a challenge. Antihistamines, UVB phototherapy, PUVA therapy and various medications have been tried with varying success.

AML is an aggressive type of blood cancer that affects the myeloid lineage cells in the bone marrow . It occurs when genetic mutations cause abnormal proliferation or differentiation of these cells, leading to their accumulation in the bone marrow at the expense of normal hematopoiesis. This results in pancytopenia, characterized by low counts of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets . The incidence rate for AML increases with age, affecting more men than women .

The stages of adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are defined by genetic abnormalities that can be identified using cytogenetic analysis or molecular testing. These staging systems help to predict prognosis and guide treatment decisions for patients with AML.

The most common symptom is fatigue due to anemia caused by bone marrow replacement with leukemic cells. Other symptoms include frequent infections due to immune system dysfunction, weight loss, night sweats, fever, abdominal pain or swelling (due to enlarged spleen), coughing, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, weakness, dizziness, headaches, blurred vision, bruising, bleeding, and lymphadenopathy .

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a type of cancer that affects white blood cells called granulocytes or monocytes . It occurs when an abnormal chromosome forms from a fusion between two other chromosomes, resulting in uncontrolled cell growth and proliferation . The condition can cause symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss, enlarged spleen, and increased susceptibility to infection. CML typically progresses through three stages: chronic phase, accelerated phase, and blast crisis phase . Treatment options include chemotherapy, targeted therapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, stem cell transplant, and supportive care .

The chronic phase (CP) is characterized by an increase in myeloid cells with normal maturation, while the accelerated phase (AP) shows dysplastic changes in myeloid precursors and increased proliferation. In blast crisis (BC), there is a transformation to acute leukemia or myelodysplasia .

The most common symptom of hairy cell leukemia is fatigue due to anemia caused by bone marrow infiltration with hairy cells . Other signs and symptoms include recurrent infections, weight loss, night sweats, fever, abdominal pain or discomfort, bleeding from the gums, easy bruising, paleness, enlarged spleen, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, petechial rash, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, and peripheral neuropathy.

The treatment of hairy cell leukaemia (HCL) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and stem cell transplantation . Chemotherapy is often used as the first line of treatment for HCL, with cladribine being considered the most effective agent . Other commonly used agents include fludarabine , pentostatin , and 2-chlorodeoxyadenosine . Radiation therapy may be used in conjunction with chemotherapy to help reduce symptoms such as splenomegaly or lymph node enlargement . Stem cell transplantation is reserved for patients who have relapsed after multiple lines of chemotherapy or who have refractory disease .

There have been several ongoing studies in childhood acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL). The National Cancer Institute has an active study called ALL-Reach, which aims to improve outcomes for children with relapsed or refractory ALL by using targeted therapy. Another study from St Jude Children's Research Hospital is evaluating the effectiveness of adding venetoclax to standard chemotherapy regimens for newly diagnosed patients with high-risk B cell precursor ALL.

The treatment of childhood acute myeloid leukemia (AML) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, stem cell transplantation, targeted therapy, and supportive care . The specific treatment plan depends on several factors, including the patient's age, genetic abnormalities, risk stratification, and response to initial treatment .

The prognosis of adult soft tissue sarcomas depends on various factors such as tumor size, grade, histologic subtype, location, depth of invasion, and presence or absence of metastasis at diagnosis . In general, high-grade sarcomas have a worse prognosis than low-grade sarcomas.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) can occur in anyone regardless of age, gender or race; however, they are more common among adults over 50 years old. Risk factors include family history of GIST, certain genetic syndromes such as neurofibromatosis type I, Lynch syndrome, familial juvenile polyposis, and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, long-term nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, smoking, obesity, and exposure to radiation.

Kaposi sarcomas (KSs) are malignant tumors that can occur in many parts of the body, including the skin, lymph nodes, visceral organs, and bone marrow . KS was first described by Moritz Kaposi in 1872 as “idiopathic multiple pigmented sarcoma” among Jewish and Italian patients living in eastern Europe . It was initially considered rare until it emerged as one of the most common AIDS-defining illnesses during the early stages of the HIV epidemic in the United States .

The most common symptom is a painless mass or lump that can be found anywhere in the body but often occurs in the head, neck, and genital regions . Other symptoms include difficulty moving certain parts of the body, weakness, swelling, and visible changes to the skin such as redness or bruising.

The treatment of childhood rhabdomyosarcoma typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation therapy depending on the tumor location and stage . For localized disease, surgical resection may be used as the primary modality with or without adjuvant radiotherapy. In cases where complete surgical removal is not possible, neoadjuvant chemotherapy can be administered to shrink the tumor prior to surgery followed by additional cycles of chemotherapy after surgery. Chemotherapy regimens often include vincristine, actinomycin D, and cyclophosphamide (VAC) in addition to other agents such as doxorubicin and ifosfamide. Radiation therapy may also play a role in some cases.

The prognosis of childhood soft tissue sarcomas depends on several factors such as tumor type, location, size, grade, stage, age at diagnosis, and whether it has metastasized to other parts of the body . Overall survival rates have improved significantly over time due to advances in treatment methods including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy . For example, the 5-year overall survival rate for children with localized rhabdomyosarcoma increased from about 60% in the early 1980s to more than 83% today . However, the prognosis remains poor for some types of soft tissue sarcomas, especially those that occur in infants or young children, recur after initial treatment, or spread to distant sites .

Diagnosis of childhood vascular tumors can be made through clinical examination, imaging tests such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or angiography, and histopathological evaluation after biopsy or surgical resection . The type of vascular tumor is determined by its appearance on imaging studies and microscopic features. For example, capillary hemangiomas typically appear as red, blue-red, or purple lesions with a blanching response to pressure on clinical examination. On ultrasound, they may show a hypoechoic mass with flow signals in color Doppler mode. Capillary malformations often present as soft, flat areas that do not blanche and have no flow signal on Doppler ultrasound.

The most common symptom of adult Hodgkin lymphoma is painless swelling or enlargement in one part of the body such as the neck, armpit, groin, or chest area. Other symptoms include weight loss, fever, chills, night sweats, weakness, fatigue, cough, shortness of breath, abdominal discomfort, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation .

The standard treatment for adult Hodgkin lymphoma is chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy depending on stage of disease . For early-stage (stages I and II) classic Hodgkin lymphoma, 6 cycles of ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) chemotherapy are recommended. If there is an increased risk of relapse due to certain adverse prognostic factors such as bulky disease >10 cm, elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels, advanced stage, or unfavorable histology, additional consolidative radiotherapy may be considered after chemotherapy .

Diagnosis of adult non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies such as CT or PET scans, and biopsy with pathological examination of tissue samples from affected areas. The diagnostic process may also include additional tests depending on the specific type of NHL being considered. It is important for healthcare professionals to work together to ensure that all relevant information is gathered and interpreted in order to make an accurate diagnosis and develop an appropriate treatment plan.

The most common symptom of ARL is lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes), which can occur in up to 90% of patients. Other symptoms include fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, weakness, abdominal pain or distension due to an enlarged spleen or liver, cough, shortness of breath, dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, oral ulcers, skin rashes, and neurological deficits such as confusion, seizures, and paralysis .

Mycosis fungoides (MF) is a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that typically presents as patches or plaques of red, scaly skin lesions . The most common symptom of MF is itching, which can be severe in some cases. Other symptoms include burning sensations, pain, and bleeding from broken skin. As the disease progresses, patients may develop tumors known as nodules, which can appear anywhere on the body but are often found on the scalp, face, ears, neck, chest, back, abdomen, groin, and legs.

The clinical staging system for mycosis fungoides (MF) was developed by the International Society for Cutaneous Lymphomas (ISCL). It is based primarily on disease extent and histopathological features .

The prognosis of primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, performance status, presence or absence of extranodal involvement, and genetic mutations. According to the International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group (IELSG), patients with PCNSL who were younger than 60 years old had an overall survival rate of about 45% after five years . However, those older than 60 years only had a 1-year survival rate of around 28%. Patients with poor performance status also have worse outcomes compared to those in good condition.

The most common symptom is painless lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes) which may occur in one or more areas of the body such as neck, armpit, groin, chest, abdomen, or behind the ears. Other symptoms include fever, weight loss, night sweats, fatigue, cough, shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing, and bone pain.

The treatment of childhood Hodgkin lymphoma typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and surgery in some cases. The specific treatment plan will depend on several factors, including the stage and location of the tumor, as well as other individual characteristics of the patient.

The most common symptom of anal cancer is rectal bleeding or blood in stool, which may be visible to the patient or only detectable by a digital rectal examination (DRE) performed by a healthcare provider. Other possible signs include persistent painless mass or lump near the anus, itching or burning in the anal area, changes in bowel habits such as diarrhea or constipation, mucousy discharge from the anus, painful or difficult passing of stools, and weight loss .

The treatment of anal cancer typically involves a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy or a multimodal approach depending on the stage at diagnosis. For early-stage disease (Stage I or II), local excision such as hemorrhoidectomy may be performed along with sentinel lymph node biopsy to determine if further treatment is needed. Radiation therapy alone or in conjunction with chemotherapy is often used for Stage III disease while a multidisciplinary approach involving all three modalities is recommended for more advanced cancers (Stages IVA and above). Surgery may involve abdominoperineal resection (APR) which removes the rectum and anus, followed by permanent colostomy to divert feces away from the anal canal.

The most common symptom of adult central nervous system (CNS) tumors is headache . Other signs include seizures , weakness or numbness in the extremities , vision changes , balance problems , nausea and vomiting , speech impairment , dizziness , memory loss , fatigue , and weight loss .

The treatment of adult central nervous system tumors typically involves a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or targeted therapies depending on the type and grade of the tumor. For low-grade gliomas (LGGs), such as pilocytic astrocytoma and diffuse astrocytoma, surgical resection is often the primary treatment option, with adjuvant radiotherapy recommended in some cases to reduce recurrence rates . However, for high-grade gliomas (HGGs) such as anaplastic astrocytoma and glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), which have a higher rate of recurrence after surgical resection alone, additional treatments including chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy may be necessary .

The prognosis of childhood brain tumors depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, type of tumor, location within the central nervous system (CNS), grade or stage of the tumor, presence or absence of metastasis, and response to treatment .

Childhood astrocytoma can occur in both children and adults of all ages, but it is more common in children under 15 years old. The exact cause of childhood astrocytoma is unknown, but there may be genetic factors that increase the risk of developing this type of brain tumor. Children with certain inherited conditions such as neurofibromatosis or tuberous sclerosis have an increased risk of developing childhood astrocytoma. Additionally, exposure to radiation early in life, particularly from diagnostic X-rays, has been linked to an increased risk of developing childhood astrocytoma later in life.

There have been several ongoing studies to investigate childhood astrocytoma treatments. One such study is the Children's Oncology Group (COG) trial ACNS0831, which aims to evaluate the efficacy of irinotecan in combination with temozolomide as a first-line treatment for children with newly diagnosed diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG). The results of this trial were published in 2019 and showed that adding irinotecan to standard therapy did not improve progression-free survival or overall survival .

Diagnosis of childhood central nervous system atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (AT/RTs) requires a combination of clinical presentation, imaging findings, histopathological examination, immunohistochemistry staining, and molecular testing .

Childhood brain stem gliomas (CBSGs), also known as pediatric brainstem gliomas or diffuse pontine gliomas, refer to a specific type of malignant tumor that arises from glial cells in the pons region of the brainstem during childhood . These tumors account for approximately 50% of all pediatric brainstem cancers and typically occur between the ages of 3 and 7 years old .

The prognosis of childhood brainstem gliomas (BSGs) depends on several factors, including age at diagnosis, tumor location within the brainstem, histologic grade, extent of surgical resection, and adjuvant therapy received .

Childhood central nervous system (CNS) embryonal tumors can occur in both genders; however, they are more common among males than females. The exact cause of these tumors remains unknown, but certain genetic conditions such as neurofibromatosis type 1 or Li-Fraumeni syndrome may increase the risk of developing CNS embryonal tumors . Additionally, exposure to radiation has been linked to an increased risk of developing some types of CNS embryonal tumors.

The treatment of childhood central nervous system embryonal tumors typically involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy depending on the specific type and stage of the tumor. Surgery is often used to remove as much of the tumor as possible, while chemotherapy and radiation therapy are used to kill any remaining cancer cells.

Diagnosis of childhood central nervous system germ cell tumors typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT), and pathological examination of tissue biopsy samples obtained during surgery .

Childhood craniopharyngiomas can occur in both children and adults of any age group but are more common in children aged 5 to 10 years old . They are also slightly more prevalent in males than females (male-to-female ratio of approximately 2 : 1) .

There have been several ongoing studies investigating new treatments for craniopharyngiomas in children. One such study is the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium (PBTC) protocol PBTC-0621, which is evaluating the use of bevacizumab as an adjuvant therapy after surgical resection of craniopharyngioma . The results of this trial were published in 2018 and showed that bevacizumab was associated with improved progression-free survival compared to placebo . Another ongoing study by the Children's Oncology Group (COG) is evaluating the use of chemotherapy prior to surgery for patients with newly diagnosed craniopharyngioma (protocol A9372).

Diagnosis of childhood ependymomas typically involves a combination of imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT), along with other diagnostic tests including cerebrospinal fluid analysis, biopsy, and histopathological examination of tissue samples obtained during surgery .

The term "adult primary liver cancer" refers to cancers that originate from cells in the liver tissue itself. These include hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), which accounts for about 90% of cases, cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer), and other rarer types such as angiosarcoma or hemangioblastoma .

The stages of adult primary liver cancer (also known as hepatocellular carcinoma or HCC) are classified using two different systems: the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging system and the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) staging system.

The most common symptom of bile duct cancer is jaundice, which can be accompanied by pruritus, dark urine, clay-colored stools, fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain or discomfort in the upper right quadrant, nausea, vomiting, fever, chills, light colored stool, and diarrhea .

Cholangiocarcinoma is a type of cancer that develops in the biliary ducts, which carry bile from the liver to the small intestine. Treatment options depend on several factors, including the stage of the cancer at diagnosis, its location within the biliary system, and whether it has spread beyond the bile ducts .

The prognosis of childhood liver cancer depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, tumor stage, type of tumor, and whether it has spread to other parts of the body. Overall survival rates have improved over time due to advances in treatment options including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and targeted therapies . However, the overall 5-year relative survival rate remains low (10–20%), with most deaths occurring within two years after diagnosis . Infants diagnosed with hepatoblastoma have better outcomes than older children, with an estimated five-year survival rate of up to 80%. Children with HCC or PNETs generally have worse prognoses compared to those with hepatoblastoma.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), which accounts for 75% to 85% of all primary liver cancers, is most commonly associated with chronic inflammation due to hepatitis B or C virus infection . Other significant risk factors include exposure to dietary aflatoxin, alcoholic cirrhosis, tobacco smoking, obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, porphyria cutanea tarda, cholestatic jaundice, and congestive heart failure .

The most common symptoms of Ewing sarcoma include pain in one bone or joint that is persistent and does not go away over time, swelling, redness, warmth around an affected area, limping, weakness, fatigue, weight loss, fever, and difficulty walking .

Osteosarcoma is a type of bone cancer that arises from osteoblasts or cells that produce bone tissue . It most commonly affects children and adolescents but can occur at any age. The primary location for this tumor is in the long bones such as the femur, tibia, humerus, and radius. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and localized tenderness around the affected area.

The stages of osteosarcoma are as follows: Stage I: Localized disease without metastasis; Stage IIA: Localized disease with local metastasis (e.g., soft tissue extension); Stage IIB: Diffuse bone marrow involvement without extracompartmental extension; Stage III: Diffuse bone marrow involvement with extracompartmental extension.

The most common symptom of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumor is diarrhea (50%), followed by abdominal pain or cramping (38%) . Other less frequent symptoms include nausea, vomiting, weight loss, fatigue, weakness, anemia, palpable abdominal mass, and iron deficiency anemia .

There have been several ongoing studies to investigate new treatments for gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors. One such study is NCT03915268, which is evaluating the efficacy of everolimus in combination with capecitabine versus placebo plus capecitabine as second-line treatment for patients with advanced neuroendocrine tumors, including gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors . Another study, NCT04716353, is investigating the use of lanreotide autogel in combination with temozolomide and capecitabine as first-line therapy for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors .

The chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are a group of clonal hematologic disorders characterized by increased proliferation of one or more myeloid cell lineages in the bone marrow . There are three main types of MPNs: polycythemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythemia (ET), and primary myelofibrosis (PMF). These diseases can occur at any age but most often affect individuals over 50 years old.

The treatment of polycythemia vera typically involves phlebotomy (removal of blood) to reduce hematocrit levels below 45% in men and 43% in women . In addition, patients with PV may be prescribed medications such as hydroxyurea or interferon-alpha to help regulate white blood cell counts and prevent clot formation . Patients should also avoid activities that can increase their risk of bleeding, such as contact sports, and take steps to manage any underlying conditions they may have, such as high blood pressure or diabetes . Regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare provider are important to monitor disease activity and adjust treatment as needed.

Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an increase in platelet count above 450 × 109 cells per liter (× 109/L), splenomegaly, bone marrow fibrosis, and increased risk of vascular events . ET can occur at any age but typically presents between 30 to 60 years old. The diagnosis requires exclusion of reactive causes such as inflammation or bleeding, which may elevate platelets transiently .

The treatment of chronic neutrophilic leukemia (CNL) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy and targeted therapies . First-line therapy usually includes hydroxyurea to reduce white blood cell counts and prevent complications such as splenomegaly and tissue damage caused by neutrophils . Other options include interferon alpha or immunomodulatory drugs like lenalidomide . Targeted agents that have shown efficacy in CNL include ruxolitinib , midostaurin  and masitinib . Masitinib is approved in Europe but not in the US . Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered if patients relapse after first-line therapy or develop refractory disease .

The diagnosis of myeloid neoplasms is made through a combination of clinical features, blood counts, bone marrow examination, cytogenetics, molecular genetics, flow cytometry, and next-generation sequencing (NGS).

The symptoms of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) can include fatigue, weakness, weight loss, abdominal pain or discomfort, frequent infections, enlarged spleen, bone pain, easy bruising, bleeding gums, and an increased risk of thrombosis .

The prognosis of juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) depends on several factors, including genetic mutations, response to initial treatment, age at diagnosis, and risk group classification. Patients with JMML typically have an aggressive disease course and poor overall survival rates.

The treatment of atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) depends on various factors such as age, overall health status, and genetic abnormalities detected in the bone marrow cells . In general, aCML is treated with targeted therapies that aim to control blood cell counts and reduce symptoms associated with anemia or other complications caused by the disease .

Endometrial cancer (EC) is one of the most common gynecological malignancies in developed countries . The incidence rate of EC varies widely across different populations worldwide, with an estimated 382,069 new cases diagnosed annually . In the United States alone, approximately 61,780 women were newly diagnosed with EC in 2020 , while in Europe, there were about 45,600 new diagnoses in 2020 .

The treatment of endometrial cancer typically involves surgery combined with chemotherapy or radiation therapy depending on the stage of the disease . For early-stage (I and II) endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, hysterectomy is recommended as primary surgical approach . In advanced stages (III and IV), patients may undergo neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to surgery in order to reduce tumor size and dissemination . Adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy can also be used after surgery if necessary .

The diagnosis of uterine sarcomas typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies such as ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and histopathological examination of biopsy samples obtained through endometrial curettage or laparoscopy. Imaging studies can help identify suspicious features that may suggest the presence of a malignant tumor, but they cannot definitively confirm the diagnosis. Histologic examination is necessary for accurate classification of uterine sarcomas into specific subtypes.

There is no clear evidence that any specific factor can completely prevent endometrial cancer. However, there are several steps women can take to reduce their risk of developing this disease or detect it early when treatment is more effective. These include maintaining a healthy body weight throughout life, limiting alcohol intake, reducing red meat consumption, increasing physical activity levels, taking oral contraceptives for at least five years if they have not had children, having regular pelvic examinations with Papanicolaou testing (Pap smear), and being screened regularly for cervical cancer .

Diagnosis of childhood extracranial germ cell tumors typically involves a combination of imaging studies, such as ultrasound or computed tomography (CT), and biopsy with histopathological examination. Imaging may reveal specific features that suggest a diagnosis of GCT, including heterogeneous enhancement, necrosis, calcification, cystic components, hemorrhage, and fat content .

An extragonadal germ cell tumor (EGCT) refers to a type of cancer that develops from cells similar to those found in testicles or ovaries but at an uncommon location outside the reproductive organs . These cancers originate from the embryonic tissues known as the germ line, which gives rise to gametes during fetal development. EGCTs most commonly occur in midline structures such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and anterior sacral region; however, they may also arise in other locations including the brain, liver, kidney, bladder, breast, and bone marrow . The most common sites for EGCTs are the gonads (testes and ovaries), followed by the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and anterior sacral region .

The stages of extragonadal germ cell tumor (EGCT) are defined by the International Germ Cell Cancer Consensus Classification . EGCTs can occur in various locations throughout the body, including the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, testicular tunics, omentum, fallopian tube, pericardium, bladder, kidney, prostate, breast, liver, lung, thyroid gland, brain, and bone marrow.

The most common symptom of uveal melanoma is blurred vision or a sudden change in vision that may be accompanied by floaters or flashes of light. Other possible signs include painless eye movement restrictions, bulging of the eyeball, changes to pupil size or shape, irregularly shaped pupils, and buphthalmos (enlargement of one or both eyes).

There have been several ongoing studies related to intraocular melanoma. One such study is the UM-T trial, which aims to evaluate the efficacy of targeted therapy with nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus standard treatment with plaque brachytherapy in patients with uveal melanoma that has spread outside the eye or cannot be removed by surgery . Another study, the COMO trial, is evaluating the use of combination immunotherapy with nivolumab plus ipilimumab as first-line treatment for metastatic uveal melanoma .

Retinoblastoma is a rare type of cancer that develops in children under 5 years old. It can be diagnosed by examining the eyes using an ophthalmoscope or other imaging techniques such as ultrasound, MRI, CT scan, or PET scan. The diagnosis may also involve genetic testing for mutations in RB1 gene.

Ovarian epithelial cancer, fallopian tube cancer, and primary peritoneal carcinoma are all types of malignant tumors that arise from cells lining the ovary, fallopian tubes, or peritoneum, respectively. They are often referred to collectively as “ovarian cancers” because they share many similarities in their clinical presentation, diagnostic workup, treatment, and prognosis.

The diagnosis of ovarian epithelial cancer (OEC), fallopian tube cancer (FTC) or primary peritoneal carcinoma (PPC) typically involves a combination of clinical history, physical examination, imaging tests such as ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, PET-CT, laparoscopy with biopsy for histopathological evaluation and immunohistochemical analysis. Imaging modalities can help in identifying tumor location, size, extent of spread, presence of metastasis and staging. Histology is crucial for confirmatory diagnosis and differentiation between these three types of malignancies which share similar features.

An ovarian germ cell tumor is a type of cancer that originates from cells in the ovary that were present at conception. These can be either malignant or benign. Malignant germ cell tumors include immature teratoma, dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and embryonal carcinomas. Benign germ cell tumors include mature cystic teratomas, also known as dermoid cysts, which are usually not cancerous but may become so if they undergo malignant transformation .

The treatment of ovarian germ cell tumors typically involves surgery to remove the tumor followed by chemotherapy to kill any remaining cancer cells. Surgery may involve removing one or both ovaries, as well as other organs such as the uterus, fallopian tubes, lymph nodes, liver, lungs, bones, etc., depending on the extent of metastasis. Chemotherapy is often recommended after surgery in order to prevent recurrence.

The prognosis of ovarian low malignant potential tumor (LMPT) is generally favorable with an overall survival rate of 95% at five years . However, it can be challenging to distinguish LMPT from other types of ovarian cancer due to their similar clinical presentation and imaging findings. Therefore, surgical resection followed by histopathological examination is recommended for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning .

The best way to prevent ovarian cancer is through early detection. Regular screening with pelvic exams, transvaginal ultrasound (TVU), and CA-125 blood test can help detect ovarian cancer in its early stages when it's most treatable. Other prevention strategies include maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol consumption, and practicing safe sex to reduce the risk of infection from HPV.

The most common symptom of gallbladder cancer is pain in the upper right abdomen that may radiate to the back or be associated with nausea and vomiting. Other possible symptoms include weight loss, indigestion, bloating, itching, dark urine, light-colored stools, yellowing of the skin (jaundice), and fatigue. These symptoms often occur late in the disease process when tumors are large and invasive, making early detection difficult.

There have been several ongoing studies to investigate new treatments for gallbladder cancer. One such study is the phase II trial of gemcitabine plus cisplatin in patients with advanced biliary tract cancers, including gallbladder cancer. The results of this trial showed that the combination therapy was effective, with an overall response rate of 50% . Another study is the phase III trial of gemcitabine plus oxaliplatin versus single-agent gemcitabine in patients with advanced biliary tract cancers. This trial demonstrated that the combination therapy resulted in improved progression-free survival compared to gemcitabine alone .

Testicular cancer is a type of cancer that originates in one or both testicles. It is most commonly diagnosed between 20 to 49 years old, with an average age at diagnosis of around 35 years old . The exact cause of testicular cancer is unknown but it has been linked to environmental factors such as pesticides and chemicals found in plastics, as well as genetic factors . Symptoms can include a painless lump or swelling in the scrotum, which may be felt by self-examination or noticed by a partner during sexual intercourse. Other symptoms can include a feeling of heaviness in the scrotal area, a sensation of pain or pressure in the lower abdomen, and/or changes in how you urinate. If left untreated, testicular cancer can spread from the testicle into the bloodstream and affect other parts of the body, including the lungs, liver, brain, bones, and lymph nodes.

The diagnosis of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) is made through a combination of clinical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging studies such as ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and histopathological evaluation of tissue samples obtained by biopsy or surgery .

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare hematologic disorder characterized by abnormal proliferation of dendritic cells called Langerhans cells. It can affect various organs including bone, skin, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, lungs, and central nervous system. The disease presents with diverse clinical manifestations depending on the affected organ(s). Diagnosis is usually made through biopsy and immunohistochemical staining to identify Langerhans cells. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy or radiation therapy for localized lesions, while combination chemotherapy may be used in disseminated cases .

The most common symptom of hypopharyngeal cancer is difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), which may cause food to feel stuck in your throat or chest, coughing while eating, weight loss, pain when swallowing, and regurgitation. Other possible signs include hoarseness, voice changes, sore throat, painful deglutition, odynophagia, globus sensation, dysphonia, and foreign body sensation .

There have been several ongoing studies investigating new treatments for hypopharyngeal cancer. One such study is evaluating the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors in combination with chemotherapy as first-line treatment for patients with advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma . Another study is examining the effectiveness of targeted therapy using vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) inhibition in combination with standard platinum-based chemotherapy for recurrent or metastatic disease . Additionally, there are also studies exploring novel approaches to radiation therapy, including intensity modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), proton beam therapy, and stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT). These therapies aim to improve outcomes while reducing side effects associated with traditional radiation techniques.

The most common symptom of laryngeal cancer is a hoarse or raspy voice. Other symptoms include difficulty swallowing, pain in the throat or ear, cough, breathing difficulties, sensation of something being stuck in the throat, vocal cord paralysis, and swelling in the neck.

There have been several ongoing studies related to laryngeal cancer. One such study is the “Lung Cancer Screening Trial” which aims to determine whether screening with low-dose computed tomography can reduce mortality in heavy smokers at high risk of developing lung cancer . Another study is the “Radiation Therapy Oncology Group 0617” trial, which investigates the effectiveness of chemotherapy and radiation therapy as an adjuvant treatment after surgical resection of locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma . The “Checkmate 143” trial is evaluating nivolumab versus docetaxel as second-line treatment for patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma who progressed after platinum-based chemotherapy .

The prognosis of lip and oral cavity cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor size, location, histologic grade, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis . Generally, early-stage cancers have better outcomes with 5-year survival rates approaching 80% to 90%. However, advanced-stage disease has poorer outcomes, with 5-year survival rates dropping below 30% in some cases .

The symptoms of metastatic squamous neck cancer with an occult primary site can vary depending on the location of the tumor in the head or neck region. Some common signs and symptoms include a painless lump or mass in the neck, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), hoarseness, numbness or tingling sensations in the face, mouth, or tongue, weakness or paralysis of facial muscles, and unilateral hearing loss . Other possible symptoms may include double vision, drooping eyelids, eye movement abnormalities, or blindness due to optic nerve involvement, as well as coughing, shortness of breath, chest pain, or weight loss if there is lung involvement . It is important for patients experiencing these symptoms to seek prompt medical attention, especially those who have risk factors such as smoking, alcohol consumption, or exposure to human papillomavirus (HPV).

There have been several studies conducted to investigate metastatic squamous cell neck cancer with an occult primary site. One study was published in 2018 by Kwong et al., which included 45 patients who were diagnosed with cervical lymph node metastases from unknown origin . The most common sites of involvement were the level II nodes (69%), followed by the level III nodes (31%) and the retropharyngeal nodes (7%). In terms of treatment, surgery alone or in combination with chemotherapy or radiation therapy was performed in 36%, 56%, and 8%, respectively. The median overall survival time was 12 months, and the five-year overall survival rate was 27%. Another study that was published in 2019 by Chan et al. included 22 patients who had similar findings . They found that the most common presenting symptoms were a neck mass (41%), dyspnea (32%), and dysphagia (23%). The prognosis of nasopharyngeal cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, histological type, age, and overall health status. In general, early-stage cancers have a better prognosis than advanced-stage cancers. Radiation therapy alone or in combination with chemotherapy has been shown to be effective in treating nasopharyngeal cancer, but it may also cause side effects such as hearing loss, swallowing difficulties, and dry mouth. Surgery may also be used depending on the stage and location of the tumor. Regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare provider are important after treatment to monitor for recurrence and manage any long-term symptoms.

Oral cancer can affect anyone; however, certain factors may increase the risk of developing this type of cancer. These include smoking tobacco (including cigarettes, pipes, water pipes or “bubble pipes,” cigars, and chewing tobacco), heavy alcohol use, human papillomavirus infection (particularly HPV 16), poor oral hygiene, having certain types of warts in your mouth, long-term irritation or inflammation caused by dentures that do not fit properly, radiation therapy to head and neck area, family history of squamous cell carcinoma, chronic sun exposure, and immunosuppression from organ transplantation .

Treatment options for oropharyngeal cancer depend on several factors such as stage of diagnosis, location of tumor, size of tumor, presence of lymph node involvement, and whether human papillomavirus (HPV) is present in the tumor cells.

Diagnosis of paranasal sinus and nasal cavity cancer typically involves a combination of clinical examination, imaging tests such as CT scans or MRIs, and biopsy of suspicious tissue. The specific approach may vary depending on the location and extent of the suspected tumor.

Salivary gland cancer refers to any malignant tumor that arises from one of the major or minor salivary glands found throughout the oral cavity . The three major salivary glands include the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands, while the minor salivary glands are located in various areas within the mouth, including the hard palate, soft palate, lip, buccal mucosa, tongue, gingiva, floor of the mouth, pharynx, and tonsils .

The stages of salivary gland cancer are determined using the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) Tumor-Node-Metastasis (TNM) staging system. This is based on the size of the primary tumour (T), whether the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes (N) and whether there is distant metastasis (M).

Pancreatic cancer refers to any type of malignant tumor that arises from cells within the pancreas. The most common form of pancreatic cancer is adenocarcinoma, which originates in the exocrine tissues of the pancreas. Other types of pancreatic cancers include neuroendocrine tumors, such as insulinomas or gastrinomas, and rare forms of pancreatic cancer, including acinar cell carcinoma and solid pseudopapillary neoplasm .

The stages of pancreatic cancer are determined by the Tumor-Node-Metastasis (TNM) classification system . This system takes into account the size and location of the tumor (T), whether the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes (N), and whether it has metastasized to distant sites in the body (M).

Diagnosis of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (PanNET) is typically made through a combination of clinical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging studies such as CT or MRI scans, and biopsy for histopathological evaluation . The most common presenting symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, fatigue, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and palpable masses in the abdomen . Laboratory testing may reveal elevated levels of serotonin, chromogranin A, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), glucagon, gastrin, somatostatin, parathyroid hormone related peptide (PTHrP), and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP). Imaging studies can help determine the size, location, extent of disease spread, and vascular involvement of PanNETs. Biopsies are usually not performed due to the risk of bleeding and metastasis; however, they may be necessary if other diagnostic methods do not provide sufficient information .

Renal cell cancer (RCC), also known as renal carcinoma or kidney cancer, refers to any type of malignant tumor that arises from the epithelial cells lining the proximal convoluted tubules in the kidneys . RCC accounts for approximately 90% of all primary kidney cancers and is one of the most common urinary tract cancers . The most common subtype of RCC is clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), which is characterized by the presence of clear cytoplasm due to glycogen and lipid content . Other types of RCC include papillary renal cell carcinoma (pRCC), chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (chRCC), collecting duct carcinomas, and unclassified histologic variants .

The symptoms of transitional cell cancer (TCC) of the renal pelvis and ureter can include pain in the flank or side, blood in the urine (hematuria), difficulty urinating, frequent urination, and pain with urination. Other possible signs may include weight loss, anemia, fatigue, fever, and hydronephrosis (fluid buildup behind the kidney). It is important to note that these symptoms can also be caused by other conditions, so it is essential for individuals experiencing any of them to consult a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.

There have been several ongoing studies related to transitional cell cancer of the renal pelvis and ureter. One study is investigating the use of pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy as first-line treatment for patients with advanced or metastatic disease . Another study is evaluating the efficacy of atezolizumab plus bevacizumab versus sunitinib monotherapy in patients with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic tumors .

The prognosis of childhood kidney tumors depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, stage of disease, histological subtype, and presence or absence of metastasis. For example, nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumor) has an overall 5-year survival rate of approximately 80% in children under the age of five years but drops to around 10% in those over the age of ten years . Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney typically has a poor prognosis with a reported median progression-free survival of less than one year . Rhabdoid carcinomas have a particularly aggressive course with a high likelihood of early dissemination and a dismal prognosis . It is important to note that these figures may vary depending on the specific type of pediatric renal tumor and its individual characteristics.

Breast cancer can affect anyone with two X chromosomes, but certain factors increase the likelihood of developing breast cancer. These include family history of breast or ovarian cancer in first-degree relatives (mothers, sisters, daughters), age (the older one gets, the more likely it is to develop breast cancer), genetic mutations such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, personal history of benign breast tumors, hormonal exposure such as early menarche and late menopause, radiation exposure, alcohol consumption, smoking, obesity, lack of physical activity, oral contraceptives use, and postmenopausal hormone replacement therapy.

The outlook for breast cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, age of patient, tumor size, grade, hormone receptor status, HER2 status, and lymph node involvement. In general, early-stage (I or II) breast cancers that are diagnosed before they have spread to other parts of the body usually have better outcomes than later-stage (III or IV) breast cancers. Treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and hormonal therapies. Regular follow-up with a healthcare provider is important for monitoring disease progression and detecting recurrence in its earliest stages when treatment may be more effective.

Men can develop breast cancer due to various factors such as genetic mutations (e.g., BRCA1 or BRCA2), hormonal imbalances, family history of breast cancer in first-degree relatives, increased age, exposure to radiation, alcohol consumption, obesity, liver diseases, testicular conditions, and drug use .
The stages of male breast cancer are determined using the same staging system as for female breast cancer. This is because the biology and prognosis of male and female breast cancers are similar .

The outlook for skin cancer varies depending on the type of skin cancer and its stage at diagnosis. If detected early through regular self-skin examinations or doctor checkups, most forms of skin cancer can be cured with simple excision or other procedures. However, if left untreated, some types of skin cancer may spread to other parts of the body and become difficult to treat. It's important to note that while melanoma accounts for less than 1% of all skin cancers diagnosed each year in the United States, it causes more than 75% of all deaths from skin cancer due to its aggressive nature .

Melanoma can affect anyone regardless of age, gender or race; however, certain factors may increase one's risk of developing melanoma. These include having fair skin, hair and eye color (red or blond hair, blue or light-colored eyes), a history of sunburns, excessive UV exposure from the sun or tanning beds, a family history of melanoma, multiple moles or unusual nevi, a weakened immune system, and a personal history of nonmelanoma skin cancer .

The treatment of melanoma depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, location of tumor, age, overall health status, and personal preferences . For early-stage localized disease (Stage I or II), surgical removal is typically recommended. This may involve wide excision to remove all visible tumors with some healthy tissue around it, known as clear margins . If the melanoma has spread regionally (Stage III) or distantly (Stage IV), additional therapies may be needed in addition to surgery. These can include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches . Immunotherapies that have been approved by the FDA for the treatment of metastatic melanoma include ipilimumab, pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and tremelimumab . Targeted therapies that have been approved for advanced melanoma include dabrafenib, trametinib, vemurafenib, cobimetinib, encorafenib, binimetinib, and combinatorial regimens including dabrafenib plus trametinib and vemurafenib plus cobimetinib . It's important to note that the specific treatment plan will depend on several individual factors, so it's always best to consult with a healthcare provider for personalized advice.

Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is a rare but aggressive form of skin cancer that can be difficult to detect in its early stages due to its fast growth rate and ability to mimic other benign skin conditions such as cysts or moles . The best way to diagnose MCC is through a combination of clinical examination, dermoscopy, biopsy, and histopathological analysis of tissue samples under a microscope . During a physical exam, doctors will look for signs of MCC, which may include small, flesh-colored, pink, red, purple, blue, brown, or black nodules or lesions with irregular borders that can appear anywhere on the body but are most commonly found on the head, neck, ears, eyelids, lips, hands, feet, ankles, and legs . Dermatoscopic evaluation involves using a handheld magnifying device called a dermoscope to examine suspicious spots or bumps more closely. This technique allows doctors to see details that are not visible to the naked eye, including structures known as milia-like pseudocysts, which are round, white areas within the tumor that resemble milkspots under a microscope . If a suspicious spot or bump is identified during either a physical exam or dermoscopic evaluation, a doctor may recommend a biopsy to remove a sample of tissue from the area for further testing . There are several ways to reduce your risk of developing skin cancer: 1) Seek shade whenever possible; 2) Wear protective clothing such as wide-brimmed hats, sunglasses, and long sleeves when outside for more than 30 minutes; 3) Use sunscreen with at least SPF 30 (sun protection factor); 4) Avoid tanning beds; 5) Check your skin regularly for any changes in moles or spots; 6) If you find any suspicious spots or lesions, see a doctor right away.

The stages of plasma cell neoplasm include monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM), and multiple myeloma (MM). MGUS is an asymptomatic condition in which abnormal antibodies or proteins are produced by cells called plasma cells but do not cause any damage to tissues. SMM is another precursor state of MM that may progress into active MM within two years if left untreated. In contrast, MM is characterized by the proliferation of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow and overproduction of monoclonal light chains or immunoglobulins .

The most common signs and symptoms of neuroblastoma include abdominal or pelvic mass (65%), abdominal pain or distension (40-72%), constipation (39%), fever (38%), weakness or fatigue (31%), loss of appetite (28%) and weight loss (28%). Other less frequent symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, bone pain, skin lesions, high blood pressure, seizures, and swelling in the neck, chest, or belly area .

The diagnosis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) typically involves several steps, including obtaining a detailed patient history, physical examination, imaging tests such as chest X-ray or computed tomography (CT), bronchoscopy with biopsy, and other diagnostic procedures depending on the location of the tumor .

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a type of aggressive neuroendocrine tumor that originates in the lungs. It accounts for about 15% of all lung cancers. SCLC cells tend to spread quickly throughout the body via blood vessels or lymphatic system, resulting in metastasis to other organs such as brain, liver, bone, and adrenal glands .

The standard treatment for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy depending on stage of disease at diagnosis . First-line treatment typically involves combination chemotherapy using cisplatin or carboplatin plus etoposide . For limited-stage SCLC, which is confined to one hemithorax, concurrent chemoradiation therapy may be used after initial chemotherapy. Second-line treatment options include topotecan monotherapy or irinotecan plus cisplatin . Targeted therapies such as immunotherapies have not been shown to improve outcomes in patients with SCLC, but ongoing clinical trials are evaluating their potential role in this setting .

Parathyroid cancer is a rare endocrine malignancy that arises from the parathyroids, which are four small glands located behind the thyroid gland in the neck . The main function of these glands is to produce parathyroid hormone (PTH), which regulates calcium levels in the blood by controlling the amount of calcium absorbed from the intestines and excreted through the kidneys .

The stages of parathyroid cancer (PC) are classified according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). PC is considered rare with an incidence rate of 0.5 per million people . It accounts for less than 1% of all endocrine malignancies and has no gender predilection .

The most common symptom of penile cancer is an unusual odorous discharge from the penis. Other symptoms include a lump or thickening on the skin of the penis, bleeding from the penis, pain in the pelvic area, difficulty urinating, painful erection, and swelling of the legs. It's important to note that these symptoms can also be caused by other conditions not related to cancer, so it's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis.

There have been several recent studies published regarding penile cancer. A 2019 study by Böhm et al. investigated the prognostic value of sentinel lymph node biopsy in patients with clinically negative inguinal nodes . The results showed that sentinel lymph node biopsy was associated with improved overall survival compared to no lymph node dissection. Another study from 2018 by Liu et al. evaluated the use of carbon ion therapy for treating locally advanced penile cancer . They found that carbon ion therapy had better local control rates than conventional radiotherapy.

The prognosis of pituitary tumors depends on various factors such as size, type, location within the sella turcica, hormone production by the tumor, patient age, and response to treatment. Generally speaking, most patients with non-invasive pituitary adenomas can be cured or have significant improvement in their symptoms after undergoing surgical resection followed by radiation therapy if necessary . However, some types of pituitary tumors may require lifelong medical management even after successful surgery due to high recurrence rates .

The most common symptom of prostate cancer is difficulty urinating, which may be accompanied by pain or burning sensation during urination, more frequent urination, incontinence, weakened stream, and pain in the lower back, hips, or pelvis. Other possible signs include blood in the semen, erectile dysfunction, decreased libido, weight loss, fatigue, constipation, and hot flashes. It's important to note that these symptoms can also occur due to other conditions not related to prostate cancer, so it's crucial for individuals experiencing any of them to consult with their healthcare provider.

There have been several ongoing studies to investigate new treatments for prostate cancer. One such study is the phase III PROSPER trial, which aims to evaluate the efficacy of apalutamide in combination with androgen deprivation therapy compared to placebo plus androgen deprivation therapy as first-line treatment for nonmetastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer . Another ongoing study is the phase IIb PALGPS-2 trial, which will assess the effectiveness of palbociclib combined with goserelin and either abiraterone acetate or enzalutamide in patients with newly diagnosed metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer . The results from these studies may provide important insights into the optimal management of this disease.

The most common symptom of colon cancer is persistent changes in bowel habits such as diarrhea or constipation. Other symptoms include abdominal pain, weight loss, blood in stool (visible or hidden), anemia, fatigue, vomiting, palpable abdominal mass, and rectal bleeding .

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials related to colon cancer treatment that are listed in ClinicalTrials.gov . These include studies of new targeted therapies such as immunotherapy or combination therapy with chemotherapeutic agents. The goal of these trials is to improve patient outcomes by developing more effective treatments while reducing side effects. It is important for patients with colon cancer to be aware of these clinical trials and consider participating if they meet eligibility criteria.

The prognosis of rectal cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor size, histologic grade, lymph node involvement, vascular invasion, and circumferential resection margin status . Patients with early-stage disease (Stage I or II) have a good chance of cure after surgery alone, while those with advanced disease require chemotherapy in addition to surgery . In recent years, there has been significant progress in the treatment of rectal cancer, including advances in surgical techniques, neoadjuvant therapy, and adjuvant therapy . As a result, survival rates have improved significantly over time, especially among patients diagnosed with Stage III disease . Despite these improvements, however, rectal cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer death worldwide .

There is no definitive way to prevent colorectal cancer (CRC). However, there are several ways that can help reduce your risk of developing CRC, including maintaining a healthy body weight, eating plenty of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean meats, fish, and low-fat dairy products while avoiding processed meat, red meat, sugary drinks, and excessive alcohol consumption . Additionally, it's important to exercise regularly, quit smoking if you smoke, limit exposure to radiation or certain chemicals, screen for CRC starting at age 50 using colonoscopy every ten years unless polyps are found, in which case screening should be done more frequently , and consider genetic testing if there is a family history of CRC .

The most common symptom of small intestinal cancer is abdominal pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen. Other symptoms include diarrhea, constipation, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, indigestion, bloating, gas, anemia, light stools, fatigue, jaundice, palpable abdominal mass, and bleeding from the GI tract .

Thymomas and thymic carcinomas are rare tumors that originate from epithelial cells of the thymus gland . The thymus gland is an organ located in the anterior mediastinum near the heart that plays a role in immune function during early childhood .
