The prognosis of urothelial cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor grade, presence or absence of lymph node metastasis, and other comorbidities . In general, patients with localized disease have a good chance of survival after treatment, while those with advanced or recurrent disease have a poorer prognosis.

The most common symptom of vulvar cancer is an itchy or sore vagina that doesn't go away for more than 2 weeks. Other symptoms include abnormal vaginal bleeding, pain in the pelvic area, painful urination, discharge from the vagina, swelling around the genitals, thickening of the skin near the vagina, and changes to the color of the skin around the vagina .

The treatment of vulvar cancer depends on several factors such as stage, size, grade, type of tumor, and whether it has spread to other parts of the body. Treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapies, or a combination of these approaches .

An aberrant subclavian artery is an anomaly in which the left or right subclavian artery originates from an abnormal site other than its usual location at the level of T1-2 vertebrae . The most common form of this anomaly involves the left subclavian artery, which originates directly from the arch of the aorta instead of branching off the brachiocephalic trunk . This can lead to several clinical complications such as stroke due to cerebral hypoperfusion, carotid-subclavian steal syndrome, and congenital heart defects .

Abetalipoproteinemia (ABL) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe impairment of lipid metabolism due to deficiency in apolipoproteins B-100 and A-I . Diagnosis of ABL can be made using several methods including plasma total cholesterol levels, stool examination for fat globules, and genetic testing .

The absence of tibia is known as congenital fibular deficiency (CFD), which is an extremely rare condition that occurs during embryonic development. It can be caused by genetic or environmental factors. Symptoms include shortening of one leg compared to the other, pain in the affected area, difficulty walking, and knee instability .

The most common symptom of acatalasemia is chest pain or angina due to myocardial ischemia . Other possible symptoms include dyspnea, fatigue, palpitations, dizziness, syncope, and arrhythmias . In rare cases, patients may also experience neurological symptoms such as headache, seizures, stroke-like episodes, cognitive impairment, and dementia .

An accessory navicular bone is an extra ossicle located at the junction of the medial part of the navicular bone with the middle phalanx of the fifth digit. It can be asymptomatic or cause pain in the midfoot region due to irritation from shoe pressure or repetitive stress . Treatment options include activity modification, orthotics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, and surgery if conservative measures fail . Surgery involves removal of the ossicle through a small incision made over it followed by fixation of the extensor tendon of the long toe flexor muscle to the base of the first metatarsal bone using sutures or wire .

The most common symptoms of achalasia include dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), regurgitation, weight loss, and chest pain or discomfort . Other less frequent symptoms may include coughing, choking sensations, heartburn, nausea, vomiting, difficulty speaking or talking while eating, and aspiration pneumonia .

Achondrogenesis is a rare genetic disorder characterized by underdevelopment or absence of cartilage during fetal development, resulting in dwarfism with short limbs and other skeletal abnormalities such as joint laxity, flat facial features, and hearing loss . There are several types of achondrogenesis that vary in severity and clinical presentation. Type 1, also known as Fraser-Sheehan syndrome, is the most common type and causes partial or complete lack of growth plates leading to disproportionate dwarfism with relatively shorter upper than lower extremities, joint contractures, and mild intellectual disability . Other forms include type 2, which presents with more severe symptoms including microcephaly, cleft palate, and sensorineural deafness; type 3, which has the most severe form of dysplasia and can be fatal within hours after birth due to respiratory failure ; and type 4, which is similar to type 1 but without intellectual disability .

Achondrogenesis type I A is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe dwarfism with disproportionate short limbs, joint laxity, and facial dysmorphia. It results from mutations in the gene encoding fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), which leads to defects in chondrocyte proliferation during endochondral ossification .

The most common symptom of achondroplasia is short stature due to abnormalities in endochondral ossification during growth . Other physical features include rhizomelia (short limbs), frontal bossing, midface flattening, trident acetabular roofs, lumbar lordosis, kyphoscoliosis, genu varum, macrocephaly, small mouth with high palate, crowded teeth, hearing loss, sleep apnea, recurrent otitis media, and limited joint mobility .

The symptoms of Achondroplasia include short stature with rhizomelia (shortening of limb segments), disproportionate head size (macrocephaly) and other skeletal abnormalities such as trident acetabular roof, lumbar lordosis, kyphoscoliosis, genu valgum, midface flattening, frontal bossing, underdeveloped nasal bridge, mandibular prognathism, foramen magnum stenosis, and hearing loss .

Acquired pure red cell aplasias (APRCA), also known as idiopathic aplastic anemia, are rare blood disorders characterized by severe pancytopenia due to failure of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow . APRCAs can be caused by various factors such as viral infections, exposure to certain drugs or chemicals, autoimmune diseases, nutritional deficiencies, and genetic conditions . The exact cause of most cases of APRCA remains unknown, making it difficult to treat effectively .

Acrodermatitis enteropathica (AE) is an autosomal recessive disorder of zinc absorption caused by mutations in the SLC39A4 gene that encodes the ZIP4 transporter protein . AE presents with dermatitic lesions and alopecia due to impaired zinc uptake from the gastrointestinal tract, leading to systemic zinc deficiency . The skin lesions typically appear as scaly papules or plaques on extensor surfaces such as the elbows, knees, hands, feet, and buttocks , which may progress to vesicles and bullae .
The symptoms of acrokeratoderma elastoidosis Costan can include hyperpigmented papules or plaques with thickened skin that may be painful to touch in the distal extremities .

Acro-meso-melic dysplasia is a rare genetic disorder that affects bone growth during development. It causes shortening of the limbs, particularly in the forearms and lower legs, as well as abnormalities in the fingers and toes. The condition can also affect other parts of the body such as the face or spine. There are several different types of acro-meso-melic dysplasias, which vary in severity and specific symptoms.

The acrorenal-mandibular (ARM) syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by renal tubular dysfunction with proximal tubulopathy, hypophosphatemia, osteomalacia or rickets, and dental enamel hypoplasia . Other features include short stature, mental retardation, sensorineural hearing loss, cataracts, hyperuricemia, hypercholesterolemia, and hepatomegaly .

Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis (AFND), also known as Sweet syndrome or acute febrile neutrophilic dermatitis, is a rare skin condition characterized by tender erythematous plaques that usually develop on the extremities, neck, scalp, and trunk . The name “Sweet syndrome” was given in honor of Dr. Robert Douglas Sweet, who first described this disease in 1964 .

The symptoms of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) typically include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, dark urine, and alcohol cravings. A severe complication is hepatic encephalopathy, which can lead to seizures, loss of consciousness, and death if not treated promptly.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a serious condition that can occur in response to an infection or other illnesses affecting the lungs. It involves fluid buildup in the alveoli of the lungs, which makes it difficult for patients to breathe. The symptoms include shortness of breath, low oxygen levels in the blood, and chest X-ray findings consistent with ARDS. Treatment typically includes supportive care such as mechanical ventilation, along with medications to reduce inflammation and prevent further damage to the lungs.

An adenoameloblastoma is an extremely rare odontogenic tumor that was first described in 1976 by Robinson et al. It accounts for less than 0.5% of all jaw cysts . The term “adenomelo” means both epithelial and ameloid components, which explains its name.

Diagnosis of adenocarcinoma of the appendix is typically made through a combination of clinical symptoms, imaging studies such as ultrasound or CT scans, and histopathological examination of biopsy samples obtained during surgery.

The main clinical manifestations of adenylosuccinate dehydrogenase (ADSL) deficiency include developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, movement disorders, dystonia, ataxia, hypotonia, microcephaly, autistic features, behavioral problems, speech impairment, feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, and visual impairment .

No, adipositis dolorosa is not considered to be an inheritable condition. It has been observed in patients with no family history of similar symptoms or conditions. However, further research may be needed to fully understand the genetic factors that contribute to this disease.

Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) refers to a structural three-dimensional deformity of the spine with Cobb angle between 10° and 45° in patients aged 10–18 years old . The cause of AIS remains unknown but it has been associated with genetic factors, hormonal imbalances, connective tissue disorders, neuromuscular diseases, skeletal dysplasia, and congenital vertebral anomalies .

The most common symptom of adrenocortical carcinoma is irregularity in menstruation or infertility due to hyperandrogenism . Other symptoms include weight loss, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, anorexia, weakness, headache, dizziness, hypertension, hypokalemia, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels.

The symptoms of adult-onset Still’s disease (AOSD) include high fever, arthritis or arthralgia, salmon pink skin rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, serositis, leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), ferritin levels, and an abnormal liver function test .

No, adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy is not considered to be inherited in an autosomal dominant or recessive pattern. However, there have been reports of familial cases with some genetic association .

Yes, afibrinogenemia is an autosomal recessive disorder, meaning that both parents must carry a copy of the defective gene for their child to have the condition. This is in contrast to dominant disorders where only one copy of the defective gene is needed for the condition to manifest.

The most common symptom of agenesis of the dorsal pancreas is recurrent acute pancreatitis attacks due to obstruction of the main pancreatic duct by stones or sludge . Other possible symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and fatigue .

Aicardi-Goutières Syndrome Type 2 (AGS2) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in genes involved in RNA metabolism or sensing pathways . AGS2 is characterized by encephalopathy with spasticity, microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, cholestatic jaundice, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and increased levels of interferon alpha .

The symptoms of Aicardi-Goutières Syndrome (AGS) Type 4 include developmental delay, microcephaly, cerebral calcifications, skin lesions such as periorbital xanthomas, and elevated levels of interferon in the blood or cerebrospinal fluid .

Ackermann syndrome is an extremely rare genetic disorder that affects the development of the skeletal system during embryonic development. The main features include short stature, delayed bone age, scoliosis, and facial dysmorphism (triangular face with pointed chin). Other possible signs and symptoms may include intellectual disability, microcephaly, hearing loss, joint laxity, and hernias .

The symptoms of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) deficiency include elevated levels of blood glucose, liver damage, and neurological problems such as seizures and developmental delay . Microcephaly is one of the most common features in patients with ALT deficiency, along with other signs including dwarfism, enamel hypoplasia, and diabetes mellitus .

The treatment of AHO is primarily supportive with no cure available at this time . Treatment options include bisphosphonates to improve bone mineral density (BMD) , calcitriol supplementation to increase calcium absorption in cases of hypocalcemia or rickets , and vitamin D supplementation if there is insufficient intake or malabsorption . Physical therapy may be recommended to help manage pain and maintain mobility . Surgery may be necessary in severe cases to correct deformities or relieve pain .

The exact cause of alopecia maculata congenita (AMC) is unknown; however, it has been associated with mutations in genes involved in cell cycle regulation . It is characterized by hypopigmented patches that usually appear at birth or during early childhood. These patches can be found anywhere on the body but most commonly occur on the scalp, upper trunk, and extremities. They may have irregular borders and vary in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters in diameter. In addition to skin pigmentation abnormalities, affected individuals may also experience hair loss (alopecia), particularly over the eyebrows, eyelashes, and scalp. Other features such as delayed growth and intellectual disability may also be present in some cases.

The exact cause of alopecia universalis is unknown. However, it has been associated with several factors such as autoimmune disorders (e.g., vitiligo), infections (e.g., syphilis), nutritional deficiencies, certain medications, genetic conditions (e.g., trichothiodystrophy), and psychological stress. It can also be idiopathic or occur without any identifiable underlying cause .

The symptoms of alopecia-intellectual disability syndrome include intellectual disability, hypogonadism, delayed puberty, amenorrhea in females, hirsutism, hypertrichosis cubiti (excessive hair growth at the elbows, knees, and other areas), seizures, and alopecia totalis or universalis (complete loss of scalp and body hair).

There is no cure for AATD at this time; however, there are several treatment options available to help manage symptoms and slow disease progression . These include augmentation therapy with intravenous (IV) or subcutaneous replacement of exogenous AAT protein , oral corticosteroids such as prednisone  and anti-inflammatory agents like NSAIDs . Patients may also benefit from supportive care measures including smoking cessation, vaccinations against common infections, and regular monitoring of lung function through spirometry . In severe cases, patients may require lung transplant evaluation if other therapies fail to improve respiratory symptoms .

Yes, alpha thalassemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs when one or more deletions of the α globin gene cluster occur in hemoglobin genes located on chromosome 16 . The inheritance pattern can be either homozygous (when both alleles have a mutation) or heterozygous (when only one allele has a mutation).

Alport syndrome is an inherited disorder of type IV collagen in the basement membrane that affects multiple organs including the kidneys, eyes, ears, skin, brain, heart, lungs, and muscles . It can be caused by mutations in any one of three genes encoding different chains of type IV collagen: COL4A3, COL4A4, or COL4A5 . The most common clinical manifestation of Alport syndrome is chronic progressive nephropathy leading to end-stage renal disease . Other symptoms include sensorineural hearing loss, ocular abnormalities such as lenticonus and maculopathy, and neurological problems such as cerebellar ataxia .

The main symptom of alveolar capillary dysplasia is shortness of breath due to hypoxemia (low oxygen levels in blood). Other common signs include cyanosis (blue or grayish-blue discoloration) of the skin and mucous membranes, tachypnea (rapid breathing), clubbing of fingers and toes, hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), failure to thrive, growth retardation, developmental delay, and fatigue. Infants with ACD may also have recurrent pulmonary infections and feeding difficulties due to poor nutrition .

Amelogenesis imperfecta refers to a group of rare genetic disorders that affect tooth enamel formation during its mineralization stage in the developing teeth . The condition can be inherited as an autosomal dominant trait or as an autosomal recessive disorder, with varying degrees of severity ranging from mild hypoplastic defects to severe hypoplasia resulting in congenital absence of tooth enamel .

There is no cure for amelogenesis imperfecta (AI), but there are several treatment options available to manage symptoms and improve quality of life. The specific treatment plan will depend on the type and severity of AI present in each individual patient.

The symptoms of amino acidurias can vary depending on the specific type of disorder involved. However, some common symptoms include intellectual disability, muscle weakness or wasting (muscular dystrophy), bone loss or fractures (osteopenia or osteoporosis), seizures, developmental delay, failure to thrive, recurrent infections, diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, irritability, poor appetite, abdominal pain, and rash. It is important for healthcare providers to consider these symptoms as potential indicators of an underlying metabolic disorder such as amino aciduria.

Amniotic band syndrome is caused by amniotic bands that wrap around fetuses during pregnancy. These bands can cause various injuries to the fetus at birth, including limb contractures, soft tissue damage, joint fusion, and even amputation of digits or limbs . The exact mechanism behind how these bands form remains unknown, but it has been suggested that they may be due to abnormalities in the amniotic fluid or placenta, such as decreased amniotic fluid levels or an excess of alpha-fetoprotein . Other factors that have been associated with amniotic band syndrome include multiple gestations, advanced maternal age, and certain genetic conditions . It is important for healthcare providers to recognize this condition early and provide appropriate treatment to minimize any long-term effects on the child's health.

The most common symptom of amyloid deposits in the cornea is a grayish-white opacity or plaque that can be seen with the naked eye . These opacities may vary in size from small to large, ranging from 1 mm to several millimeters in diameter. They typically appear as single lesions but multiple plaques may also occur. In addition to visual disturbances caused by these opacities, other ocular manifestations include dry eyes, photophobia, foreign body sensation, tearing, blurred vision, and glare .

Amyotonia congenita is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by muscle stiffness or weakness that occurs after rest and improves with continued activity . The main symptom of AC is muscle stiffness or rigidity, which typically affects large muscles such as those in the arms and legs, but can also affect smaller muscles like those used for eye movement. This stiffness often leads to difficulty walking, climbing stairs, running, writing, and other activities requiring coordinated movements. Other common symptoms include fatigue, pain, and cramps.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord . The diagnosis of ALS can be challenging as there is no single test or gold standard for its detection. Currently, the diagnosis of ALS requires a combination of clinical history, physical examination, electrodiagnostic testing, and imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

An anaplastic astrocytoma is a type of malignant brain tumor that arises from glial cells called astrocytes. It is classified as grade III by the World Health Organization (WHO). This classification system was developed to reflect the different degrees of aggressiveness and prognosis associated with various types of brain tumors .

Andermann syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by intellectual disability, hypotonia, and dysmorphic features such as microcephaly, short stature, small hands and feet, and low-set ears . It was first described in 1964 by Dr. Robert Andermann, who reported two siblings with severe developmental delay, growth retardation, and distinctive facial features . The condition results from mutations in the KIAA0586 gene, which encodes a protein involved in DNA repair pathways . Diagnosis of Andermann syndrome can be made through genetic testing or clinical evaluation if there is a strong suspicion of the diagnosis . Treatment for this condition focuses primarily on supportive care to manage symptoms and improve quality of life.

Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS) refers to a group of genetic disorders in which cells cannot respond normally to the male sex hormone, testosterone . AIS results from mutations in the androgen receptor gene located on chromosome Xq11-q12 that prevent the target tissues from responding to testosterone and other androgens . There are three types of AIS: complete form (CAIS), partial form (PAIS), and mild or reversible form (MAIS). CAIS occurs when there is no response at all to androgens. PAIS occurs when some tissues respond partially to androgens but not others. MAIS occurs when there is only slight resistance to androgens.

Anencephaly is a neural tube defect that occurs early in pregnancy, resulting in an infant born without large parts of the brain, skull, and scalp. The condition can cause severe developmental abnormalities including missing limbs (known as amelia), spinal cord defects, and heart problems. Symptoms include absent eyes, nose, ears, and mouth; no movement or response to touch; absence of breathing control; and lack of skin covering the brain tissue.

Angelman syndrome is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of function of UBE3A gene located at chromosome 15q11-q13 . The condition was first described in 1965 by Dr. Harry Angelman as “Proud Syndrome” or “Happy Puppet Syndrome.” It affects approximately one in every 20,000 births worldwide and has been associated with autism spectrum disorders .

The symptoms of angiomatosis, diffuse corticomeningeal, of Dreyfuss and Van Bogaert (DDB) can include headaches, seizures, mental retardation, developmental delay, cerebral edema, hydrocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, and stroke .

The main symptom of Ankyloblepharon filiforme is a membrane that connects the eyelids to each other or to the nose, which can cause eye irritation and discharge. Imperforate anus may also be present in some cases.

The main symptom of ankylosed teeth is limited or absent tooth mobility. Other symptoms include sensitivity to cold temperatures, pain when biting down (bruxism), difficulty chewing, and discomfort in the jaw muscles.

Congenital anonychia is a rare condition that can be treated with surgical procedures such as nail transplantation or toe-to-digit free tissue transfer . The choice of treatment depends on several factors, including the extent of the affected area and whether there are other associated anomalies present.

Anophthalmia is defined as congenital absence or complete loss of both eyes without any ocular tissue remaining in its place . Congenital antiplasmin deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the PLG gene that encodes plasminogen . Plasminogen is converted to plasmin, which breaks down fibrin clots during blood coagulation. Deficiencies in plasminogen can lead to excessive bleeding and delayed wound healing.

The treatment of antisynthetase syndrome typically involves a combination of medications to manage symptoms and control disease activity . First-line therapies include corticosteroids such as prednisone or methylprednisolone, which can help reduce inflammation and suppress immune system overactivity. Other immunosuppressive agents may also be used in conjunction with steroid therapy, including cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, and hydroxychloroquine. In severe cases, biologics such as rituximab or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) may be considered. Additionally, patients should receive supportive care measures to manage specific organ involvement and prevent complications associated with the condition.

Apert Syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the gene FBN1 that encodes for fibrillin-1 protein. The main features include craniofacial abnormalities such as midface hypoplasia with depressed nasal bridge, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, maxillary hypoplasia, micrognathia, underdeveloped sinuses, cleft lip or palate, and ocular proptosis . Other common features include short stature, joint laxity, pectus carinatum (outward bulging of chest), scoliosis, hernias, and syndactyly of fingers and toes .

The exact cause of Aplasia cutis congenital is unknown; however, it has been associated with genetic factors such as mutations in genes involved in epidermal development (e.g., P63 gene) or environmental factors such as exposure to certain medications during pregnancy . It can also be related to chromosomal abnormalities, including trisomy 21 .
The symptoms of apparent mineralocorticoid excess (AME) include hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin activity, and increased levels of plasma aldosterone or cortisol .

The mainstay of treatment for aquagnetic pruritus is topical emollients such as petroleum jelly or mineral oil to hydrate the skin and reduce transepidermal water loss . In addition, topical corticosteroids may be used in mild cases to relieve itching . If these measures fail, systemic antihistamines can be considered .
answers_noisy: Doctors use several tests to diagnose leukemia in adults. These include a complete blood count (CBC), which measures the number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets; peripheral smear examination, which is used to identify abnormalities in circulating blood elements such as immature forms or blast cells; bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, which can help determine whether an excess of blasts is present in the bone marrow; and cytogenetic analysis, which involves examining chromosomes for numerical and structural changes . In addition, doctors may perform other diagnostic procedures depending on the type of leukemia suspected. For example, in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), genetic testing may be performed to detect specific chromosomal translocations associated with these diseases .

The condition you may be referring to is acute myeloid leukemia (AML). AML is an aggressive form of leukemia in which abnormal myeloid cells rapidly accumulate in the bone marrow and bloodstream. This can lead to pancytopenia, infections due to low white blood cell counts, bleeding from low platelet levels, and anemia caused by a lack of healthy red blood cells. Symptoms typically develop over weeks or months, but some people with AML experience symptoms within 2–3 days .

The different stages of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are classified according to the French-American-British (FAB) classification system. There are four main types of AML: M1, M2, M3, and M4/M5. M1 is characterized by hypergranularity and eosinophilia; M2 is defined by hypogranularity with minimal eosinophilia; M3 has a specific morphology called “blastic”; and M4 and M5 have increased blasts in bone marrow .

Leukemia is a type of cancer that affects the bone marrow cells. It can cause symptoms such as feeling very tired (fatigue), frequent infections, anemia, bruising easily, bleeding from the nose, and pain in the joints, bones, or kidneys .

The condition you are referring to is called myeloid dysplastic syndromes (MDS). It is a type of bone marrow disorder in which abnormal hematopoietic stem cells produce excess immature white blood cells, leading to their accumulation in the bone marrow and peripheral blood. This can result in anemia, bleeding, and increased risk of infection due to decreased numbers of normal red blood cells, platelets, and neutrophils, respectively. MDS is considered a form of leukemia but not all patients with MDS will progress to acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) .

The different stages of multiple myeloma (MM) are defined by the International Staging System (ISS), which is based on serum lactate dehydrogenase levels, β2-microglobulin levels, and cytogenetic abnormalities .

The condition you may be referring to is called myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). MDS is a type of bone marrow disorder in which abnormal hematopoietic stem cells produce an excess of immature red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets . This can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, frequent infections, bleeding, and bruising. Other possible symptoms include weight loss, appetite changes, enlarged spleen or liver, and pain in the upper left side of the abdomen. It's important to note that these symptoms could also be caused by other conditions, so it's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis.

The condition you are referring to is called chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). CML is treated with targeted therapy drugs rather than chemotherapy in most cases. These medications work by blocking signals from an abnormal protein produced by a rearrangement of chromosomes 9 and 22 known as BCR-ABL1. This helps prevent uncontrolled growth of CML stem cells.

There is ongoing research to develop more effective treatments for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Some of these include using targeted therapies such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, and immunotherapies . Additionally, there has been an increased focus on developing personalized treatment approaches based on genetic profiling of individual patients’ tumors . This allows for more precise targeting of specific molecular pathways in order to achieve better outcomes while minimizing side effects from chemotherapy.

The symptoms of leukemia may vary depending upon its type (acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML) or chronic leukemias). In general, patients with leukemia present with prolonged fever, weight loss, weakness, fatigue, abdominal discomfort, swollen spleen, anemia, bleeding, bruises, petechial rashes, jaundice, infections, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy .

The type of treatment typically depends on the specific diagnosis. For example, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in children is usually treated with chemotherapy alone, while acute myeloid leukemia (AML) may be treated with chemotherapy or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation . Other types of bone marrow disorders such as multiple myeloma and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma may also require radiation therapy or targeted therapies depending on the stage and subtype of disease . It is important to note that the specific treatment plan will depend on several factors including age, overall health status, and individual characteristics of the patient.

Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are rare cancers of mesenchymal origin. The overall 5-year survival rate for STS patients is approximately 60%, but this varies depending on several factors such as tumor size, grade, location, histologic subtype, and whether the tumor has metastasized at diagnosis .

Certain types of tumors can be caused by genetic factors, but most cases occur randomly due to environmental exposures such as smoking, dietary habits, and lifestyle choices. They usually have an irregular shape with varying shades of brown or black coloring. It is important to note that not all moles become melanoma, but changes in existing moles or the development of new ones should prompt further evaluation by a healthcare professional.

The type of symptoms that children with rhabdomyosarcoma may experience can vary depending on the location of the tumor within the body. For example, if the tumor is located in the head or neck region, it may cause difficulty swallowing, facial asymmetry, problems opening the mouth, or nasal obstruction. If the tumor is located in the abdomen or pelvis, it may cause abdominal pain, constipation, urinary difficulties, or difficulty having bowel movements. If the tumor is located in the extremities, it may cause pain, weakness, or numbness in one part of the limb. Other general symptoms such as fever, weight loss, anemia, and fatigue may also be present .

The correct term for the condition you mentioned is rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS). RMS is a type of soft tissue sarcoma that can occur in children and adults. It typically arises from skeletal muscle precursor cells and most commonly affects infants and young children .

The prognosis depends on various factors such as age at diagnosis, tumor size, location, histology, grade, and metastasis status . Soft tissue sarcomas in children have an overall 5-year survival rate of approximately 70%, but this varies widely depending on the specific type of sarcoma .

Doctors can diagnose vascular malformations through physical examination, imaging studies such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) or digital subtraction angiogram (DSA). The diagnosis may also be made during surgery. If the malformation causes symptoms, further testing may include functional studies to assess organ perfusion, such as echocardiography, electrocardiography, pulmonary function test, abdominal ultrasound, and ophthalmologic examinations.

Lymphoma is a type of cancer that affects the lymphatic system, which is responsible for fighting infections and regulating fluid levels in tissues . The most common symptoms of lymphoma include painless swelling of the lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy), weight loss, fatigue, fever, night sweats, chills, coughing, shortness of breath, abdominal discomfort, vomiting, diarrhea, chest pain, and difficulty breathing . It can also cause bone pain, weakness, numbness, and paralysis. If you experience any of these symptoms, especially if they persist over time, it's important to see your doctor so they can help determine the underlying cause and provide appropriate treatment.

Lymphoma is a type of cancer that affects cells in the immune system called lymphocytes. There are different types of lymphomas depending on where they occur in the body. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) is one type of lymphoma that occurs outside of the brain and spinal cord. The treatment of NHL typically involves chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or both . Chemotherapy can be given as oral medications or through an intravenous line at the hospital. Radiation therapy may also involve receiving daily treatments at the hospital. In some cases, surgery may also be used to remove any affected tissue. It is important to work closely with your healthcare provider to determine the best course of action for your specific situation.

Doctors use several methods to diagnose non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL). First, they may perform a physical exam to check for enlarged lymph nodes in various parts of your body. They will also ask you about any symptoms you have been experiencing, such as fever, weight loss, night sweats, fatigue, difficulty breathing, pain, or bleeding.

If someone living with HIV develops Kaposi sarcoma (KS), they may experience skin lesions such as red, purple, or brown patches or nodules on their skin. These lesions can be found anywhere on the body but often appear on the legs, feet, face, mouth, hands, and nails. Other symptoms of KS include pain associated with these lesions, difficulty breathing due to tumors in the lungs, gastrointestinal bleeding caused by tumors in the digestive tract, and swelling in the abdomen .

The conditions you may be referring to include cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCLs) such as mycosis fungoides (MF), which is a form of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma that typically presents with an itchy rash, and paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP), which can occur secondary to various types of malignancies including hematological neoplasms like CTCLs. These two conditions have some overlapping clinical features but are distinct entities.

The condition you may be referring to is called cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). CTCL is a type of cancer that affects the skin cells. It can present as different stages depending on the severity of symptoms and spread of the disease.

The prognosis for patients diagnosed with primary central nervous system (CNS) tumors depends on several factors, including the type and grade of the tumor, location within the CNS, age at diagnosis, overall health status, and treatment received .

In some advanced stages, surgical removal of affected lymph nodes may also be necessary. It is important to consult with a healthcare professional for personalized advice as treatment options vary depending on individual factors such as age, overall health status, and stage of cancer.

There are ongoing clinical trials of various treatments for pediatric non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL). These include studies evaluating novel targeted therapies such as immunotherapy agents, small molecule inhibitors, and cellular therapy approaches including chimeric antigen receptor T cells . The National Cancer Institute has several ongoing clinical trials in children with NHL that can be found at their website .
