The prognosis for patients with anal cancer depends on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, age, overall health status, presence or absence of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and whether or not they have undergone treatment. In general, early-stage anal cancers tend to have better outcomes than later stages. For example, five-year survival rates range from about 80% in Stage I to less than 15% in Stage IV. It's also important to note that while there may be some differences between men and women in terms of their risk factors for developing anal cancer, once diagnosed, both genders generally have similar prognoses.

There are several things you can do to reduce your risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC) later in life. Firstly, maintaining a healthy body weight is important as obesity increases the risk of CRC by 60%. Secondly, eating plenty of fruits and vegetables may help lower this risk. Thirdly, limiting alcohol consumption reduces the risk of CRC. Fourthly, smoking cessation decreases the risk of CRC. Lastly, screening for CRC using stool-based tests such as fecal occult blood test (FOBT), flexible sigmoidoscopy, or colonoscopy can detect polyps early which helps treat them before they become cancerous .

The symptoms that may indicate a serious problem in the abdomen include severe or persistent pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea with blood or mucus, difficulty passing gas, dizziness, fainting, swelling, redness, or tenderness in the belly area, and changes in urination habits. If you experience any of these symptoms, it's important to seek immediate medical attention as they could be signs of appendicitis, bowel obstruction, pancreatitis, gastrointestinal bleeding, kidney stones, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cyst rupture, or other potentially life-threatening conditions.

Thymomas and thymic carcinomas are both tumors that originate from epithelial cells in the thymus gland, but they differ in their histological features and clinical behavior. Thymomas are typically slow-growing and can be divided into five subtypes (A, AB, B1, B2, and B3) based on their cellular morphology and immunohistochemical characteristics . Type A thymomas have a high degree of heterogeneity, with varying degrees of spindle cells, lymphocytes, polygonal cells, and multinucleated giant cells. Type AB thymomas resemble type A thymomas but contain areas of acinar or papillary architecture. Type B1 thymomas consist mainly of polygonal cells arranged in an acinar pattern, while type B2 thymomas are composed of polygonal cells with round nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, which form solid nests without papillary structures. Type B3 thymomas are characterized by large polygonal cells with abundant clear to pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, which may appear foamy.

Currently, there are several ongoing clinical trials that aim to improve outcomes for patients with advanced thymic carcinomas (TCs). These include phase II single-arm trials evaluating the efficacy of chemotherapy regimens such as cisplatin plus gemcitabine 15 , carboplatin plus paclitaxel 16 , and irinotecan plus fluorouracil 17 . Other trials are investigating targeted therapies such as pembrolizumab 18 , nivolumab 19 , and everolimus 20 .

The prognosis of UC depends on various factors such as tumor stage, grade, location, presence or absence of lymph node metastasis, recurrence rate, and overall survival. In general, patients with low-grade nonmuscle invasive bladder cancer have a good prognosis, while those with high-risk features such as high-grade disease, multifocality, concurrent carcinoma in situ, and recurrent disease may be at risk for progression to muscle-invasive disease and metastases . Patients diagnosed with muscle-invasive bladder cancer have a poorer prognosis than those with superficial bladder cancer. Approximately 50% of patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer develop distant metastatic disease within five years of treatment, despite initial complete resection and adjuvant chemotherapy .

It is important for women to be aware of any unusual changes in their menstrual cycle, such as heavy periods with clots, irregular cycles, or no period at all. Women should also look out for signs of vaginal discharge, which can range from white or clear to yellowish-green or gray. If there is a foul odor coming from the vagina, this could indicate bacterial infection. Pain during urination may suggest a urinary tract infection (UTI). Any redness, swelling, or pain in the vulva area should be noted. A sore or rash on the labia or inside the vagina may indicate herpes or another sexually transmitted disease. Bleeding between periods or after sexual intercourse may be a sign of endometriosis or cervical cancer. Persistent lower back pain could be caused by ovarian cancer.

Vulvar cancer is treated with surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy or combination of these modalities depending upon stage at presentation. For early-stage disease involving the labia majora alone, radical local excision may be curative; however, more advanced disease requires additional treatment such as pelvic lymph node dissection or adjuvant radiotherapy. In patients with locally advanced tumors not amenable to surgical resection, concurrent chemoradiation therapy is indicated. Chemotherapy regimens include platinum-based agents combined with other drugs such as topotecan, paclitaxel, docetaxel, etc.

An aberrant coronary artery is when one or more of the major coronary arteries (left main, left anterior descending, right coronary artery, circumflex) originate from the opposite sinus of Valsalva instead of their normal position in the aortic root . This can lead to compression of the free wall of the heart during diastole, which may cause angina, myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, or sudden cardiac death . The treatment for this condition depends on the severity of symptoms and whether there are other underlying conditions present. In some cases, medications such as beta-blockers, nitrates, or antiplatelet agents may be prescribed to manage symptoms. If these treatments are not effective, revascularization procedures such as bypass surgery or percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty with stent placement may be necessary .

A physician may order stool tests such as fecal elastase-1 (FE-1), calprotectin, or microscopic examination to assess for steatorrhea, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) or other causes of diarrhea. In addition, they may also request blood tests including serum albumin, folate, vitamin B12, iron studies, total cholesterol, triglycerides, calcium, alkaline phosphatase, amylase, lipase, thyroid function test, and liver function test to evaluate nutrient deficiencies, pancreatic insufficiency, biliary obstruction, celiac disease, or other systemic diseases that can cause malabsorption. An upper endoscopy is recommended if there is suspicion of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).

The most common symptom in infants born with a congenital absence of the distal tibia is painless swelling or deformity at the site where the foot should be located. Other possible signs include asymmetry of the lower limbs, abnormalities in the positioning of the feet during fetal ultrasound scans, and shortening of one leg compared to the other.

Patients with conditions that affect digestion may experience various gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms such as diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, bloating or cramps, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, fatigue, weight loss, heartburn, indigestion, belching, gas, and flatulence.

There are several possible treatment options available depending on the cause of the extra bone or bump in the foot arch. If it is due to osteochondroma (the most common benign tumor of bone), surgical excision may be recommended if symptoms persist despite conservative treatments such as rest, ice, anti-inflammatory medications, orthotics, and physical therapy. Other potential treatment options include radiofrequency ablation, cryoablation, arthroscopic synovectomy, and open synovectomy. However, if the extra bone or bump is caused by a stress fracture, nonoperative management with weight bearing restriction and activity modification may be sufficient. It is important to consult with a healthcare provider for proper diagnosis and appropriate treatment plan.

Dysphagia is characterized by difficulty or discomfort during swallowing. In addition to food getting stuck while swallowing (known as odynophagia), other common symptoms include pain with swallowing, sensation of something sticking into the throat, coughing or choking after eating, feeling of aspiration or “wet” voice or breathing, sensations of the food going down the wrong way (e.g., into the larynx or lungs instead of esophagus). Other associated symptoms may be weight loss, poor nutrition, dehydration, malnutrition, halitosis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Skeletal dysplasias refer to a group of congenital disorders characterized by abnormalities in bone growth or development. These conditions can affect the shape, size, proportion, or mineralization of bones throughout the body. They may be inherited as autosomal dominant, recessive, X-linked, or mitochondrial traits .

The condition you are referring to is called congenital arthrogryposis (CA). It can be caused by genetic factors or environmental conditions during pregnancy. Genetic forms of CA are usually dominant or recessive traits that run in families. Environmental causes include maternal illnesses such as diabetes mellitus, certain medications taken during pregnancy, and intrauterine infection.

Short limb dwarfism is characterized by proportional shortening of both upper and lower extremities with normal trunk length and head size. The most common feature is rhizomelia, which involves proximal shortening of the long bones in the arms or legs. Other symptoms may include joint contractures, scoliosis, pectus carinatum (chest deformity), and facial dysmorphic features such as micrognathia (small jaw) and midface hypoplasia.

The typical clinical features of patients with dysmorphic syndrome and severe immunodeficiency include recurrent respiratory tract infections such as pneumonia or bronchitis, otitis media, sinusitis, skin abscesses, sepsis, diarrhea, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive, developmental delay, short stature, microcephaly, facial asymmetry, hypertelorism, epicanthus, broad nasal bridge, thin upper lip, retrognathia, and hypotonia .

This condition is known as acquired aplastic anemia (AA). It occurs due to bone marrow failure that leads to decreased production of blood cells. The exact cause of AA remains unknown but may be linked to viral infections or exposure to certain chemicals. Patients with AA often experience symptoms such as weakness, pale skin, easy bruising, and bleeding. Diagnosis involves a physical examination, blood tests, and bone marrow aspiration. Treatment typically includes hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Patients who experience these symptoms may be suffering from a drug reaction known as DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms). This is an allergic reaction that can occur within 2 weeks of starting a new medication. It typically resolves once the offending agent is discontinued.

The typical symptoms of psoriasis include red, scaly patches with silvery-white scales that may be painful to touch. These lesions can occur anywhere on the body but most commonly appear on the scalp, ears, elbows, knees, and trunk. Itching is often associated with psoriatic skin lesions. Psoriasis can also manifest as small, white spots resembling dandruff flakes on the surface of the tongue (known as “psoraliasis guttata”).

The rare bone disorder that causes abnormality in limbs during fetal development is called congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT). It can also be referred to as congenital tibial dyschondrodysplasia. CPT is not a simple growth disorder but rather an uncommon genetic disease that affects one in 50,000 live births worldwide .

Congenital Osteochondrodysplasia (COCD) is a rare genetic disorder that affects bone and cartilage formation during embryonic development. It can result from mutations in genes involved in chondrocyte differentiation or maturation, leading to defective endochondral ossification. The most common clinical features of COCD include short stature, disproportionate limb length, joint laxity, and skeletal deformities such as scoliosis and kyphosis. In addition, patients may also exhibit craniofacial anomalies, including microcephaly, midface hypoplasia, and dental malocclusion. Hand abnormalities such as brachydactyly, syndactyly, and camptodactyly have been reported in some cases. Urinary tract dysfunction has not been described as part of the disease spectrum; however, it could be related to other associated conditions such as spinal cord compression.

Yes, this condition is known as leukocytoclastic vasculitis or small vessel vasculitis. It can be caused by viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV) and parvovirus B19, bacterial infections such as Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus, autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), drug reactions, and other conditions. The symptoms of leukocytoclastic vasculitis typically include sudden onset of palpable purpuric lesions on the extremities, face, trunk, and mucous membranes. Other common symptoms may include fever, arthralgia, myalgias, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and fatigue. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is characterized by inflammation of the small vessels leading to endothelial damage, which causes extravasation of fibrinogen and plasma proteins into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, resulting in the formation of palpable purpuric nodules .

Rare chemical poisoning symptoms can also include seizures, coma, respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias or arrest, hypothermia, hyperthermia, diarrhea, dermatitis, bronchospasm, pneumonitis, renal failure, liver damage, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria, and death depending on the type of substance ingested.

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is an acute inflammatory condition of both lungs characterized by increased permeability of alveolar capillaries leading to pulmonary edema and hypoxemia . It can be caused by various factors such as pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, blood transfusion, drowning, smoke inhalation, or drug overdose . The main difference between ARDS and other forms of breathing failure is that patients with ARDS have severe hypoxemia due to low lung compliance and high airway resistance . Other signs include tachypnea, use of accessory muscles for breathing, cyanosis, and crackles on auscultation .

The jaw/gum growth you described could be an ameloblastoma, which is a benign (noncancerous) tumor that develops in the jawbone. It can occur at any age but most commonly affects young adults between 20 and 40 years old. Ameloblastomas usually do not cause pain unless they grow very large or become infected. They typically appear as slow-growing swellings under the gums near the front of the lower jaw. If left untreated, these lesions may continue to enlarge and potentially damage surrounding teeth and bone structures.

There are several diagnostic procedures available for detection of abnormalities in the small bowel including capsule endoscopy, double balloon enteroscopy (DBE), push enteroscopy, single-balloon enteroscopy, and surgical enteroscopy. Capsule endoscopy is considered first line investigation due to its noninvasive nature. DBE is used when there is bleeding or if previous endoscopies were negative. Push enteroscopy can be performed as an outpatient procedure but requires general anaesthesia for deep insertion into the small bowel. Surgical enteroscopy may also be required in some cases.

The condition you may be referring to is mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes (MELAS) syndrome. MELAS syndrome is caused by mutations in the mtDNA gene that encodes tRNALysine 1 (MT-TL1). It can present with various clinical features such as headaches, vomiting, seizures, strokes, dementia, myocardial infarction, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, and other neurological disorders. Other common symptoms include cognitive impairments, muscle weakness, vision loss, hearing loss, gastrointestinal problems, and cardiac disease. These symptoms usually begin during childhood or adolescence but can also occur later in life.

Yes, there is an inherited component in developing firm, tender nodules beneath the skin. The condition of multiple familial trichodiscomas (MFT) is characterized by small, flesh-colored or slightly pink papules that develop into firm dome-shaped nodules under the skin. These lesions typically appear during childhood and can affect any part of the body but most commonly occur on the face, neck, scalp, back, and chest. MFT is caused by mutations in the gene TP63, which encodes for p63 protein. P63 plays a crucial role in cell differentiation and proliferation, particularly in epithelial tissues such as the skin. Mutations in this gene lead to abnormal keratinocyte development, resulting in the formation of these characteristic skin nodules.

Scoliosis refers to an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine that can occur at any age but is more common during childhood and adolescence. It affects both boys and girls with equal frequency and typically presents as either idiopathic or neuromuscular. Idiopathic scoliosis has no known cause while neuromuscular scoliosis may be associated with cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, spina bifida, poliomyelitis, or other neurological conditions. The exact pathogenesis of scoliosis remains unknown; however, it appears to involve genetic factors, biomechanics, growth patterns, and connective tissue disorders.

An overgrowing endocrine tumor can cause various symptoms depending on which gland is affected. For example, if it affects the thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism), one may experience rapid heartbeat, sweating, heat intolerance, anxiety, tremors, weakness, fatigue, and weight loss. If it affects the adrenal glands (Cushing's syndrome), one may have high blood pressure, mood swings, weight gain in the face, neck, and trunk, thin skin, purple stains on the skin, osteoporosis, muscle weakness, and irregular menstruation. If it affects the pancreas (hyperparathyroidism), one may have stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, kidney stones, bone pain, tiredness, and weakness. If it affects the pituitary gland (acromegaly), one may have enlarged hands and feet, headache, vision problems, excessive sweating, sleep apnea, and impotence. These are just some examples, but there could be other symptoms as well. It is important for individuals experiencing these symptoms to consult with their healthcare provider to determine the underlying cause and receive appropriate treatment.

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is one of the most common chronic diseases in childhood, affecting 1 out of every 1000 children worldwide . JIA can present with different symptoms depending upon its subtype; however, there are some general signs that may indicate the presence of this condition. The most common symptom of JIA is pain or swelling in one or more joints which persists for at least six weeks without any apparent cause. This pain and swelling usually occur in multiple joints over time. Other symptoms include limited range of motion, stiffness lasting longer than an hour after waking up, fatigue, fever, rash, and loss of appetite .

The yellowish spot or "flecks" that may be observed in the central retina of elderly individuals is known as drusen . Drusen can appear as small white dots or larger yellow-white patches and typically do not cause any vision problems unless they grow in size or number. They occur due to an accumulation of waste products from aging cells within the macula region of the eye. While their presence alone does not necessarily indicate disease, it could serve as an early sign of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), which is one of the leading causes of blindness among older adults worldwide.

Platelet deficiencies can be either congenital or acquired conditions. Congenital platelet disorders are caused by genetic mutations that affect platelet production or function. These include isolated quantitative platelet defects (such as thrombocytopenia) and qualitative platelet defects (such as Glanzmann's thrombasthenia). Acquired platelet deficiencies may occur due to certain medications, infections, immune-mediated diseases, bone marrow failure, or nutritional deficiencies.

Congenital malformation involving abnormal development of organs in the abdominal cavity may cause various symptoms such as abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, constipation or diarrhea, hematochezia, melena, palpable mass, jaundice, dyspepsia, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), anemia, fever, chills, etc.

The second type of rare pediatric brain-body disorder that presents similarly to an infectious disease at birth but is not caused by an actual infection is called Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy with Lactic Acidosis and Stroke-like episodes (MELAS).

The typical symptoms of type IV congenital disorder include intellectual disability, seizures, hypotonia or hypertonia, developmental delay, dysmorphic features, facial asymmetry, microcephaly, macrocephaly, cleft palate, hearing loss, vision impairment, cardiac defects, renal anomalies, skeletal abnormalities, gastrointestinal problems, and feeding difficulties.

Typical symptoms of acute kidney injury (AKI) include decreased urine output, edema, fatigue or weakness, shortness of breath, hypertension, oliguria, anemia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, seizures, confusion, and skin discoloration. These symptoms may lead to further complications such as electrolyte imbalances, fluid overload, cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, uremic encephalopathy, and death if left untreated.

People with microcephaly may exhibit developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, muscle weakness, vision problems, hearing loss, and other neurological issues. Growth retardation can manifest as short stature or weight gain compared to peers of similar age and sex. Poor dental enamel is characterized by hypoplastic teeth that appear chalky white without any signs or symptoms unless accompanied by caries or infection. Diabetes mellitus presents with polyuria (frequent urination), polydipsia (increased thirst), nocturia (waking up at night to urinate), increased appetite, fatigue, blurred vision, slow healing wounds, recurrent infections, and unexplained weight loss.

The appropriate management of patients with an inherited growth disorder characterized by abnormalities in skeletal development, such as dwarfism, facial dysmorphism, and limb deformity, depends on the specific diagnosis. In general, it involves multidisciplinary care that addresses both physical and psychosocial needs throughout childhood and into adulthood. Treatment may include pharmacological therapy to stimulate linear growth (e.g., human growth hormone), surgical procedures to correct skeletal anomalies or other associated conditions, and rehabilitation services to improve mobility and function. Psychological support and counseling may also be necessary to help individuals cope with the emotional and social effects of their condition. It is important to note that each patient's treatment plan should be tailored to their individual needs and circumstances, taking into account the severity of their symptoms, underlying genetic cause, and potential comorbidities.

Patients with alopecia totalis typically present with complete loss of scalp hair as well as body hair, eyebrows, eyelashes, and beard (if applicable). They may also experience pruritus and burning sensation in the affected areas. Patchy hair loss, worsening eyesight, and abnormal growth patterns are not common symptoms associated with alopecia totalis.

Rapid alopecia is hair loss that occurs over a short period of time (typically less than 6 months). It can be caused by several factors including certain medications such as chemotherapy drugs used to treat cancer or anticoagulants; hormonal changes during pregnancy or menopause; autoimmune conditions like lupus; scalp infections; nutrient deficiencies; and stressful life events.

The condition is known as Cockayne syndrome (CS). It is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects multiple organ systems including skin, brain, eyes, skeleton, and endocrine system. CS can present at birth or develop during childhood. Common features of CS include microcephaly, growth retardation, intellectual disability, hearing loss, cataracts, photosensitivity, and alopecia. Other less common manifestations may include diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, seizures, cardiac defects, renal failure, and hematological abnormalities.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects 1 in every 2000 people worldwide . It is caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene, which encodes AAT protein, resulting in decreased levels of functional AAT in plasma and tissues . The most common phenotypes associated with AAT deficiency include PI*SZ, PI*SS, and PI*ZZ genotype variants .

Yes, certain types of anemia can be inherited from parents to their children. Hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease (SCD) and thalassemias are hereditary disorders caused by mutations in genes encoding proteins involved in oxygen transport or hemoglobin synthesis . SCD is caused by a single base substitution in exon 1 of the gene for beta globin (HBB), resulting in production of abnormal HbS molecules with altered properties . Thalassemias result from deletions or point mutations in one or more of the alpha-globin (HBA) or beta-globin (HBB) genes , leading to decreased levels of normal adult hemoglobin (HbA). These conditions often present early in life but may also manifest later in adulthood depending upon the severity of the genetic defects.

A newborn baby presenting with pulmonary airway disease may show signs of respiratory distress such as difficulty breathing, rapid or labored breathing, wheezing, coughing, nasal flaring, cyanosis (blue coloration) around lips and nails, grunting, chest retractions, poor feeding, and low oxygen saturation levels.

Yes, this is known as amelogenesis imperfecta (AI). AI refers to a group of rare genetic disorders characterized by abnormal tooth development resulting in defective formation or calcification of enamel . The most common form of AI is hypoplastic type which presents with thin or absent enamel that can be yellowish-brown in color. Other types of AI present with other dental anomalies such as small teeth, taurodontism, and dentin dysplasia .

Congenital hypoplasia of tooth enamel is caused by abnormal amelogenesis during tooth development. It presents as white or brownish-white opacities with normal dentin beneath the affected enamel. The condition may affect one or more teeth and usually does not cause any pain unless associated with caries. Treatment options depend on the severity of the condition and include fluoride therapy to prevent dental caries, restorative procedures such as composite resins, porcelain veneers, or crowns, and cosmetic treatments such as microabrasion, bleaching, and laser treatment .

Children with OI may present with blue sclerae, bone deformities such as bowing of long bones, short stature, dentinogenesis imperfecta (teeth that appear thin or chalky), hearing loss, joint hyperlaxity, and skull deformities. They can also have recurrent fractures, fatigue easily, bruise easily, and have poor growth rates .

Fetal knot is an extremely rare condition that occurs when one or both of the umbilical cords wraps around the neck of the fetus, forming a noose-like structure known as a "knot." The exact cause of this phenomenon remains unknown; however, it has been linked to various factors such as abnormal placental implantation, multiple births, advanced maternal age, polyhydramnios, oligohydramnios, macrosomia, and twin reversed arterial perfusion sequence (TRAP) sequence. It can lead to reduced blood flow to the fetal brain, resulting in hypoxic stress, which may result in intrauterine death if not detected early and managed appropriately.

The symptoms you describe may be indicative of dry eye syndrome (DES). DES is a common condition that can cause discomfort, blurred vision, or even temporary loss of vision. It occurs when your tears aren’t able to keep the surface of your eyes sufficiently moist. This could be due to reduced production of tears by your lacrimal glands, or because of evaporation of tears from the surface of your eyes before they can be replenished.

Newborns with low muscle tone may present with poor sucking ability, difficulty feeding, weak cry, hypotonia (floppy limbs), decreased movement, abnormal reflexes, delayed motor development milestones, and respiratory distress.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. There is no definitive test for ALS diagnosis; however, doctors will usually conduct several tests to rule out other possible causes of symptoms. The most common initial test is an electromyography (EMG), which measures electrical activity in muscles during rest or contraction. If EMG results are inconclusive, a spine MRI may be ordered to check for any abnormalities in the motor neurons. Other tests such as blood tests, nerve conduction studies, and muscle biopsies may also be recommended depending on the individual's specific symptoms and medical history. It is important to note that while these tests can help with diagnosis, they cannot confirm whether a person has ALS. Ultimately, a combination of clinical evaluation, family history, and laboratory findings must be considered before making a final diagnosis.

Based on the information provided in the image, it appears that this is a diffuse astrocytic glioma with high-grade characteristics. It cannot be determined whether this is GBM without further testing such as immunohistochemistry staining for IDH1 mutation status.

Congenital myopathies (CMs) refer to a group of rare genetic disorders that affect muscle tissue in infants at birth or during early childhood . These conditions can cause weakness, hypotonia, and abnormal movement patterns. The exact prevalence of CMs remains unknown but it has been estimated to be between 1 in 50,000 and 1 in 200,000 live births worldwide .

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) refers to a group of autosomal recessive genetic disorders caused by mutations in genes involved in cortisol synthesis in the adrenal gland . The most common form of CAH is 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which accounts for approximately 90%–95% of all cases . This condition results from an enzyme defect that impairs the conversion of pregnenolone into progesterone and testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT), leading to excessive production of steroid precursors such as 17α-OH progesterone and androgens .

Fetal brain malformations can be diagnosed prenatally through ultrasound scans or MRI imaging. The severity of these conditions varies depending on the type of anomaly present. Microcephaly is characterized by an abnormally small head due to underdevelopment of the brain tissue. This condition may result in developmental delays, intellectual disabilities, seizures, and other neurological issues.

Based on the information provided, it is possible that your child may be experiencing symptoms associated with Angelman syndrome (AS). AS is a rare neurogenetic disorder caused by the loss of function in genes located on chromosome 15q11-q13 . The most common features of AS include developmental delay, intellectual disability, speech impairment, movement disorders such as ataxia and chorea, epilepsy, sleep disturbances, and happy affect . It can also present with behavioral characteristics including socialization deficits, hyperactivity, and hypersensitivity to sensory stimuli .

Cerebrovascular malformations (CVM) can cause various neurological symptoms such as headaches, seizures, cognitive impairment, focal deficits, and psychiatric disorders. These symptoms may appear at any age but are more common in adults than children.

The baby's eyes may appear closed or partially closed with no visible pupils. There may be signs of irritation around the eyes such as redness, swelling, tearing, discharge, and crusting. Depending on the severity of the condition, there could also be decreased vision or complete blindness.

An impacted tooth is one that has failed to erupt into its normal position in the mouth due to physical interference by adjacent structures or other teeth. This can lead to overcrowding of the dental arch, malocclusion, and even infection in some cases. It is important for both oral health and overall well-being to have any impacted teeth removed as soon as possible.

The condition of being born without fingernails or toenails is known as anonychia. This can be caused by genetic factors such as ectodermal dysplasia or environmental factors like fetal alcohol syndrome. In some cases, it may also result from trauma during pregnancy. Without nails, there is no protection for the underlying nail bed, which can lead to fragile skin and easy tearing. There may also be abnormalities in other parts of the body, including hair, teeth, sweat glands, and bones. Treatment options include protective dressings and bandages, as well as cosmetic procedures such as tattooing or permanent makeup.

A child born with anophthalmia (without eyes) or microphthalmia (smaller than average sized eyes), may also experience vision impairment or blindness depending on the severity of their eye malformation. They may require corrective surgeries to reconstruct their eyelids and facial structures as they age. Children born with congenital limb deficiencies such as amelia (complete absence of one or more limbs) or symbrachydactyly (limbs that are shortened with missing digits) may develop musculoskeletal problems including pain, limited range of motion in joints, and difficulty walking. These children will likely need orthopedic treatments such as prosthetics, braces, and surgery throughout childhood and into adulthood.

Congenital coagulation disorders are caused by inherited errors of blood clotting factor synthesis or function that result in increased or decreased levels of specific proteins involved in hemostasis . These diseases may present as mild to severe hemorrhages or thromboses depending upon the type of defect. The most commonly encountered coagulation disorders include von Willebrand disease (VWD), Hemophilia A & B, Factor V deficiency, Factor VII deficiency, Factor VIII deficiency, Factor IX deficiency, Factor X deficiency, Factor XI deficiency, Factor XII deficiency, Factor XIII deficiency, Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, afibrinogenemia, dysfibrinogenemia, hypofibrinogenemia, and platelet qualitative disorder .

Myositis refers to inflammation of skeletal muscles that can be caused by various factors such as autoimmune diseases, viruses, drugs, or toxins. The most common form of myositis is polymyositis (PM), which affects multiple muscle groups, typically proximal limb girdle muscles. Treatment options vary depending on the underlying cause but may include corticosteroids, immunomodulatory agents, intravenous immune globulin, plasmapheresis, or rituximab .

Craniosynostosis is characterized by abnormal fusion of one or more sutures of the skull leading to premature closure of the calvarial suture(s). The most common symptom of craniosynostosis is an asymmetric head shape with compensatory growth in the direction opposite to the restricted expansion (e.g., plagiocephaly), but it can also be detected through subtle changes in the shape of the occipital region (i.e., trigonocephaly) or through early-onset frontal bossing (i.e., acrocephaly). Other signs may include midface retrusion, exorbitism, hypertelorism, facial asymmetry, and macrocephaly .

Congenital skin patches can be caused by genetic factors or environmental exposures during pregnancy. Genetic factors include mutations in genes involved in melanocyte development or function, such as Pmel17, KIT, MITF, SLC45A2, OCA2, TYR, TRP-1, and TRP-2. Environmental exposures during pregnancy may also cause these types of birthmarks, including UV light exposure, certain medications, and some chemicals.

Hypernatremia is characterized by high sodium levels in the blood (serum) that can be caused either by excessive fluid loss or by an increase in antidiuretic hormone production. The most common cause of hypernatremia is dehydration from diarrhea, vomiting, fever, diabetes insipidus, or prolonged fasting . Symptoms may include dry mouth, fatigue, lethargy, confusion, irritability, muscle weakness, twitching, seizures, nausea, headache, dizziness, cramps, constipation, oliguria, polyuria, and weight loss .

The itchy sensation you experience after taking a bath could be caused by several factors such as dryness of the skin due to loss of moisture during bathing or exposure to irritants in water (e.g., chlorine). It can also be due to certain medications that cause photosensitivity when exposed to sunlight. Other possible causes include allergic reactions to soaps, detergents, shampoos, or other products used for personal hygiene.
reference_answers: Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose adult ALL. The following tests and procedures may be used: - Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as infection or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patient's health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken. - Complete blood count (CBC) with differential : A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following: - The number of red blood cells and platelets. - The number and type of white blood cells. - The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells. - The portion of the blood sample made up of red blood cells. - Blood chemistry studies : A procedure in which a blood sample is checked to measure the amounts of certain substances released into the blood by organs and tissues in the body. An unusual (higher or lower than normal) amount of a substance can be a sign of disease. - Peripheral blood smear : A procedure in which a sample of blood is checked for blast cells, the number and kinds of white blood cells, the number of platelets, and changes in the shape of blood cells. - Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy : The removal of bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone or breastbone. A pathologist views the bone marrow, blood, and bone under a microscope to look for abnormal cells. The following tests may be done on the samples of blood or bone marrow tissue that are removed: - Cytogenetic analysis: A laboratory test in which the cells in a sample of blood or bone marrow are looked at under a microscope to find out if there are certain changes in the chromosomes of lymphocytes. For example, in Philadelphia chromosome positive ALL, part of one chromosome switches places with part of another chromosome. This is called the Philadelphia chromosome. - Immunophenotyping : A process used to identify cells, based on the types of antigens or markers on the surface of the cell. This process is used to diagnose the subtype of ALL by comparing the cancer cells to normal cells of the immune system. For example, a cytochemistry study may test the cells in a sample of tissue using chemicals (dyes) to look for certain changes in the sample. A chemical may cause a color change in one type of leukemia cell but not in another type of leukemia cell.

Key Points - Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes abnormal myeloblasts (a type of white blood cell), red blood cells, or platelets. - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - There are different subtypes of AML. - Smoking, previous chemotherapy treatment, and exposure to radiation may affect the risk of adult AML. - Signs and symptoms of adult AML include fever, feeling tired, and easy bruising or bleeding. - Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose adult AML. - Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes abnormal myeloblasts (a type of white blood cell), red blood cells, or platelets. Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. This type of cancer usually gets worse quickly if it is not treated. It is the most common type of acute leukemia in adults. AML is also called acute myelogenous leukemia, acute myeloblastic leukemia, acute granulocytic leukemia, and acute nonlymphocytic leukemia. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the bone marrow makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a white blood cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - White blood cells that fight infection and disease. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. In AML, the myeloid stem cells usually become a type of immature white blood cell called myeloblasts (or myeloid blasts). The myeloblasts in AML are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells. Sometimes in AML, too many stem cells become abnormal red blood cells or platelets. These abnormal white blood cells, red blood cells, or platelets are also called leukemia cells or blasts. Leukemia cells can build up in the bone marrow and blood so there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. When this happens, infection, anemia, or easy bleeding may occur. The leukemia cells can spread outside the blood to other parts of the body, including the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), skin, and gums. This summary is about adult AML. See the following PDQ summaries for information about other types of leukemia: - Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia/Other Myeloid Malignancies Treatment - Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia Treatment - Adult Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia Treatment - Hairy Cell Leukemia Treatment There are different subtypes of AML. Most AML subtypes are based on how mature (developed) the cancer cells are at the time of diagnosis and how different they are from normal cells. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a subtype of AML that occurs when parts of two genes stick together. APL usually occurs in middle-aged adults. Signs of APL may include both bleeding and forming blood clots.

Key Points - Once adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. - There is no standard staging system for adult AML. Once adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. The extent or spread of cancer is usually described as stages. In adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the subtype of AML and whether the leukemia has spread outside the blood and bone marrow are used instead of the stage to plan treatment. The following tests and procedures may be used to determine if the leukemia has spread: - Lumbar puncture : A procedure used to collect a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the spinal column. This is done by placing a needle between two bones in the spine and into the CSF around the spinal cord and removing a sample of the fluid. The sample of CSF is checked under a microscope for signs that leukemia cells have spread to the brain and spinal cord. This procedure is also called an LP or spinal tap. - CT scan (CAT scan): A procedure that makes a series of detailed pictures of the abdomen, taken from different angles. The pictures are made by a computer linked to an x-ray machine. A dye may be injected into a vein or swallowed to help the organs or tissues show up more clearly. This procedure is also called computed tomography, computerized tomography, or computerized axial tomography. There is no standard staging system for adult AML. The disease is described as untreated, in remission, or recurrent. Untreated adult AML In untreated adult AML, the disease is newly diagnosed. It has not been treated except to relieve signs and symptoms such as fever, bleeding, or pain, and the following are true: - The complete blood count is abnormal. - At least 20% of the cells in the bone marrow are blasts (leukemia cells). - There are signs or symptoms of leukemia. Adult AML in remission In adult AML in remission, the disease has been treated and the following are true: - The complete blood count is normal. - Less than 5% of the cells in the bone marrow are blasts (leukemia cells). - There are no signs or symptoms of leukemia in the brain and spinal cord or elsewhere in the body. Recurrent Adult AML Recurrent AML is cancer that has recurred (come back) after it has been treated. The AML may come back in the blood or bone marrow.

Signs and symptoms of chronic lymphocytic leukemia include swollen lymph nodes and tiredness. Usually CLL does not cause any signs or symptoms and is found during a routine blood test. Signs and symptoms may be caused by CLL or by other conditions. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following: - Painless swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin. - Feeling very tired. - Pain or fullness below the ribs. - Fever and infection. - Weight loss for no known reason.

Key Points - Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a disease in which the bone marrow makes too many white blood cells. - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - Signs and symptoms of chronic myelogenous leukemia include fever, night sweats, and tiredness. - Most people with CML have a gene mutation (change) called the Philadelphia chromosome. - Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose chronic myelogenous leukemia. - Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a disease in which the bone marrow makes too many white blood cells. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (also called CML or chronic granulocytic leukemia) is a slowly progressing blood and bone marrow disease that usually occurs during or after middle age, and rarely occurs in children. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the bone marrow makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a white blood cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. - Granulocytes (white blood cells) that fight infection and disease. In CML, too many blood stem cells become a type of white blood cell called granulocytes. These granulocytes are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells. They are also called leukemia cells. The leukemia cells can build up in the blood and bone marrow so there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. When this happens, infection, anemia, or easy bleeding may occur. This summary is about chronic myelogenous leukemia. See the following PDQ summaries for more information about leukemia: - Adult Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia Treatment - Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia/Other Myeloid Malignancies Treatment - Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia Treatment - Hairy Cell Leukemia Treatment

Key Points - After chronic myelogenous leukemia has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread. - Chronic myelogenous leukemia has 3 phases. - Chronic phase - Accelerated phase - Blastic phase After chronic myelogenous leukemia has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread. Staging is the process used to find out how far the cancer has spread. There is no standard staging system for chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). Instead, the disease is classified by phase: chronic phase, accelerated phase, or blastic phase. It is important to know the phase in order to plan treatment. The information from tests and procedures done to detect (find) and diagnose chronic myelogenous leukemia is also used to plan treatment. Chronic myelogenous leukemia has 3 phases. As the amount of blast cells increases in the blood and bone marrow, there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. This may result in infections, anemia, and easy bleeding, as well as bone pain and pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs on the left side. The number of blast cells in the blood and bone marrow and the severity of signs or symptoms determine the phase of the disease. Chronic phase In chronic phase CML, fewer than 10% of the cells in the blood and bone marrow are blast cells. Accelerated phase In accelerated phase CML, 10% to 19% of the cells in the blood and bone marrow are blast cells. Blastic phase In blastic phase CML, 20% or more of the cells in the blood or bone marrow are blast cells. When tiredness, fever, and an enlarged spleen occur during the blastic phase, it is called blast crisis.

Signs and symptoms of hairy cell leukemia include infections, tiredness, and pain below the ribs. These and other signs and symptoms may be caused by hairy cell leukemia or by other conditions. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following: - Weakness or feeling tired. - Fever or frequent infections. - Easy bruising or bleeding. - Shortness of breath. - Weight loss for no known reason. - Pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs. - Painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin.

Key Points - There are different types of treatment for patients with hairy cell leukemia. - Five types of standard treatment are used: - Watchful waiting - Chemotherapy - Biologic therapy - Surgery - Targeted therapy - New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials. - Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. - Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. - Follow-up tests may be needed. There are different types of treatment for patients with hairy cell leukemia. Different types of treatment are available for patients with hairy cell leukemia. Some treatments are standard (the currently used treatment), and some are being tested in clinical trials. A treatment clinical trial is a research study meant to help improve current treatments or obtain information on new treatments for patients with cancer. When clinical trials show that a new treatment is better than the standard treatment, the new treatment may become the standard treatment. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. Some clinical trials are open only to patients who have not started treatment. Five types of standard treatment are used: Watchful waiting Watchful waiting is closely monitoring a patient's condition, without giving any treatment until signs or symptoms appear or change. Chemotherapy Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells or by stopping them from dividing. When chemotherapy is taken by mouth or injected into a vein or muscle, the drugs enter the bloodstream and can reach cancer cells throughout the body (systemic chemotherapy). When chemotherapy is placed directly into the cerebrospinal fluid, an organ, or a body cavity such as the abdomen, the drugs mainly affect cancer cells in those areas (regional chemotherapy). The way the chemotherapy is given depends on the type and stage of the cancer being treated. Cladribine and pentostatin are anticancer drugs commonly used to treat hairy cell leukemia. These drugs may increase the risk of other types of cancer, especially Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Long-term follow up for second cancers is very important. Biologic therapy Biologic therapy is a cancer treatment that uses the patients immune system to fight cancer. Substances made by the body or made in a laboratory are used to boost, direct, or restore the bodys natural defenses against cancer. This type of cancer treatment is also called biotherapy or immunotherapy. Interferon alfa is a biologic agent commonly used to treat hairy cell leukemia. See Drugs Approved for Hairy Cell Leukemia for more information. Surgery Splenectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the spleen. Targeted therapy Targeted therapy is a treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells without harming normal cells. Monoclonal antibody therapy is a type of targeted therapy used to treat hairy cell leukemia. Monoclonal antibody therapy uses antibodies made in the laboratory from a single type of immune system cell. These antibodies can identify substances on cancer cells or normal substances that may help cancer cells grow. The antibodies attach to the substances and kill the cancer cells, block their growth, or keep them from spreading. Monoclonal antibodies are given by infusion. They may be used alone or to carry drugs, toxins, or radioactive material directly to cancer cells. A monoclonal antibody called rituximab may be used for certain patients with hairy cell leukemia. Other types of targeted therapies are being studied. New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials. Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Clinical trials are part of the cancer research process. Clinical trials are done to find out if new cancer treatments are safe and effective or better than the standard treatment. Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment. Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward. Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment. Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials. Follow-up tests may be needed. Some of the tests that were done to diagnose the cancer or to find out the stage of the cancer may be repeated. Some tests will be repeated in order to see how well the treatment is working. Decisions about whether to continue, change, or stop treatment may be based on the results of these tests. Some of the tests will continue to be done from time to time after treatment has ended. The results of these tests can show if your condition has changed or if the cancer has recurred (come back). These tests are sometimes called follow-up tests or check-ups. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy CAR T-cell therapy is a type of immunotherapy that changes the patient's T cells (a type of immune system cell) so they will attack certain proteins on the surface of cancer cells. The CAR T cells are grown in the laboratory and given to the patient by infusion. The CAR T cells multiply in the patient's blood and attack cancer cells. CAR T-cell therapy is being studied in the treatment of childhood ALL that has relapsed (come back) a second time. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. Signs and symptoms of childhood AML, childhood CML, JMML, or MDS include fever, feeling tired, and easy bleeding or bruising. These and other signs and symptoms may be caused by childhood AML, childhood CML, JMML, or MDS or by other conditions. Check with a doctor if your child has any of the following: - Fever with or without an infection. - Night sweats. - Shortness of breath. - Weakness or feeling tired. - Easy bruising or bleeding. - Petechiae (flat, pinpoint spots under the skin caused by bleeding). - Pain in the bones or joints. - Pain or feeling of fullness below the ribs. - Painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, groin, or other parts of the body. In childhood AML, these lumps, called leukemia cutis, may be blue or purple. - Painless lumps that are sometimes around the eyes. These lumps, called chloromas, are sometimes seen in childhood AML and may be blue-green. - An eczema -like skin rash. The signs and symptoms of TMD may include the following: - Swelling all over the body. - Shortness of breath. - Trouble breathing. - Weakness or feeling tired. - Pain below the ribs.

There are different types of treatment for children with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML), or myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). Different types of treatment are available for children with AML, CML, JMML, or MDS. Some treatments are standard (the currently used treatment), and some are being tested in clinical trials. A treatment clinical trial is a research study meant to help improve current treatments or obtain information on new treatments for patients with cancer. When clinical trials show that a new treatment is better than the standard treatment, the new treatment may become the standard treatment. Because cancer in children is rare, taking part in a clinical trial should be considered. Some clinical trials are open only to patients who have not started treatment. Treatment is planned by a team of health care providers who are experts in treating childhood leukemia and other diseases of the blood. Treatment will be overseen by a pediatric oncologist, a doctor who specializes in treating children with cancer. The pediatric oncologist works with other healthcare providers who are experts in treating children with leukemia and who specialize in certain areas of medicine. These may include the following specialists: - Pediatrician. - Hematologist. - Medical oncologist. - Pediatric surgeon. - Radiation oncologist. - Neurologist. - Neuropathologist. - Neuroradiologist. - Pediatric nurse specialist. - Social worker. - Rehabilitation specialist. - Psychologist. Some cancer treatments cause side effects months or years after treatment has ended. Regular follow-up exams are very important. Some cancer treatments cause side effects that continue or appear months or years after cancer treatment has ended. These are called late effects. Late effects of cancer treatment may include: - Physical problems. - Changes in mood, feelings, thinking, learning, or memory. - Second cancers (new types of cancer). Some late effects may be treated or controlled. It is important that parents of children who are treated for AML or other blood diseases talk with their doctors about the effects cancer treatment can have on their child. (See the PDQ summary on Late Effects of Treatment for Childhood Cancer for more information). The treatment of childhood AML usually has two phases. The treatment of childhood AML is done in phases: - Induction therapy: This is the first phase of treatment. The goal is to kill the leukemia cells in the blood and bone marrow. This puts the leukemia into remission. - Consolidation /intensification therapy: This is the second phase of treatment. It begins once the leukemia is in remission. The goal of therapy is to kill any remaining leukemia cells that may not be active but could begin to regrow and cause a relapse. Treatment called central nervous system (CNS) sanctuary therapy may be given during the induction phase of therapy. Because standard doses of chemotherapy may not reach leukemia cells in the CNS (brain and spinal cord), the cells are able to find sanctuary (hide) in the CNS. Intrathecal chemotherapy is able to reach leukemia cells in the CNS. It is given to kill the leukemia cells and lessen the chance the leukemia will recur (come back). CNS sanctuary therapy is also called CNS prophylaxis. Seven types of standard treatment are used for childhood AML, childhood CML, JMML, or MDS. Chemotherapy Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells or by stopping them from dividing. When chemotherapy is taken by mouth or injected into a vein or muscle, the drugs enter the bloodstream and can reach cancer cells throughout the body (systemic chemotherapy). When chemotherapy is placed directly into the cerebrospinal fluid (intrathecal chemotherapy), an organ, or a body cavity such as the abdomen, the drugs mainly affect cancer cells in those areas (regional chemotherapy). Combination chemotherapy is treatment using more than one anticancer drug. The way the chemotherapy is given depends on the type of cancer being treated. In AML, the leukemia cells may spread to the brain and/or spinal cord. Chemotherapy given by mouth or vein to treat AML may not cross the blood-brain barrier to get into the fluid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord. Instead, chemotherapy is injected into the fluid-filled space to kill leukemia cells that may have spread there (intrathecal chemotherapy). See Drugs Approved for Acute Myeloid Leukemia for more information. Radiation therapy Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment that uses high-energy x-rays or other types of radiation to kill cancer cells or keep them from growing. There are two types of radiation therapy: - External radiation therapy uses a machine outside the body to send radiation toward the cancer. - Internal radiation therapy uses a radioactive substance sealed in needles, seeds, wires, or catheters that are placed directly into or near the cancer. The way the radiation therapy is given depends on the type of the cancer being treated. In childhood AML, external radiation therapy may be used to treat a chloroma that does not respond to chemotherapy. Stem cell transplant Stem cell transplant is a way of giving chemotherapy and replacing blood-forming cells that are abnormal or destroyed by the cancer treatment. Stem cells (immature blood cells) are removed from the blood or bone marrow of the patient or a donor and are frozen and stored. After the chemotherapy is completed, the stored stem cells are thawed and given back to the patient through an infusion. These reinfused stem cells grow into (and restore) the body's blood cells. Targeted therapy Targeted therapy is a type of treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells without harming normal cells. Types of targeted therapy include the following: - Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy blocks signals needed for tumors to grow. TKIs block the enzyme (tyrosine kinase) that causes stem cells to become more white blood cells (granulocytes or blasts) than the body needs. TKIs may be used with other anticancer drugs as adjuvant therapy (treatment given after the initial treatment, to lower the risk that the cancer will come back). - Imatinib is a type of TKI that is approved to treat childhood CML. - Sorafenib, dasatinib, and nilotinib are being studied in the treatment of childhood leukemia. - Monoclonal antibody therapy: Monoclonal antibody therapy uses antibodies made in the laboratory, from a single type of immune system cell. These antibodies can identify substances on cancer cells or normal substances that may help cancer cells grow. The antibodies attach to the substances and kill the cancer cells, block their growth, or keep them from spreading. Monoclonal antibodies are given by infusion. They may be used alone or to carry drugs, toxins, or radioactive material directly to cancer cells. - Gemtuzumab is a type of monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of a subtype of AML called acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). Gemtuzumab is not available in the United States unless special approval is given. Monoclonal antibodies may be used with chemotherapy as adjuvant therapy. - Proteasome inhibitor therapy: Proteasome inhibitors break down proteins in cancer cells and kill them. - Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor used to treat childhood APL. See Drugs Approved for Leukemia for more information. Other drug therapy Lenalidomide may be used to lessen the need for transfusions in patients who have myelodysplastic syndromes caused by a specific chromosome change. Arsenic trioxide and all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) are anticancer drugs that kill leukemia cells, stop the leukemia cells from dividing, or help the leukemia cells mature into white blood cells. These drugs are used in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia. See Drugs Approved for Acute Myeloid Leukemia for more information. Watchful waiting Watchful waiting is closely monitoring a patients condition without giving any treatment until signs or symptoms appear or change. It is sometimes used to treat MDS or TMD. Supportive care Supportive care is given to lessen the problems caused by the disease or its treatment. Supportive care may include the following: - Transfusion therapy: A way of giving red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets to replace blood cells destroyed by disease or cancer treatment. The blood may be donated from another person or it may have been taken from the patient earlier and stored until needed. - Drug therapy, such as antibiotics or antifungal agents. - Leukapheresis: A procedure in which a special machine is used to remove white blood cells from the blood. Blood is taken from the patient and put through a blood cell separator where the white blood cells are removed. The rest of the blood is then returned to the patient's bloodstream. Treatment of newly diagnosed childhood acute leukemia with a granulocytic sarcoma (chloroma) may include chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy. Treatment of therapy -related AML is usually the same as for newly diagnosed AML, followed by stem cell transplant. Certain factors affect treatment options and prognosis (chance of recovery). The treatment options and prognosis (chance of recovery) depend on the following: - The type of soft tissue sarcoma. - The size, grade, and stage of the tumor. - How fast the cancer cells are growing and dividing. - Where the tumor is in the body. - Whether all of the tumor is removed by surgery. - The patient's age and general health. - Whether the cancer has recurred (come back).

Genetic factors can increase the risk of having a gastrointestinal stromal tumor. Anything that increases your risk of getting a disease is called a risk factor. Having a risk factor does not mean that you will get cancer; not having risk factors doesn't mean that you will not get cancer. Talk with your doctor if you think you may be at risk. The genes in cells carry the hereditary information received from a persons parents. The risk of GIST is increased in people who have inherited a mutation (change) in a certain gene. In rare cases, GISTs can be found in several members of the same family. GIST may be part of a genetic syndrome, but this is rare. A genetic syndrome is a set of symptoms or conditions that occur together and is usually caused by abnormal genes. The following genetic syndromes have been linked to GIST: - Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). - Carney triad.

Kaposi sarcoma is a disease in which malignant tumors (cancer) can form in the skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes, and other organs. Kaposi sarcoma is a cancer that causes lesions (abnormal tissue) to grow in the skin; the mucous membranes lining the mouth, nose, and throat; lymph nodes; or other organs. The lesions are usually purple and are made of cancer cells, new blood vessels, red blood cells, and white blood cells. Kaposi sarcoma is different from other cancers in that lesions may begin in more than one place in the body at the same time. Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) is found in the lesions of all patients with Kaposi sarcoma. This virus is also called Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV). Most people infected with HHV-8 do not get Kaposi sarcoma. Those infected with HHV-8 who are most likely to develop Kaposi sarcoma have immune systems weakened by disease or by drugs given after an organ transplant. There are several types of Kaposi sarcoma, including: - Classic Kaposi sarcoma. - African Kaposi sarcoma. - Immunosuppressive therapyrelated Kaposi sarcoma. - Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma. - Nonepidemic Kaposi sarcoma. Tests that examine the skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are used to detect (find) and diagnose Kaposi sarcoma. The following tests and procedures may be used: - Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking skin and lymph nodes for signs of disease, such as lumps or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patient's health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken. - Chest x-ray : An x-ray of the organs and bones inside the chest. An x-ray is a type of energy beam that can go through the body and onto film, making a picture of areas inside the body. This is used to find Kaposi sarcoma in the lungs. - Biopsy : The removal of cells or tissues so they can be viewed under a microscope by a pathologist to check for signs of cancer. One of the following types of biopsies may be done to check for Kaposi sarcoma lesions in the skin: - Excisional biopsy : A scalpel is used to remove the entire skin growth. - Incisional biopsy : A scalpel is used to remove part of a skin growth. - Core biopsy : A wide needle is used to remove part of a skin growth. - Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy : A thin needle is used to remove part of a skin growth. An endoscopy or bronchoscopy may be done to check for Kaposi sarcoma lesions in the gastrointestinal tract or lungs. - Endoscopy for biopsy: A procedure to look at organs and tissues inside the body to check for abnormal areas. An endoscope is inserted through an incision (cut) in the skin or opening in the body, such as the mouth. An endoscope is a thin, tube-like instrument with a light and a lens for viewing. It may also have a tool to remove tissue or lymph node samples, which are checked under a microscope for signs of disease. This is used to find Kaposi sarcoma lesions in the gastrointestinal tract. - Bronchoscopy for biopsy: A procedure to look inside the trachea and large airways in the lung for abnormal areas. A bronchoscope is inserted through the nose or mouth into the trachea and lungs. A bronchoscope is a thin, tube-like instrument with a light and a lens for viewing. It may also have a tool to remove tissue samples, which are checked under a microscope for signs of disease. This is used to find Kaposi sarcoma lesions in the lungs. After Kaposi sarcoma has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if cancer cells have spread to other parts of the body. The following tests and procedures may be used to find out if cancer has spread to other parts of the body: - Blood chemistry studies : A procedure in which a blood sample is checked to measure the amounts of certain substances released into the blood by organs and tissues in the body. An unusual (higher or lower than normal) amount of a substance can be a sign of disease. - CT scan (CAT scan): A procedure that makes a series of detailed pictures of areas inside the body, such as the lung, liver, and spleen, taken from different angles. The pictures are made by a computer linked to an x-ray machine. A dye may be injected into a vein or swallowed to help the organs or tissues show up more clearly. This procedure is also called computed tomography, computerized tomography, or computerized axial tomography. - PET scan (positron emission tomography scan): A procedure to find malignant tumor cells in the body. A small amount of radioactive glucose (sugar) is injected into a vein. The PET scanner rotates around the body and makes a picture of where glucose is being used in the body. Malignant tumor cells show up brighter in the picture because they are more active and take up more glucose than normal cells do. This imaging test checks for signs of cancer in the lung, liver, and spleen. - CD34 lymphocyte count: A procedure in which a blood sample is checked to measure the amount of CD34 cells (a type of white blood cell). A lower than normal amount of CD34 cells can be a sign the immune system is not working well. Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. The prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options depend on the following: - The type of Kaposi sarcoma. - The general health of the patient, especially the patient's immune system. - Whether the cancer has just been diagnosed or has recurred (come back). Classic Kaposi Sarcoma Key Points - Classic Kaposi sarcoma is found most often in older men of Italian or Eastern European Jewish origin. - Signs of classic Kaposi sarcoma may include slow-growing lesions on the legs and feet. - Another cancer may develop. Classic Kaposi sarcoma is found most often in older men of Italian or Eastern European Jewish origin. Classic Kaposi sarcoma is a rare disease that gets worse slowly over many years. Signs of classic Kaposi sarcoma may include slow-growing lesions on the legs and feet. Patients may have one or more red, purple, or brown skin lesions on the legs and feet, most often on the ankles or soles of the feet. Over time, lesions may form in other parts of the body, such as the stomach, intestines, or lymph nodes. The lesions usually don't cause any symptoms, but may grow in size and number over a period of 10 years or more. Pressure from the lesions may block the flow of lymph and blood in the legs and cause painful swelling. Lesions in the digestive tract may cause gastrointestinal bleeding. Another cancer may develop. Some patients with classic Kaposi sarcoma may develop another type of cancer before the Kaposi sarcoma lesions appear or later in life. Most often, this second cancer is non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Frequent follow-up is needed to watch for these second cancers. Epidemic Kaposi Sarcoma Key Points - Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is found in patients who have acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). - Signs of epidemic Kaposi sarcoma can include lesions that form in many parts of the body. - The use of drug therapy called cART reduces the risk of epidemic Kaposi sarcoma in patients infected with HIV. Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is found in patients who have acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Epidemic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in patients who have acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). AIDS is caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which attacks and weakens the immune system. When the body's immune system is weakened by HIV, infections and cancers such as Kaposi sarcoma can develop. Most cases of epidemic Kaposi sarcoma in the United States have been diagnosed in homosexual or bisexual men infected with HIV. Signs of epidemic Kaposi sarcoma can include lesions that form in many parts of the body. The signs of epidemic Kaposi sarcoma can include lesions in different parts of the body, including any of the following: - Skin. - Lining of the mouth. - Lymph nodes. - Stomach and intestines. - Lungs and lining of the chest. - Liver. - Spleen. Kaposi sarcoma is sometimes found in the lining of the mouth during a regular dental check-up. In most patients with epidemic Kaposi sarcoma, the disease will spread to other parts of the body over time. Fever, weight loss, or diarrhea can occur. In the later stages of epidemic Kaposi sarcoma, life-threatening infections are common. The use of drug therapy called cART reduces the risk of epidemic Kaposi sarcoma in patients infected with HIV. Combined antiretroviral therapy (cART) is a combination of several drugs that block HIV and slow down the development of AIDS and AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma.
