Aplasia cutis congenital is a rare skin disorder characterized by absent or hypoplastic scalp tissue at birth. It can occur as an isolated defect or in association with other developmental anomalies such as craniofacial malformations, neural tube defects, and skeletal abnormalities. The condition may be caused by genetic factors, environmental exposures, or a combination of both. Treatment typically involves surgical reconstruction to close the open wound and prevent infection.

The symptoms of Aplasia cutis congenital (ACC) include absent or hypoplastic skin with variable subcutaneous tissue defects affecting one or more limb(s). Other associated features may include oral anomalies such as micrognathia, cleft lip or palate, dental agenesis, ocular abnormalities, hearing impairment, cardiac malformations, renal dysfunction, and skeletal deformities .

Aquagenic pruritus is caused by an abnormal reaction of the skin to water exposure or contact with moist substances such as sweat. It can be triggered by swimming in chlorinated pools or bathing in tap water. The condition is more common among women than men and typically affects young adults.
answers_noisy: Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (ALL) is a type of cancer that affects the bone marrow and blood cells called lymphocytes or white blood cells. ALL occurs when there is an abnormal proliferation of immature B-cells or T-cells in the bone marrow .

Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (ALL) is a type of cancer that affects the bone marrow and blood cells. ALL can occur in both children and adults, but there are some differences between childhood and adult ALL. In general, ALL progresses through different stages known as phases. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is diagnosed by bone marrow aspiration and biopsy . The diagnosis of AML requires the presence of at least 20% blasts in the bone marrow with characteristic cytological features, as well as immunophenotyping showing aberrant expression of myeloid markers such as CD13, CD33, or MPO. Additional tests that may be performed include karyotype analysis to identify chromosomal translocations associated with specific subtypes of AML, molecular testing to detect mutations in genes involved in signaling pathways commonly altered in AML, and flow cytometry to determine the immunophenotype of the blast population.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL) is a type of cancer that affects white blood cells called B-cells or lymphocytes. It causes an overproduction of these cells in the bone marrow, leading to their accumulation in the bloodstream. This can result in enlarged spleens and livers, as well as other complications such as infection, autoimmune disease, and cytopenias. CLL typically develops slowly, with symptoms appearing only when the disease has progressed significantly. The exact cause of CLL remains unknown, but it is thought to be related to genetic factors, environmental exposures, and lifestyle habits. Diagnosis involves a combination of physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging studies, and biopsies. Treatment options for CLL include chemotherapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and stem cell transplantation.

There are currently several clinical trials being conducted to evaluate new treatments for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Some of these trials are evaluating targeted therapies such as ibrutinib, venetoclax, idelalisib, and lenalidomide, while others are testing immunotherapy approaches using CAR-T cells or bispecific antibodies. To learn more about ongoing clinical trials in this area, you can visit websites such as www.clinicaltrials.gov or www.lls.org/research.

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is diagnosed by identifying the Philadelphia chromosome or its molecular equivalent in peripheral blood cells or bone marrow aspirate using cytogenetics or polymerase chain reaction (PCR), respectively . The presence of BCR-ABL1 fusion gene can be detected through fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).

Hairy cell leukemia (HCL) is a rare type of blood cancer that affects white blood cells called lymphocytes. It was named "hair cell" because some lymphocytes in patients with this condition have long projections resembling hairs under a microscope.

Hairy cell leukemia (HCL) is a type of cancer that affects white blood cells called lymphocytes. It is named because these lymphocytes have hair-like structures on their surfaces when examined under a microscope. The exact cause of HCL is not known, but it usually develops slowly over time.

Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is diagnosed through a combination of clinical symptoms, physical examination findings, blood tests, bone marrow aspiration or biopsy, and imaging studies such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid analysis .

Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer that affects the bone marrow cells called myeloblasts. These cells do not mature properly into white blood cells, such as neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, erythroid progenitors, megakaryocyte precursors, and platelets .

Childhood acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is classified into two main categories: infant AML and childhood AML. Infant AML typically occurs in children under 1 year old and has distinct genetic features that differ from those seen in older children with AML.

Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are rare malignant tumors that can occur in any part of the body but most commonly arise from muscles or fatty tissue . The symptoms of STS vary depending on their location within the body. For example, an STS arising in the extremities may cause pain, swelling, or numbness in the affected limb, while an abdominal STS may present with abdominal discomfort or bloating. Other common symptoms include difficulty walking, weakness, weight loss, and lumps or masses beneath the skin.

Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are rare malignant tumors that can occur in any part of the body but most commonly arise from muscles, fat, blood vessels, or connective tissue . The treatment approach for STS is multidisciplinary and depends on several factors such as histologic subtype, grade, size, location, resectability, and presence of metastatic disease at presentation .

Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a malignant tumor of endothelial cells that can occur in any organ system but most commonly affects the skin. The treatment of KS depends on several factors, including the stage of disease, location of lesions, patient age and overall health status, and personal preference .

Rhabdomyosarcomas (RMS) are malignant tumors that arise from immature skeletal muscle cells . They account for approximately 4% of all pediatric cancers and occur most commonly in children under the age of 15 years old . There are two main histological subtypes of RMS: embryonal and alveolar. Embryonal RMS is more common than alveolar RMS and typically affects infants and young children less than five years of age . Alveolar RMS occurs primarily in older children and adolescents .

Childhood soft tissue sarcomas can present with various symptoms depending on their location in the body. The most common childhood soft tissue sarcomas include rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), osteosarcoma, Ewing's sarcoma, synovial sarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, liposarcoma, fibrosarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, clear cell sarcoma, extra-skeletal chondroblastoma, desmoplastic small round cell tumor, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors .

Childhood soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are rare tumors that can occur anywhere in the body but most commonly arise from bone or soft tissues such as muscles, fat, nerves, blood vessels, and connective tissues . The treatment of childhood STS typically involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy depending on the specific type and stage of the tumor . Surgery is usually the first line of treatment and involves removing the tumor along with any affected surrounding tissue to prevent recurrence . Chemotherapy may be used before or after surgery to help shrink large tumors or kill remaining cancer cells . Radiation therapy may also be used if the tumor cannot be completely removed surgically or if there is a high risk of recurrence . In addition to these treatments, targeted therapies such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immunotherapies have been developed for certain types of STS that target specific molecular pathways involved in cancer cell growth and survival .

Adult Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL) is a type of cancer that affects the lymphatic system in adults. It is characterized by large cells called Reed-Sternberg cells and their variants, which can be found in the lymph nodes or other organs such as the spleen, liver, bone marrow, or lungs . The exact cause of HL is unknown, but certain genetic factors may increase the risk of developing this disease.

There are several ongoing clinical trials for adult Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). One such trial is evaluating the use of brentuximab vedotin in combination with bendamustine as first-line treatment for patients with advanced stage classical HL . Another trial is investigating the efficacy of nivolumab plus relapsed or refractory HL that has progressed after three or more lines of chemotherapy . Additionally, a phase III randomized controlled trial is comparing the safety and effectiveness of bendamustine plus vinblastine versus bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine, and prednisone (BEACOPP) as first-line therapy for advanced stage classic HL .

Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) is a type of cancer that affects the lymphatic system. It can occur in people of any age group but is most common in adults over 65 years old . The exact cause of NHL is unknown, but certain factors may increase the risk of developing this disease. These include family history of lymphoid malignancies, genetic predisposition, autoimmune diseases such as Sjogren’s syndrome, chronic inflammation due to infection with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), exposure to radiation, smoking tobacco products, obesity, and weakened immune function from conditions such as HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, and immunosuppressive medications .

The treatment of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and stem cell transplantation. Chemotherapy is used to kill cancer cells throughout the body, while radiation therapy uses high doses of X-rays or other types of radiation to destroy cancer cells in a specific area. Stem cell transplantation can be used as part of the initial treatment plan or after other treatments have failed.

The different stages of AIDS-related lymphomas include early stage (stage I or II), intermediate stage (stage III), and advanced stage (stages IV). Early stage lymphomas usually present as localized masses in the abdomen, thorax, or bone marrow. Intermediate stage lymphomas can involve multiple sites within one organ system, such as the gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system, or skin. Advanced stage lymphomas typically affect multiple organs throughout the body.

The prognosis of mycosis fungoides (MF) depends on several factors, including stage at diagnosis, age, and presence or absence of extracutaneous involvement . MF is considered to be one of the most common types of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), with an estimated incidence rate of 0.5–1 per million person-years in Western countries .

Primary central nervous system (PCNSL) lymphomas occur in the brain or spinal cord and are usually associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis, or prior treatment with chemotherapy or radiation therapy.

Childhood Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is a type of cancer that affects the lymphatic system. It usually occurs during childhood or adolescence, but can also occur at any age. The lymphatic system is made up of a network of vessels called lymph nodes, which filter fluid from body tissues to help fight infection .

Childhood Hodgkin Lymphoma (cHL) is classified into two stages according to the Ann Arbor Staging System . Stage I refers to disease confined within one lymph node region or organ; while stage II indicates involvement of adjacent lymph nodes or organs.

Childhood non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHL) can be diagnosed using various tests such as blood tests, imaging studies like CT scans or MRI, bone marrow biopsy, and staging of the disease which is important for treatment planning .

Anal cancer is a type of cancer that arises from cells in or around the anus. It usually begins as abnormal growths called anal squamous cell carcinomas (SCC). These tumors typically develop slowly over time, but they can also grow rapidly if left untreated. The exact cause of anal SCC is not known, but certain factors such as human papillomavirus infection, smoking, and exposure to other chemicals have been linked to increased risk for developing this form of cancer. Early detection through regular screening tests like digital rectal examinations and biopsies can help identify and treat anal SCC early when treatment options may be more effective.

Anal cancer is a rare type of cancer that develops in the anus or rectum. It usually begins as abnormal cells called dysplasia, which may eventually turn into cancer if not treated. There are four stages of anal cancer, with Stage 0 being the earliest and Stage IV being the most advanced.

Central nervous system (CNS) tumors can occur in people of any age group but are generally rare except for certain types such as meningiomas which account for 38% of all CNS tumors . The incidence rate of brain and other CNS tumors increases with age, from less than one per 100,000 persons under the age of 20 to over six per 100,000 persons aged 75 or older .

The classification of adult central nervous system (CNS) tumours is based on histological features and molecular characteristics. There are four main types of CNS tumours in adults: gliomas, meningiomas, pituitary adenomas, and brain metastases. Glioma is the most common type of primary brain tumour in adults, accounting for about 80% of all intracranial neoplasms .

Childhood astrocytomas are tumors that arise from cells called astrocytes, which are found throughout the brain and spinal cord. These tumors can occur at any age but are more common during childhood and adolescence. The most common type of childhood astrocytoma is pilocytic astrocytoma (PA), accounting for about 5% to 10% of all pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors .

Childhood astrocytomas can vary in their prognosis depending on several factors such as age at diagnosis, tumor location, histologic grade, and treatment received. Low-grade gliomas (LGG) tend to have a better overall survival rate compared to high-grade gliomas (HGG). For example, children with LGG located in the posterior fossa had an estimated 5-year progression-free survival of approximately 90%, while those with HGG had a much lower estimated 5-year progression-free survival of about 30% .

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials for childhood central nervous system (CNS) atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors (AT/RT). These include studies of targeted therapies such as histone deacetylase inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and immunotherapies such as CAR-T cell therapy.

Childhood brainstem gliomas can present with various symptoms depending on their location within the brainstem. Some common symptoms include headaches, vomiting, vision problems, facial weakness or drooping, difficulty walking, dizziness, balance issues, speech difficulties, swallowing problems, seizures, and hearing loss. Other less frequent symptoms may include double vision, eye movement abnormalities, numbness in arms or legs, constipation, and changes in personality or behavior . It is important to note that these symptoms may also be caused by other conditions unrelated to brain tumors; therefore, it is crucial for parents and caregivers to consult a healthcare professional if they notice any concerning symptoms in children.

Childhood brain tumors can be treated with surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or a combination of these treatments depending on the type and stage of the tumor. The treatment plan is typically determined by a team of specialists called a pediatric brain tumor board.

The prognosis of childhood central nervous system (CNS) embryonal tumours varies depending on the specific type of tumour and its location within the CNS. In general, these types of tumours have a poor overall survival rate compared to other brain tumours in children.

Childhood CNS germ cell tumours can be caused by several factors, including genetic predisposition, exposure to environmental chemicals such as pesticides or solvents, and certain lifestyle choices such as smoking during pregnancy . However, it is important to note that these factors alone cannot fully explain all cases of childhood cancer, and there may also be other contributing factors not yet identified.

Childhood central nervous system (CNS) germ cell tumours are rare but aggressive neoplasms that arise from primordial germ cells during early embryonic development . The most common type of CNS germ cell tumour is medulloblastoma, which accounts for approximately 20% of all paediatric brain cancers . Other types include ependymomas, choriocarcinomas, teratomas, and mixed germ cell tumours.

Childhood craniopharyngiomas have an overall survival rate of 90% to 100%. However, they can cause significant morbidity due to their location near vital structures such as the optic nerves, pituitary gland, hypothalamus, and brainstem. The prognosis depends on several factors including age at diagnosis, tumor size and extent of resection, presence of hydrocephalus, and radiographic appearance (solid vs cystic). Solid tumors tend to be more aggressive than cystic ones. Children with residual tumors after surgery may require additional treatment such as radiation therapy or chemotherapy. Long-term follow-up is necessary because recurrence can occur many years after initial treatment.

Ependymomas can occur anywhere along the central nervous system (CNS), including the brain, spinal cord, and cerebrospinal fluid pathways. The exact cause of childhood ependymoma is unknown; however, several risk factors have been identified that may contribute to its development.

Primary liver cancer is often diagnosed through a combination of imaging tests such as ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET). A biopsy may also be performed to obtain tissue samples for examination under a microscope. The specific diagnostic approach depends on various factors, including the patient's symptoms, risk factors, and whether there is evidence of cirrhosis or other underlying liver diseases.

Bile duct cancer, also known as cholangiocarcinoma, is a type of cancer that develops in the bile ducts within or outside of the liver. The exact cause of this disease is unknown, but there are several risk factors associated with its development, including primary sclerosing cholangitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis, hepatitis C infection, alcoholic liver disease, obesity, tobacco use, and exposure to certain chemicals such as thorotrast and DDC.

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to cholangiocarcinoma that aim to evaluate novel therapies and improve patient outcomes. Some of these include studies evaluating immunotherapy agents such as pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapeutic drugs like gemcitabine and cisplatin, as well as targeted therapy agents like regorafenib . Other ongoing trials are investigating the use of radiation therapy in combination with other treatments, including immunotherapy and targeted therapy agents .

Childhood liver cancer is rare in children under 10 years old. The most common type of childhood liver cancer is hepatoblastoma (HB), which usually occurs between ages 2 and 4. Symptoms may include abdominal pain or swelling, jaundice, weight loss, vomiting, anemia, fatigue, pale stools, dark urine, bruising, bleeding, palpable mass in right upper quadrant, fever, and weakness. It's important to note that these symptoms could also be caused by other conditions such as viral infection, so it's crucial for parents to consult with their child's healthcare provider if concerned about any potential symptoms.

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials that aim to improve the treatment of childhood liver cancers. Some examples include the Children’s Oncology Group (COG) study NCT03672548, which is evaluating the use of targeted therapies as an adjuvant therapy after surgical resection of localized hepatoblastoma; the COG study NCT01995608, which is investigating the optimal timing of surgery in children with newly diagnosed hepatic blastomas; and the European Paediatric Soft Tissue Sarcoma Society (E-PaSTS) study NCT03090787, which is assessing the efficacy of chemotherapy regimens for patients with relapsed or refractory rhabdomyosarcomas.

Ewing sarcoma (ES) is a type of bone or soft tissue tumor that usually develops in children and young adults. It arises from undifferentiated mesenchymal cells and is characterized by specific chromosomal rearrangements involving the EWSR1 gene. The most common sites for ES to occur include the pelvis, ribs, femur, vertebrae, and paraspinal soft tissues.

The treatment of Ewing sarcoma typically involves a combination of chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation therapy. Chemotherapy is used to shrink tumors before surgical removal or to kill any remaining cancer cells after surgery. Surgery may involve amputation in some cases but more often limb-sparing procedures can be performed with reconstruction using metal rods or other implants. Radiation therapy is usually given after surgery to help prevent recurrence. Newer treatments such as targeted therapies and immunotherapies are also being investigated for use in treating Ewing sarcoma.

The diagnosis of osteosarcoma typically involves several steps, including physical examination, imaging studies (such as X-rays, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)), biopsy to obtain tissue samples for analysis under a microscope by pathologists, and additional testing such as blood tests to look for signs of cancer in the body.

Carcinoid tumors (also known as neuroendocrine tumors) are rare neoplasms that arise from cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system, which is found throughout the body including the gastrointestinal (GI) tract . In the GI tract, most carcinoid tumors occur in the small intestine, followed by the appendix, colon, stomach, and rectum. These tumors can be classified into two types based on their location within the bowel wall: 1. Epidermal or mucosal carcinoids, which originate from the epithelium and account for about 80% of all cases; and 2. Submucosal or muscularis propria carcinoids, which develop from the deeper layers of the bowel wall and account for approximately 20% of cases .

The stages of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumours (GI-NETs) are as follows: Stage 0 - confined to the mucosa; Stage I - invasion into submucosal layer; Stage II - further penetration into muscularis propria or peripancreatic connective tissue; Stage III - metastasis to regional lymph nodes; Stage IV - distant organ metastases.

Chronic Myeloproliferative Neoplasms (MPNs) are a group of clonal hematologic disorders characterized by abnormal proliferation of one or more myeloid lineages in the bone marrow . The incidence rate is approximately 5-7 cases per million people annually, with no gender predilection .

Polycythemia Vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an increase in red blood cells due to clonal proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells. The symptoms of PV can vary depending on the underlying causes such as genetic mutations, environmental factors, and lifestyle habits. Some common symptoms include fatigue, pruritus, headaches, dizziness, visual disturbances, shortness of breath, chest pain, palpitations, and weight loss. Other less frequent symptoms may include fever, sweating, night sweats, bone pain, joint pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, erectile dysfunction, and bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract. Itching is caused by increased serum levels of histamine, which is released during inflammation. Fatigue is often associated with anemia resulting from erythrocyte hyperviscosity, leading to decreased oxygen delivery to tissues. Shortness of breath results from hypoxia-induced vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension. Chest pain may be related to coronary artery disease induced by hypercoagulability. Headache occurs because of high viscosity and low volume of cerebrospinal fluid. Visual disturbance is usually attributed to central retinal vein occlusion

Primary myelofibrosis (PMF) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by bone marrow fibrosis, splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms such as fatigue, early satiety, weight loss, and anemia . The prognosis of PMF varies depending on several factors, including age at diagnosis, risk stratification according to the International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS), driver mutation status, and treatment received .

The treatment of essential thrombocythemia (ET) depends on various factors such as age, risk stratification, comorbidities, symptoms, platelet count, and history of vascular events. Low-dose aspirin is recommended in all patients with ET to reduce cardiovascular risk .

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL) is a rare type of myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by sustained peripheral blood eosinophilia and bone marrow eosinophil hyperplasia . The treatment options for CEL include corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, interferon-alpha, immunomodulatory drugs such as danazol or cyclosporine A, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, monoclonal antibody therapy, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and splenectomy .

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a type of cancer that affects the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. It causes an overproduction of white blood cells called granulocytes or polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs). CML can also cause an increase in red blood cells and platelets .

Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) is a rare type of blood cancer that affects children under 2 years old . It occurs when abnormal cells grow in bone marrow and spread to other parts of the body such as liver or spleen. The symptoms include an enlarged spleen, bruising easily, bleeding gums, pale skin, fatigue, fever, weight loss, and recurrent infections. JMML can be diagnosed by analyzing blood samples for specific genetic mutations. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy followed by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation .

Atypical chronic myeloid leukaemia (aCML) is a rare type of blood cancer that affects the bone marrow and causes an overproduction of white blood cells . The symptoms can vary depending on how advanced the disease is and whether there are complications such as infections or bleeding. Some common symptoms include fatigue, weakness, weight loss, fever, night sweats, pain in the abdomen, joints, back, chest, or skull, bruising easily, frequent infections, and bleeding from the gums. Other less common symptoms may include headaches, dizziness, confusion, seizures, yellowing of the skin, swelling of the legs or feet, shortness of breath, cough, difficulty breathing, and pain when breathing. It's important to note that these symptoms could be caused by other conditions as well, so it's crucial for anyone experiencing them to consult with a healthcare provider for proper diagnosis and treatment.

The treatment of MDS/MPN-U depends on several factors such as age, overall health status, risk stratification, and genetic mutations present in the patient's cells. For patients who have low-risk disease or those with higher-risk disease but who are not candidates for hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT), hypomethylating agents (HMA) such as azacitidine or decitabine may be recommended .

Endometrial cancer (EC) is one of the most common gynecological malignancies in developed countries . The prognosis depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, histologic type, tumor grade, stage, myometrial invasion depth, lymphovascular space invasion, and lymph node metastasis status .

Uterine sarcomas (US) are rare malignancies that account for approximately 1% to 2% of all gynecologic cancers . The incidence rate of US in the United States has been reported as 0.6 per million women annually , with an estimated age-standardized incidence rate of 3.5 cases per 100,000 person-years worldwide .

Uterine sarcomas are rare malignant tumors that arise from the cells of the myometrium (uterine smooth muscle) or other components of the endometrial stroma . The most common type is leiomyosarcoma, which accounts for approximately 50% of all cases. Other types include endometrial stromal sarcoma, undifferentiated uterine sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, and extrauterine sarcoma.

Germ cell tumours (GCTs) are rare malignancies that occur in both children and adults. In children, GCTs account for approximately 2% of all cancers diagnosed before age 15 years . The most common sites of GCTs in children are the gonads (approximately 40%) and extragonadal locations (60%). Extragonadal GCTs arise from any site outside the reproductive organs and include midline structures such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, pineal region, and sacrococcygeal area.

Childhood extracranial germ cell tumours (EGCTs) are rare malignancies that arise from cells of embryonic origin outside of the central nervous system . The most common sites of EGCTs in children include testis, ovary, mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and gonadal germ cells . Treatment options for childhood EGCTs vary depending on the site of origin and stage at diagnosis but typically involve surgical resection followed by chemotherapy or radiation therapy .

Extragonadal germ cell tumours (EGCT) can be diagnosed by imaging tests such as ultrasound, CT scan or MRI. Imaging studies may also reveal metastatic sites in addition to the primary site of the tumour. EGCTs are often detected incidentally during imaging investigations performed for other reasons.

Intraocular or uveal melanoma refers to a type of cancer that originates from the pigment-containing cells called melanocytes located within the eye. These melanomas typically develop in the choroid, which is the layer of tissue between the sclera and retina, but can also occur in the iris and ciliary body. The exact cause of uveal melanoma is not known, but certain genetic mutations have been identified as risk factors for developing this type of cancer. Uveal melanoma is usually diagnosed at an early stage when patients present with symptoms such as blurred vision, floaters, flashes of light, pain, or a sudden change in pupil size. Treatment options include radiation therapy, brachytherapy, enucleation, and cryotherapy .

Intraocular or uveal melanoma is a type of cancer that originates from the pigment-containing cells called melanocytes found within the uvea, which is composed of three layers of tissue located between the sclera and retina . The most common location for this type of tumor to occur is in the choroid layer of the uvea; however, it can also develop in the iris and ciliary body .

Retinoblastoma (RB) is a rare malignant tumor that affects young children, typically before 5 years of age. It arises from the cells of the developing eye and can occur in one or both eyes. RB occurs most commonly in white children but has also been reported in other races and ethnic groups. The incidence rate varies by geographic region, with higher rates observed in North America and Europe compared to Asia and Africa .

Retinoblastoma is a rare type of cancer that affects young children. The treatment options depend on several factors such as the size and location of the tumor, whether it has spread to other parts of the body, and the child's overall health.

The treatment of ovarian epithelial, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancers typically involves surgery followed by chemotherapy. Surgery may involve removal of the uterus (hysterectomy), removal of one or both ovaries (oophorectomy), removal of the fallopian tubes (salpingectomy), removal of tissue in the pelvis (pelvex), removal of lymph nodes from around the abdomen (lymphadenectomy), and removal of any tumors found outside the pelvis (debulking). Chemotherapy is often given after surgery to kill remaining cancer cells.

Ovarian germ cell tumors (OGCTs) are rare cancers that originate from early embryonic cells in the ovaries or fallopian tubes . They account for approximately 1% of all ovarian malignancies and typically occur during childhood or adolescence but may also arise later in life . The most common type of OGCT is dysgerminoma, which accounts for about half of all cases. Other types include teratoma, endodermal sinus tumor, yolk sac tumor, mixed germ cell tumor, and choriocarcinoma .

Low-grade ovarian tumors typically do not cause any symptoms until they reach a large size or become advanced stage. The most common presenting symptoms include abdominal pain (which may be sharp or dull), bloating or feeling full quickly after eating, urinary urgency, frequent urination, constipation, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, weight loss, indigestion, heartburn, back pain, pelvic pressure or pain, irregular menstrual periods, and postmenopausal bleeding.

Ovarian low-grade potential epithelial tumors (LGPETs) are rare in clinical practice, accounting for only 1% of all ovarian neoplasms . The current treatment options include surgery and chemotherapy. However, due to their indolent nature, LGPETs have been treated with conservative surgical approaches such as unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (USO), cystectomy, or even observation alone .

Gallbladder cancer (GBC) is a rare type of biliary tract cancer that originates from cells in the lining of the gallbladder. The exact cause of GBC remains unknown, but several risk factors have been identified, including age over 50 years old, female gender, cholelithiasis or gallstones, chronic inflammation due to infection with Salmonella typhi or Helicobacter pylori, genetic predisposition, obesity, diabetes mellitus, liver fluke infestation, exposure to certain chemicals such as thorotrast contrast agent, polyvinyl chloride plastics, and tobacco smoking .

The stages of gallbladder cancer (GBC) are determined by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC), which uses the tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) system to classify cancers . The TNM classification is based on the size of the primary tumor (T stage), whether there are affected lymph nodes (N stage), and if distant metastases are present (M stage).

Testicular cancer is typically treated with surgery to remove the tumor from the testicle (called an orchiectomy). Depending on the type of cancer, additional treatments such as chemotherapy or radiation therapy may be recommended after surgery .

Gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) refers to a group of pregnancy-related disorders that arise from abnormal proliferation of placental cells known as trophoblasts. GTD includes hydatidiform mole, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, and placental site trophoblastic tumor .

The treatment of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) depends on the type and extent of the disease. Low-risk GTN is treated with single-agent chemotherapy, typically methotrexate or dactinomycin. High-risk GTN requires combination chemotherapy, which may include multiple agents such as methotrexate, actinomycin D, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, cisplatin, etoposide, and carboplatin. In some cases, surgery may be necessary to remove large tumors or ectopic pregnancies.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) can be diagnosed with a combination of clinical features, laboratory tests, imaging studies, and biopsies. The diagnosis of LCH requires a high index of suspicion because its symptoms vary widely depending on which organs are affected.

Hypopharyngeal cancer refers to malignant tumors occurring in the lower part of the pharynx, which includes the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, soft palate, tonsils, oropharynx, pyriform sinus, esophageal entrance, and upper portion of the larynx . The term “hypo” means low or inferior, so hypopharyngeal cancer literally means “cancer below (or inferior to) the throat.”

The stages of hypopharyngeal cancer are usually broken down as follows: Stage 0 (carcinoma in situ): This stage refers to the earliest form of cancer that is only present on the surface layer of tissue in the pharynx. It has not yet invaded deeper layers or spread to other parts of the body.Stage I: Cancer has invaded through the top muscle layer into the middle muscle layer but has not reached the lymph nodes or other tissues around the pharynx.Stage II: Cancer has invaded through all three layers of tissue surrounding the pharynx, including fatty tissue and muscles. However, it has not yet spread to any nearby lymph nodes.Stage III: Cancer has spread beyond the pharynx and may have involved one or more nearby lymph nodes.Stage IVA: Cancer has spread to one or more lymph nodes above the diaphragm, such as those near the neck area.

Laryngeal cancer refers to malignant tumors that occur in the larynx, which is part of the respiratory system located at the back of the throat. The larynx connects the airway from the nose to the lungs with the esophagus for swallowing food and drink. It consists of several parts including the glottis (the area where sound is produced during speech), the epiglottis (a structure that prevents food and liquid from entering the trachea when swallowing), and the supraglottic region (above the vocal folds).

The different stages of laryngeal cancer are as follows: Stage 0 (carcinoma in situ): This stage is characterized by an abnormal growth of cells that is confined to the top layer of cells in the larynx. It has not yet invaded deeper into the tissue or spread to other parts of the body.Stage I: At this stage, the tumor has grown through the top layer of cells but has not yet extended beyond the larynx.Stage II: In this stage, the tumor has grown further than Stage I but remains within the larynx.Stage III: The tumor at this stage may have started spreading outside of the larynx, either into tissues near the larynx or into nearby lymph nodes.Stage IVA: At this stage, the tumor has spread to tissues near the larynx or to lymph nodes above the diaphragm.

The symptoms of cancer of the lips include ulcers that do not heal easily, lumps or bumps in the lips, changes to the pigmentation of the skin such as mottling or discoloration, thickening of the skin, and persistent pain or numbness. In the case of cancer of the tongue, it may present with difficulty swallowing, a change in speech, a lump or bump, bleeding from the mouth, an ulcer that does not heal easily, and persistent pain or numbness. For cancer of the gums, symptoms may include swelling of the gum tissue, bleeding from the gums when brushing teeth, loose teeth, and persistent pain or numbness.

There are several ongoing clinical trials of novel treatments for head and neck cancers, including those involving immunotherapy (such as checkpoint inhibitors), targeted therapies, and combination therapy approaches. These include studies evaluating the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab in combination with chemoradiation for locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck . Other studies are investigating the use of targeted agents such as cetuximab in combination with other therapies for recurrent or metastatic disease . Clinical trial information can be found at https://clinicaltrials.gov/.

Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma with an unknown primary site (SCCUP) is a rare type of head and neck cancer that occurs when cancer cells from an unidentified location in the body spread to lymph nodes or other tissues in the neck . The most common sites of origin for SCCUP include the esophagus, lung, cervix, vulva, vagina, penis, skin, bladder, kidney, prostate, breast, thyroid gland, salivary glands, stomach, colon, rectum, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, bile ducts, soft tissue, bone marrow, and brain .

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) can cause various symptoms depending on its location in the upper airway and neck region. The most common symptom is a painless mass or swelling in the neck that may be visible as an enlarged lymph node under the chin. Other symptoms include difficulty swallowing, nasal congestion, hearing loss, tinnitus, facial numbness, headache, cough, sore throat, runny nose, postnasal drip, bleeding from the nose, hoarseness, voice changes, and trouble breathing through the mouth.

There are several ongoing clinical trials for nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) treatment that aim to evaluate novel therapies such as targeted agents, immunotherapy, and combination treatments. Some of these include the phase III NRG Oncology-Head and Neck 103 trial which is evaluating pembrolizumab plus chemoradiation versus chemoradiotherapy alone in patients with stage IB-IVA NPC , the phase II PHOENIX trial which will assess the efficacy of nivolumab plus ipilimumab after induction chemotherapy in patients with locally advanced NPC , and the phase III ECOG-ACRIN EA642 trial which aims to determine whether durvalumab added to concurrent chemoradiation followed by adjuvant chemotherapy improves progression-free survival compared to placebo .

Oropharyngeal cancers (OPCs) account for approximately 10% of all head and neck malignancies worldwide . The incidence rate of OPC varies by country; in high-income countries such as the United States, Canada, Australia, and Western Europe, the annual age-standardized incidence rates range from 3 to 9 per 100,000 persons . In contrast, low-to middle-income countries have higher incidences, with rates ranging between 8 and 25 per 100,000 people .

Paranasal sinus and nasal cavity cancers occur less frequently than other types of head and neck tumors. The incidence rate is approximately 1 to 2 cases per year in the United States (US) . However, this type of cancer has been increasing over time, with an average annual increase of about 3% from 2009 to 2017 .

The treatment of paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity cancer depends on several factors, including the stage and location of the tumor, as well as other health conditions that may affect the patient's overall health status. In general, surgery is often used to remove the entire tumor in early stages of the disease, while radiation therapy and chemotherapy may be recommended for more advanced cases or when surgical removal is not possible.

Salivary gland tumors (SGTs) are rare neoplasms of the head and neck region with an incidence rate of 0.7 per 100,000 person-years . The parotid glands account for approximately half of all SGTs, while the submandibular and minor salivary glands each comprise about one-quarter of cases . Malignant SGTs represent only 35%–40% of all SGTs; however, their diagnosis is crucial as they have significant implications for patient prognosis and treatment planning .

There is no definitive way to prevent oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancer, but there are several ways to reduce your risk of developing these types of cancers. Here are some tips for preventing oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancer:

Pancreatic cancer is diagnosed through a combination of clinical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging studies, and tissue biopsies. The most common diagnostic tools include ultrasound, computed tomography (CT) scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS), positron emission tomography (PET), and fine-needle aspiration (FNA). These tests can help detect suspicious lesions in the pancreas, provide detailed images for further evaluation, and assist in determining whether the tumor has metastasized to other parts of the body. In addition to these noninvasive methods, EUS-guided FNA allows doctors to obtain samples from specific areas within the pancreas for microscopic analysis. This procedure involves inserting an endoscope equipped with an ultrasound probe into the small intestine and using it to guide a thin needle into the target area. Once inside the tumor, cells are suctioned out by the needle tip and collected for testing. If the results indicate malignancy, additional tests such as CT scanning may be performed to determine if the cancer has spread beyond the pancreas.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs) are rare neoplasms that arise from cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system within the pancreas . These tumors can be further classified as functional or non-functional depending on whether they secrete hormones and cause specific symptoms related to those secretions or not, respectively. PanNETs account for approximately 1% of all pancreatic malignancies and have an annual incidence rate of about one per million people worldwide .

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pNET) treatment typically involves surgery to remove the primary tumor if it has not metastasized. The goal of surgical resection is to completely remove all visible tumor tissue while preserving as much normal pancreatic tissue as possible.

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials investigating various treatment options for patients with advanced RCC. Some of these include combination therapies such as nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NCT03562948), atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (NCT0417149) and axitinib plus avelumab (NCT04006716). Other trials are evaluating targeted agents such as cabozantinib (NCT04066422) and lenvatinib (NCT04037035). Additionally, there are also trials focused on immunotherapy including pembrolizumab alone (NCT03761095) and in combination with other agents such as axitinib (NCT04066422) and nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NCT03562948). It is important to note that this list is not exhaustive and more information about current clinical trials can be found at ClinicalTrials.gov by searching for “renal cell carcinoma”.

The stages of transitional cell cancer (TCC) of the renal pelvis and ureter are as follows: Stage I: Tumor is confined to the inner layer of the kidney or ureter.Stage II: Tumor extends beyond the inner lining but remains within the kidney or ureter.Stage III: Tumor has invaded through the muscle wall of the kidney or ureter.Stage IV: Tumor has metastasized to other parts of the body such as lymph nodes, lungs, liver, bones, etc.

The symptoms of childhood kidney cancer depend on the type of tumour and its location within the kidneys or surrounding structures. Some children may not experience any noticeable symptoms at all, especially in cases where small renal masses are incidentally discovered during imaging studies for unrelated conditions .

Yes, there are ongoing research studies and clinical trials for childhood kidney cancers such as Wilms tumor. These include studies of targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and combination treatments. Some examples of current clinical trials in children with Wilms tumor include the Children's Oncology Group (COG) study AEWSO1321, which is evaluating the use of the PARP inhibitor veliparib in combination with chemotherapy in patients with relapsed or refractory solid tumors, including Wilms tumor; the COG study AEWS1421, which is investigating the use of the MEK inhibitor selumetinib in combination with chemotherapy in patients with newly diagnosed intermediate-risk Wilms tumor; and the COG study AEWO1721, which is assessing the efficacy and safety of the PD-L1 inhibitor atezolizumab in combination with chemotherapy in patients with relapsed or refractory solid tumors, including Wilms tumor.

Breast cancer can cause several symptoms such as lumps or thickening under the armpit, changes to the nipple (such as flattening), pain in one breast that persists for more than two weeks, redness of the skin on the breast, a change in the shape of the breast, and discharge from the nipples. It's important to note that these symptoms may also be caused by other conditions not related to breast cancer, so it's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis.

Yes, there are ongoing research studies and clinical trials in breast cancer. Some of these include exploring new targeted therapies such as immunotherapy and combination treatments with existing therapies to improve outcomes and reduce side effects. ClinicalTrials.gov is a website that lists all current registered clinical trials around the world, including those related to breast cancer. It is recommended to check this site regularly for updates on new research and clinical trial opportunities.

Male breast cancer (MBC) is rare, accounting for less than 1% of all breast cancers . The diagnosis of MBC typically involves a combination of clinical examination, mammography, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB), core needle biopsy (CNB), and surgical excision biopsy.

Skin cancer can affect anyone, but certain factors increase the likelihood of developing skin cancer. These include having fair skin, a history of sunburns, exposure to ultraviolet radiation (UV), including sunlight and tanning beds, having multiple moles or nevi, having a family member with skin cancer, age, and immunosuppression.

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials investigating various treatments for skin cancer. Some of these include combination therapies with immunotherapy and targeted therapy in patients with advanced melanoma (NCT03519482), the use of pembrolizumab as an adjuvant treatment after surgical removal of stage III melanoma (NCT03679544), and the evaluation of novel therapeutic agents such as nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NCT03640048) and niraparib (NCT04028314). Other ongoing trials are evaluating the efficacy of new topical treatments for actinic keratosis (NCT03944224) and non-melanocytic pigmented lesions (NCT04110524).

Melanoma can appear as an abnormal skin lesion that has irregular borders, uneven coloring with shades of brown, blue, or black, and can be raised or flat. It may also present as dark lines (called "mock melanomas") in the palms, soles, and mucous membranes of the mouth and genitals .

Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is a rare but aggressive form of skin cancer that typically affects older adults over 60 years old . It most commonly occurs in sun-exposed areas such as the head, neck, and extremities. Risk factors include fair skin, chronic sun exposure, immunosuppression, HIV infection, organ transplantation, and genetic syndromes associated with MCC development, including dysplastic nevus syndrome, xeroderma pigmentosum, and basal cell nevus syndrome .

Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is an aggressive form of skin cancer that typically presents as a rapidly growing red-purple nodule or plaque with a shiny surface . Treatment options depend on several factors, including stage at diagnosis, tumor size, location, and whether there has been spread to other parts of the body.

Plasma cell neoplasms can be diagnosed by examining bone marrow aspirate samples using cytomorphology (morphologic examination of cells under a microscope) and immunohistochemistry (IHC; staining for specific proteins to identify different types of blood cells). In addition, flow cytometry may also be used to analyze the surface markers expressed by plasma cells in order to determine their lineage and diagnose certain subtypes of plasma cell disorders.

Neuroblastoma (NB) is a malignant tumor that arises from immature cells called neuroblasts, which normally develop into sympathetic ganglion neurons in early fetal life . NB can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain but most commonly presents as an abdominal mass in infants under 18 months old. It accounts for about 7% of all pediatric cancers and has a bimodal age distribution with peaks at less than one year and four years old. The incidence rate varies by race, being highest among Caucasian children and lowest among African American children.

Neuroblastoma is a type of cancer that develops from immature nerve cells called neuroblasts. It can occur anywhere in the body where these cells are found but most commonly arises in the abdomen near the adrenal gland or along the intestines . There are four main stages of neuroblastoma based on the location and extent of tumor involvement as well as whether it has spread to other parts of the body (known as metastasis). Stage 1 tumors are localized and confined to one area outside the adrenal glands; stage 2 tumors have invaded nearby structures such as blood vessels or lymph nodes; stage 3 tumors have spread beyond the region around the organ where it started and may involve regional lymph nodes; and stage 4 tumors have spread throughout the body via the bloodstream or bone marrow .

NSCLC can occur in anyone, but certain factors increase the likelihood of developing this type of lung cancer. These include smoking tobacco (cigarettes, cigars, pipes, water pipes), exposure to secondhand smoke, radon gas, asbestos, arsenic, nickel chromium, coal products, soot, diesel engine exhaust, air pollution, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and other chemicals. Other risk factors include family history of lung cancer, a personal history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or bronchiectasis, and prior radiation therapy to the chest area.

The treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) typically involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or targeted therapies depending on various factors such as stage, location, and patient characteristics. Surgery is often recommended for early-stage NSCLC to remove the tumor and any affected tissue. Chemotherapy may be used before or after surgery in some cases to shrink the tumor prior to surgical removal or kill remaining cancer cells, respectively. Radiation therapy uses high-energy X-rays or other particles to destroy cancer cells and is sometimes given after surgery or with chemotherapy. Targeted therapies use drugs that specifically target proteins involved in the growth and spread of certain types of cancer cells. These treatments include tyrosine kinase inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, and small molecule inhibitors.

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is diagnosed through a combination of imaging studies, such as chest X-ray or computed tomography (CT), and laboratory tests, including biopsy samples that undergo microscopic examination after staining with special dyes to detect cells' nucleic acids (DNA). Imaging studies help identify abnormalities in the lungs, while laboratory tests confirm whether those abnormalities are caused by SCLC tumor cells.
There is no definitive way to prevent lung cancer. However, there are several things you can do that may help reduce your risk of developing lung cancer:

Parathyroid cancer is a rare endocrine malignancy that arises from the parathyroid glands, which regulate blood calcium levels by secreting parathyroid hormone (PTH). The diagnosis of parathyroid cancer typically involves a combination of clinical findings, laboratory tests, imaging studies, and pathological examination.

Penile cancer refers to malignant tumors or growths of cells arising from the tissues of the penis. These include squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), which originates from the epithelial tissue of the glans, foreskin, urethra, and shaft; basal cell carcinomas, adenocarcinomas, sarcomas, melanomas, Paget's disease, and other rare forms .

Symptoms of pituitary tumours depend on the type of hormone produced by the adenoma (if any), as well as its size and location within the sella turcica. The most common symptoms include headaches, visual disturbances, ophthalmoplegia, fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, decreased libido, amenorrhea, erectile dysfunction, impotence, hirsutism, acne, galactorrhoea, polyuria, polydipsia, hypoglycaemia, hypertension, and hyperprolactinaemia .

There are several ongoing clinical trials investigating novel therapies for pituitary tumors (https://clinicaltrials.gov). Some of these include studies evaluating targeted agents such as bevacizumab (NCT03185426), cabozantinib (NCT03975269), everolimus (NCT03185426), and sunitinib (NCT03356139) in patients with recurrent or refractory pituitary adenomas. Other studies are examining the use of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) using lutetium-177 labeled somatostatin analogs in patients with aggressive pituitary adenomas that express somatostatin receptors (NCT03909689). Additionally, there are also ongoing phase 3 randomized controlled trials comparing stereotactic radiotherapy to surgery followed by radiation therapy in patients with nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma (NCT03343305) and evaluating the efficacy of pasireotide in patients with Cushing's disease who have failed prior transsphenoidal surgery (NCT03724038).

Colon cancer refers to malignant tumors that occur in the large intestine (colon). It is one of the most common types of cancer worldwide, with an estimated 1 million new cases diagnosed each year . The exact cause of colon cancer is not known, but several factors have been identified as increasing the risk of developing this disease, including smoking, high alcohol consumption, obesity, lack of physical activity, dietary habits, family history of colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel diseases such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, and certain genetic conditions such as familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) .

Colon cancer is divided into four main stages (0-IV) based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, metastasis to distant organs, and other factors. Stage 0 refers to abnormal cells found only in tissue samples taken during screening or as part of an investigation for another condition. This stage does not indicate the presence of cancer but rather that there may be a higher risk of developing cancer later.

Rectal cancer typically presents with symptoms such as changes in bowel habits (e.g., diarrhea or constipation), blood in the stool, pain during defecation, anemia, weight loss, and abdominal discomfort . It is important to note that these symptoms may also be caused by other conditions unrelated to rectal cancer, so it is crucial for individuals experiencing any of these symptoms to consult a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.

There are currently several ongoing clinical trials investigating novel treatments for colorectal cancer (CRC). Some of these studies involve targeted therapies such as anti-angiogenic agents, immunotherapies including checkpoint inhibitors, and combination therapy with chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery.

Small intestinal cancer refers to malignant tumors that occur in the small intestine, which includes the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. The most common type of small intestinal cancer is adenocarcinoma, accounting for approximately 50% of cases. Other types include neuroendocrine tumor (NET), lymphomas, stromal tumors, carcinoid tumors, sarcomas, and germ cell tumors .

There are four stages (or levels) of small intestinal cancer according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). The AJCC system classifies cancers into different stages based on various factors such as tumour size, lymph node involvement, distant metastasis, and other characteristics that help predict prognosis and guide treatment decisions .

The prognosis of thymomas depends on various factors such as tumor stage, histologic type, patient age, performance status, and surgical resection margin . WHO type A thymomas have been associated with better survival outcomes compared to other types .

Urethral cancer is a rare type of cancer that affects both men and women but is more common in males than females . The most common symptom of urethral cancer in men is pain or burning when urinating (dysuria), which may be accompanied by blood in the urine (hematuria) or discharge from the penis . Other symptoms include difficulty urinating, painful erection, and swelling or a lump in the area around the base of the penis . In women, the most common symptom of urethral cancer is increased frequency of urination with or without hematuria . Other possible symptoms include dyspareunia, vaginal discharge, and pelvic pain . It is important to note that these symptoms can also be caused by other conditions unrelated to cancer; therefore, if an individual experiences any of these symptoms for the first time, they should consult their healthcare provider as soon as possible so that further evaluation can be performed.

There is currently ongoing research into various treatments for urothelial carcinoma (UC). Some of these include immunotherapy with atezolizumab in combination with chemotherapy, as well as studies evaluating new targeted therapies such as erdafitinib and tepotinib .

The stages of vulvar cancer are determined by the Tumor-Node-Metastasis (TNM) classification system . This system takes into account the size of the tumor (T), whether there is lymph node involvement (N), and if distant metastases are present (M).

Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are enlargements of the lower part of the aorta that can lead to serious complications such as rupture or dissection. The most common symptoms of AAA include back pain in the upper abdomen or chest area, which may be severe and constant, or come and go over several days. Other possible symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, fever, palpitations, shortness of breath, weakness, dizziness, loss of consciousness, and numbness or tingling in one leg. It is important for individuals experiencing these symptoms to seek immediate medical attention, especially those with risk factors for AAA.

Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) deficiency is caused by mutations in the gene that encodes apolipoprotein B100 (APOB), which is found on chromosome 2 . This protein plays an important role in chylomicron metabolism and low-density lipoproteins (LDL). The absence of functional APOB leads to impaired clearance of triglycerides from plasma, resulting in hypertriglyceridemia and accumulation of foamy material within arterial walls, leading to premature coronary heart disease.

Abruzzo-Erickson syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by intellectual disability, seizures, hypotonia, hyperlaxity of joints, connective tissue abnormalities, and facial dysmorphism. The main symptoms include developmental delay, learning disabilities, behavior problems, and epilepsy. Other features may include blue sclerae, flat feet, pectus carinatum (an outward bulge in the chest), scoliosis, hernias, and skin laxity. There is no cure for this condition, but treatment can help manage the associated health issues.

Acantholysis is not typically associated with any specific treatment or cause. It can be caused by various factors such as autoimmune disorders, infections, medications, trauma, or malignancies . In most cases, acantholysis resolves spontaneously without intervention; however, if there is an underlying cause that needs to be addressed, topical corticosteroids may help reduce inflammation and promote healing . If the condition persists despite conservative management, oral steroids may also be considered.

An accessory navicular bone is an extra ossicle located at the junction between the talus and calcaneus bones. It can be asymptomatic or may cause pain and swelling in the medial side of the foot near the ankle joint. The symptoms typically occur during weight-bearing activities such as walking or running.

Acroceruloplasminemia (ACP) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by neurological symptoms such as parkinsonism, dystonia, ataxia, and cognitive impairment . The diagnosis of ACP involves several steps that include clinical evaluation, laboratory tests, imaging studies, and genetic testing.

Achalasia is a condition in which food does not pass properly from the esophagus to the stomach due to weakness of the muscles that control the passage of food through the lower part of the esophagus (esophagogastric junction). The treatment options include medications such as nitroglycerin, pneumatic dilation, myotomy, and surgery. Nitroglycerin can be used to relieve symptoms but does not cure the disease. Pneumatic dilation involves passing a tube down into the esophagus under fluoroscopic guidance and using air to dilate the narrowed area at the bottom of the esophagus. Myotomy is a surgical procedure in which a small incision is made along one side of the esophagus and the muscle layers are cut open to release the pressure behind the blockage.
Achondrogenesis is an inherited condition that occurs due to errors in gene expression during embryonic development. It is not something that happens randomly.

Achondrogenesis Type II is an extremely rare genetic disorder that causes severe dwarfism and congenital joint contractures. It is caused by mutations in the gene encoding fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) . The condition can be diagnosed prenatally through ultrasound imaging or postnatally based on characteristic physical features such as short stature, disproportionate head size, flattened facial profile, underdeveloped midface, low-set ears, and bowing long bones with enlarged metaphyses . Infants with this condition may also have respiratory distress due to thoracic deformity, feeding difficulties, and developmental delay.

Achondroplasia (ACH) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene that results in short stature and other skeletal abnormalities . There is no cure for ACH, but there are treatments available to manage symptoms and improve quality of life.

Acquired Hemophilia (AH) refers to the development of bleeding symptoms in an individual without prior history or family history of bleeding disorders. It can be classified into two types: AH type I, which occurs spontaneously with no identifiable cause; and AH type II, which develops after exposure to certain drugs or viruses .

Acrocapitofemoral dysplasia (ACFD) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by abnormalities in the development of the hip joint. The main symptoms include pain in the groin or thigh region that may be exacerbated by activity, limited range of motion at the hip joint, and a positive Trendelenburg gait . Other signs and symptoms can include limping, difficulty walking, and restricted movement of the affected leg during flexion. ACFD typically affects one side of the body, although bilateral cases have been reported.
Acrodysplasia is not a commonly used term in medicine. It may be that you meant to ask about the symptoms of acromegaly or Marfan syndrome.

Acromegaly is a rare endocrine disorder caused by excess growth hormone (GH) secretion from the pituitary gland . The name "acromegaly" comes from the Greek words "akros," meaning most distant or farthest, and "mega," meaning large, because of the enlargement that occurs at the ends of bones and soft tissues .

Acrocephalosyndactyly type 2 (ASD2) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the MPS7 gene that encodes alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase (alpha-NAGAL), which breaks down glycosaminoglycans such as chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate . The condition was first described by Pierre Marie and Paul Sainton in 1896 and later classified by Jean-Pierre Leber who reported three siblings with similar features including macrocephaly, short limbs, syndactlylized fingers, and mental retardation .

Acute alcohol sensitivity (also known as “alcohol intolerance” or “alcohol hangover”) refers to a condition in which certain individuals experience unpleasant symptoms after consuming only small amounts of alcohol . These symptoms can include nausea, vomiting, headache, flushing, sweating, rapid heartbeat, tremor, fatigue, dizziness, weakness, depression, anxiety, and difficulty concentrating . The exact cause of these symptoms is not fully understood, but they may be related to the way that alcohol is metabolized by the body .

Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatitis (AFND) is an acute skin condition characterized by tender erythematous papules, plaques or nodules that usually appear on the limbs, trunk, palms and soles . The rash typically lasts for one to two weeks and may be accompanied by fever, malaise, arthralgia and myalgias. AFND can occur in both children and adults but is more common among young adults aged between 15 and 30 years old .

Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS), an enzyme involved in heme biosynthesis . The diagnosis of AIP typically involves a combination of clinical presentation, laboratory testing, and genetic testing.

The term "ADCY5-related dystonia" refers to a type of movement disorder that can be caused by mutations in the gene ADCY5 (adenylate cyclase 5). This protein plays an important role in regulating dopamine signaling in the brain. Mutations in this gene have been associated with various types of movement disorders, including Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and dystonias .

Adenocarcinomas of the appendix are malignant tumors that originate from epithelial cells lining the inside of the appendix. They can be divided into two main categories: low-grade (well differentiated) and high-grade (poorly differentiated). Low-grade adenocarcinomas tend to grow slowly and may not spread beyond the wall of the appendix, while high-grade adenocarcinomas are more aggressive and have a higher likelihood of spreading to other parts of the body. The exact cause of adenocarcinomas of the appendix is unknown, but certain risk factors such as chronic inflammation due to appendicitis, family history of colorectal cancer, and exposure to radiation have been identified. Symptoms of adenocarcinomas of the appendix include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, weight loss, anemia, and fever. Diagnosis typically involves imaging tests such as CT scans and ultrasounds, along with endoscopic procedures such as colonoscopy and sigmoidoscopy. Treatment options for adenocarcinomas of the appendix depend on various factors including stage at diagnosis, location of the tumor within the appendix, and patient preferences. Surgery is often recommended as the primary treatment modality, although chemotherapy and

Adenoid cystic carcinomas (ACCs) are rare malignant tumors that can occur in various parts of the body, including the salivary glands, respiratory tract, breast, prostate, skin, and central nervous system . The incidence rate of ACC varies depending on its location; for example, approximately 10% of all primary brain tumors are ACCs , while only about 2–5% of all salivary gland tumors are ACCs .

Adipositis dolorosa is an uncommon condition characterized by painful lipodystrophy that typically affects middle-aged women . The exact cause of adiposopathy remains unknown; however, it has been associated with various conditions such as diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, chronic alcohol use, and certain medications (e.g., tamoxifen) .

ADNP syndrome (also known as Angelman-Davis neurogenetic syndrome) is a rare genetic disorder that affects both physical and mental development. It was first described by Drs. Harry Angelman and William Davis in 1965 . The condition results from mutations or deletions of the UBE3A gene located on chromosome 15q11-q13. This region of the genome contains several other genes involved in brain development, including OCA2, GABRB3, and HERC2 .

Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) is considered to have a genetic component as it tends to occur more frequently within families than would be expected by chance alone . However, the exact pattern of inheritance has yet to be determined. Studies suggest that there may be both environmental and genetic factors involved in AIS development, with heritability estimates ranging from 40% to 85%.

The symptoms of Adams-Oliver syndrome (AOS) typically include congenital upper limb malformations such as absence or hypoplasia of one hand or parts of the hand, often with cutaneous involvement; shortening or absence of digits; and skin abnormalities such as capillary malformation, hyperpigmentation, or scarring. Other common features may include facial asymmetry, craniofacial defects, cardiovascular anomalies, and developmental delay .

Vitelliform macular dystrophy (VMD) is an autosomal dominant retinal disease that typically presents with yellow-white deposits in the central macula . Symptoms include progressive visual impairment due to central scotoma and metamorphopsia , but not usually blurred vision. The condition can be diagnosed using fundus examination, optical coherence tomography (OCT), fluorescein angiography, and genetic testing. OCT shows characteristic well-circumscribed drusenoid deposits located at the level of the outer nuclear layer and ellipsoid zone . Fluorescein angiography reveals hypofluorescent lesions corresponding to the location of the drusenoid deposits . Genetic testing may reveal mutations in the PRPH2 gene .

Afibrinogenemia is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency in plasma fibrinogen levels due to mutations in genes encoding for the different subunits of fibrinogen (FGA, FGB, and FGG). The symptoms of afibrinogenemia include excessive bruising, epistaxis, hemarthrosis, menorrhagia, postpartum hemorrhage, and life-threatening bleeding after trauma or surgery . Patients may also present with petechial hemorrhages, ecchymoses, and purpura.

Total intestinal aganglionosis is also known as Hirschsprung disease (HSCR). It is caused by the absence or incomplete development of ganglion cells along the length of the colon. The symptoms typically include constipation that worsens over time, abdominal distension, failure to thrive, poor feeding, and vomiting. Other common symptoms may include excessive crying due to colic-like pain, paleness, fever, dehydration, and anemia from blood loss into the bowel. A physical examination may reveal an enlarged spleen or liver, a distended abdomen, and a lack of stool in the diaper.

The Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS) is a rare genetic disease characterized by an overactivation of interferon pathways in response to nucleic acids . AGS can be classified into two types: Type I or primary AGS, which has no underlying cause, and Type II or secondary AGS, which occurs as a result of another condition that causes this hyperactivity .

The symptoms of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS) can vary depending on the underlying genetic mutation. However, some common features include developmental delay, microcephaly, cerebral calcifications, skin lesions such as periorbital xanthomas and erythematous papules, ocular abnormalities including chorioretinopathy and optic nerve hypoplasia, and elevated levels of interferon in blood and cerebrospinal fluid .

Ainhum is an acute inflammatory disease of the skin that occurs in children under 2 years old. It usually affects the scalp but can also affect other parts of the body such as the face or neck. The exact cause of Ainhum is unknown, but it may be related to viral infection or allergic reactions.

Alagille syndrome (ALGS) is a rare genetic disorder that affects multiple organ systems in the body. It was first described by Dr. Armand Trousseau in 1893 but later named after Dr. Robert Jules Alagille who further characterized this condition in 1941 . ALGS has an estimated prevalence of one in 70,000 to 125,000 live births worldwide , with no known racial predilection.

Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO) is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in the GNAS1 gene, which encodes for the alpha subunit of the stimulatory guanine nucleotide-binding protein (Gs). This mutation leads to decreased production of cAMP, resulting in abnormal bone development .

The symptoms of Alopecia epilepsy-oligophrenia syndrome of Moya no one is not well understood as there has been only one reported case in the literature to date. However, some general information about this condition can be provided.

Alopecia universalis (AU) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by complete loss of scalp and body hair . It can be classified as either alopecia areata type 2 or patternless alopecia totalis with no other specific diagnostic criteria . The exact cause of AU remains unknown; however, genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and stress have been suggested to play a role in its development .

There are several treatment options available for alopecia universalis depending on its cause. If the condition is due to an underlying autoimmune disorder such as alopecia totalis or alopecia universalis congenita, topical corticosteroids may be used in conjunction with oral steroid-sparing agents such as hydroxychloroquine . In addition, phototherapy (ultraviolet B) can also be considered .

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is an inherited condition that typically develops early in life. It occurs when there is a mutation in one of the AAT genes located on chromosome 14 . This genetic defect results in low levels of functional AAT protein, which leads to unchecked activation of neutrophil elastase. The most common form of this disease is caused by a single nucleotide substitution at codon 342 (Glu342Lys), also known as the Z allele. Other less frequent variants include Glu264Lys (S allele) and Glu358Lys (M allele).

Alpha thalassemia is a genetic disorder that affects the production of hemoglobin in red blood cells. Hemoglobin is an important protein found inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body. There are two types of alpha globin chains (α1 and α2) that combine with two copies each of beta globin chains (β1 and β2) to form adult hemoglobin (HbA).

Alpha thalassemia is an inherited blood disorder that can cause symptoms such as mental retardation, developmental delay, short stature, microcephaly, abnormal facial features (such as triangular face, large mouth), hearing loss, heart defects, and other problems . The severity of these symptoms depends on whether they are caused by one mutated gene (called heterozygous alpha thalassemia) or two mutated genes (called homozygous alpha thalassemia). Homozygous alpha thalassemia is usually more severe than heterozygous alpha thalassemia.

Yes, Alport syndrome is an inherited condition that typically follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. This means that both parents must have at least one copy of the mutated gene to pass it on to their children. If both parents carry the same genetic mutation, there is a 25% chance with each pregnancy that the child will be born with Alport syndrome.

Ambra syndrome (AS) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the AMBRA1 gene that encodes for the protein ambra 1 . This protein plays a role in regulating cellular processes such as lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and autophagy .
