The main clinical features of AS include intellectual disability, hypotonia, seizures, ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria, and cerebellar atrophy . Other symptoms may also be present, including developmental delay, microcephaly, spasticity, visual impairment, and cardiomyopathy .

Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) is an inherited condition that affects tooth enamel development. It occurs when there is a defect in one of several genes involved in the process of amelogenesis, which is the formation of tooth enamel. AI can be passed down through families as an autosomal dominant trait, meaning that a person with AI has a 50% chance of passing the gene onto their children. However, some cases of AI occur spontaneously due to de novo mutations. The specific genetic cause of AI varies depending on the type of AI. There are currently over 20 different types of AI that have been identified, each associated with a different gene mutation. Some forms of AI may also be caused by environmental factors such as exposure to certain medications during pregnancy.

Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) is a group of rare genetic disorders that affect tooth enamel development. AI can be caused by mutations in any one of several genes involved in ameloblast differentiation or function. The most common form of AI is non-syndromic hypoplastic/hypomaturated type 2, which is characterized by thin, soft, and discolored teeth with normal dentin. This condition usually causes mild symptoms such as painless chewing difficulties due to poor occlusion and esthetic problems.

Amniotic bands are thin strands of amniotic tissue that can become wrapped around one or more limbs during fetal development. When these bands remain intact until birth, they can cause physical abnormalities known as amniotic band syndrome (ABS). ABS occurs in approximately 1 out of every 15,000 live births .

Amyloid A (AA) amyloidosis is an autoimmune disorder in which abnormal AA protein deposits in organs such as the kidneys, liver, heart, or spleen. It can be caused by chronic inflammatory conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and hepatitis B. The exact cause of AA amyloidosis is unknown but may involve genetic factors, immune system dysfunction, and environmental triggers.

Amyopathic dermatomyositis (ADM) is a rare form of inflammatory myopathy that affects the skin without muscle involvement . It was first described in 1976 by Bohan et al., who reported cases of patients with cutaneous lesions similar to those seen in classic DM but without evidence of proximal weakness or other signs of systemic disease .

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disease that affects nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. The exact cause of ALS is unknown, but it is thought to involve a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Some genes have been identified as increasing the risk for developing ALS, including mutations in the superoxide dismutase 1 gene (SOD1). Other possible causes include exposure to heavy metals or pesticides, smoking, head injuries, and military service. It is also more common in men than women.

The amytrohpic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-Parkinsonism-Dementia Complex 1 (APDC-1) is a rare genetic disorder that causes both ALS and Parkinson's disease (PD). It is caused by mutations in the SOD1 gene .

Anaplastic gangliogliomas (AGGs) are rare central nervous system neoplasms with mixed glial and neuronal differentiation . They were first described by Cushing et al. in 1948 as “anaplastic oligodendrogliomas” , but they have since been classified under the category of diffuse astrocytic gliomas according to the World Health Organization’s classification of central nervous system tumors .

Andersen-Tawil syndrome (ATS) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder that affects the heart and skeletal muscles. The main symptoms include ventricular arrhythmias such as supraventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, long QT syndrome, syncope, palpitations, dizziness, and presyncope . Other less common symptoms may include muscle weakness, fatigue, myalgia, exercise intolerance, dysphagia, gastrointestinal problems, and skin rashes . ATS can be diagnosed through clinical evaluation, electrocardiograms, echocardiography, and genetic testing.

Sideroblastic anemia is characterized by fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, paleness, shortness of breath, chest pain, cold sensitivity, and bruising . Spinocerebellar ataxia causes progressive loss of balance and coordination, dysarthria (slurred speech), dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), diplopia (double vision), nystagmus (rapid involuntary eye movements), and dysmetria (impaired ability to control voluntary movements) .

Anencephaly is characterized by the absence or incomplete development of the brain and skull bones. It can also be associated with other birth defects such as hydrocephalus (fluid buildup in the brain), spinal cord defects, heart defects, kidney defects, and limb abnormalities.

Angelman syndrome (AS) is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to mutations in the UBE3A gene located at chromosome 15q11-q13 . Most cases of AS occur spontaneously without any known family history of the condition. However, if one parent has a heterozygous mutation in the UBE3A gene, there is a 25% chance with each pregnancy that the fetus will have two copies of the mutated allele and develop AS . Therefore, while AS can occur randomly, it also has some hereditary components.

Aniridia is a rare genetic disorder characterized by the absence of iris tissue in one or both eyes. There is no cure for aniridia, but there are several treatments available to help with vision and ocular health. The main treatment options include corneal prostheses, contact lenses, glasses, and surgery. Corneal prostheses can be used to restore some visual function and protect the eye from ultraviolet light. Contact lenses can also be worn to improve vision and reduce glare. Glasses may be prescribed to correct refractive errors associated with aniridia. Surgery may involve procedures such as cataract removal, iris reconstruction, and retinal detachment repair. In addition to these treatments, regular follow-up examinations with an eye care professional are important to monitor eye health and make necessary adjustments to treatment plans.

Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is considered to have a genetic component as certain genes may increase the risk of developing AS . However, the exact cause of AS remains unknown. It has been found that there is a higher prevalence of HLA-B27 among people with AS compared to those without AS . Additionally, other gene variants such as IL17A, IL23R, TNFAIP3, NOD2, and ERAP1 have also been associated with increased susceptibility for AS .

Anonychia congenita (also known as absent nails at birth) refers to the absence of one or more fingernails or toenails at birth. It can occur in isolation or be associated with other nail abnormalities such as malformed or misshapen nails. The exact cause of anonychia congenita is unknown but may be related to genetic factors, environmental exposures during pregnancy, or maternal nutritional deficiencies .

Anophthalmos is an extremely rare congenital disorder characterized by complete absence of both optic nerves due to failure of involution of the primary optic vesicles during embryonic development . It can be unilateral or bilateral. The condition may occur as an isolated defect or as part of a syndrome associated with other ocular or systemic anomalies such as microphthalmos (partial hypoplasia of the eyeball), coloboma (congenital split in the iris, lens, retina, or optic nerve), Peters anomaly (aniridia, corneal opacity, cataract, and abnormal anterior chamber drainage) , and CHARGE association (colobomatous eye malformation, heart defects, choanal atresia, growth and psychomotor delay, genitourinary anomalies).

An anterior polar cataract is a type of lens opacity that typically affects the central part of the pupil area. It can cause blurred vision due to light scattering within the lens. Symptoms may include hazy or foggy vision with halos around bright objects such as headlights at night, glare from lamps or sunshine, poor contrast sensitivity, double vision, and difficulty driving at night .

The antisynthetase syndrome (ASS) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by myositis, interstitial lung disease (ILD), Raynaud's phenomenon, fever, arthritis, and mechanic hands. It is caused by antibodies directed against proteins involved in protein synthesis.

The symptoms associated with aortic arch anomalies depend on the specific type of malformation present. For example, in patients with coarctation of the aorta, there may be high blood pressure in the upper extremities due to decreased blood flow through the descending aorta below the point of obstruction. In contrast, individuals with an unbalanced transposition of the great arteries (i.e., D-TGA) typically exhibit cyanosis, hypoxemia, tachypnea, dyspnea, and poor growth.

Aplasia cutis congenital (ACC) refers to a condition in which skin fails to develop during embryonic development, resulting in one or more areas of absent or hypoplastic dermal tissue at birth . These lesions can occur anywhere on the body but most commonly affect the scalp, face, neck, upper extremities, and back. The size of these defects varies widely from small macules to large areas involving multiple body parts.

Aplasia cutis congenital (ACC) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by absent skin in one or more areas of the body at birth. The most common sites for ACC lesions to occur include the scalp, forehead, posterior neck, upper back, and lower extremities .

Aquagenic pruritus (AP) is a rare skin condition characterized by an intense itch that occurs immediately or within 1 hour of contact with water. The exact cause of AP is unknown, but it may be related to abnormalities in the structure of keratin filaments in the outermost layer of the skin.
answers_repaired: Adult Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (ALL) is a type of cancer that affects white blood cells known as lymphocytes or leukemic cells. These cells grow out of control in the bone marrow, displacing normal red blood cells and platelets. ALL can occur at any age but it is more common among adults aged 65 years and older . The symptoms include fatigue, weight loss, fever, frequent infections, swollen lymph nodes, pallor, bruising, bleeding, and pain in the joints, bones, or chest. Diagnosis involves a physical examination, blood tests, bone marrow aspiration, and biopsy. Treatment typically includes chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) is classified as either childhood ALL or adult ALL, with distinct clinical features and treatment approaches for each group. Adult ALL typically affects individuals over 15 years old and accounts for approximately 20% of all cases of leukemia in adults . The diagnosis of ALL involves several steps including blood tests to determine the number and type of white blood cells, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, cytogenetic analysis, molecular testing, and imaging studies such as CT scans and MRIs. Once diagnosed, adult patients may be treated with chemotherapy alone or in combination with radiation therapy depending on their age, overall health status, and other factors. Treatment usually lasts for several months and can include multiple cycles of chemotherapy followed by periods of rest. In general, the goal of treatment is to achieve remission and then maintain it long-term through ongoing monitoring and follow-up care.

The diagnosis of adult AML is typically made through a combination of blood tests (complete blood count with differential, peripheral smear), bone marrow aspiration or biopsy, cytogenetic analysis, molecular testing, and immunophenotyping using flow cytometry.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is a type of cancer that affects the blood cells known as B-lymphocytes or white blood cells. It is characterized by an overproduction of these cells in the bone marrow, which can lead to their accumulation in other parts of the body such as the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes . The disease typically progresses slowly, with symptoms appearing only when there is significant damage to organs due to high levels of CLL cells. Common signs include enlargement of the lymph nodes, fatigue, weight loss, recurrent infections, and anemia. Diagnosis involves a combination of physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging studies, and biopsies. Treatment options vary depending on factors such as age, overall health status, and severity of the disease but may involve chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, or stem cell transplantation.

There are several ongoing clinical trials for CLL that focus on different aspects of treatment such as monitoring response to therapy, evaluating new drug combinations, and assessing long-term outcomes after treatment with specific therapies. Some examples include NCT03162879 (evaluation of ibrutinib plus venetoclax in relapsed/refractory patients), NCT04558499 (comparison of acalabrutinib vs ibrutinib in previously untreated patients), and NCT04538269 (assessment of ublituximab plus venetoclax in relapsed/refractory patients).

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a type of cancer that affects the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The diagnosis of CML involves several steps including physical examination, complete blood count with differential, peripheral smear evaluation, BCR-ABL1 fusion gene testing, cytogenetic analysis, and molecular testing .

Hairy cell leukemia (HCL) is a malignant disorder characterized by abnormal proliferation of B-cells in the bone marrow, resulting in pancytopenia, splenomegaly, and other complications such as autoimmune phenomena and recurrent infections. The disease was named for its characteristic morphology at the microscopic level, whereby the neoplastic cells have cytoplasmic extensions resembling hair fibers.

Hairy cell leukemia (HCL) is a rare type of B-cell lymphoma that affects the bone marrow and bloodstream. It was first described in 1958 by William Dameshek . The disease is characterized by the presence of abnormal B cells known as hairy cells due to their unique cytoplasmic projections.

ALL is usually diagnosed through a combination of physical examination, blood testing, bone marrow aspiration or biopsy, and imaging studies such as ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, or PET scan. A complete blood count can reveal high white blood cell counts with immature cells called blast cells. Other diagnostic tests include peripheral blood flow cytometry to identify specific markers on the surface of leukemic blasts, chromosome analysis to detect abnormalities in the genetic material of cancer cells, and molecular testing to determine the presence of certain mutations associated with ALL. Imaging studies may be done to look for signs of enlarged spleen or liver, which could indicate leukostasis, or blockage of small blood vessels by leukemic cells. The diagnosis of ALL requires a team of specialists including pediatric hematologists, radiologists, pathologists, and laboratory technicians working together to interpret all available test results and make an accurate diagnosis.

Childhood AML is an aggressive type of cancer that affects immature cells in bone marrow called hematopoietic stem or progenitor cells. It can be classified as de novo (primary), secondary to another condition such as Down syndrome or prior chemotherapy treatment for another cancer, or therapy-related due to exposure to radiation or certain medications during treatment .

Childhood AML is staged according to the French-American-British (FAB) classification system, which categorizes it into eight subtypes based on morphological characteristics observed under a microscope after blood or bone marrow samples have been examined by cytology. These include M0 (blasts with granular cytoplasm), M1 (blasts without granules but with agranular cytoplasmic structure), M2 (blasts with fine, homogeneous, slightly basophilic cytoplasm), M3 (blasts with ringed sideroblasts), M4 (blasts with bilobed nuclei), M5 (blasts with multilobed nuclei), M6 (granulocytic differentiation), and M7 (monocytic differentiation). The World Health Organization (WHO) has recently updated this classification system to incorporate genetic markers such as chromosomal abnormalities, gene mutations, and epigenetic alterations .

The most common symptom of an adult soft tissue sarcoma is pain in the affected area that may be accompanied by swelling or lump. Other possible signs include bleeding, weakness, numbness, tingling, difficulty walking, changes in skin color, and discharge from the tumor site.

The treatment of soft tissue sarcomas typically involves a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy or targeted therapies depending upon the type and stage of cancer. For localized soft tissue sarcomas in adults, surgical resection is often curative. Radiation therapy may be used before or after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence. Chemotherapy is usually reserved for high-grade tumors that cannot be completely removed by surgery or have spread to other parts of the body (metastatic). Targeted therapies such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors and mTOR inhibitors may also be used alone or in combination with chemotherapy for certain types of advanced soft tissue sarcomas.

There are several ongoing clinical trials for GISTs that aim to evaluate novel therapies such as avapritinib, ripretinib, cabozantinib, and regorafenib. Avapritinib has shown promising results in phase 1 and 2 studies, with high response rates and durable disease control . Ripretinib was recently approved by the FDA for patients who progressed on imatinib therapy after initially responding to it. Cabozantinib is another multikinase inhibitor that is being evaluated in combination with pembrolizumab in a phase 1b trial . Regorafenib is also an active drug in this setting, but its efficacy beyond second-line remains unclear due to conflicting data from previous studies .

The treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma depends on various factors such as stage, location, severity, and patient's overall health status. Treatment options include topical therapy with cream containing 5% aloes or intralesional injections of interferon alpha, systemic chemotherapy (e.g., vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide), radiation therapy, surgical excision, cryosurgery, laser therapy, photodynamic therapy, immunomodulatory agents (e.g., rituximab), and antiretroviral therapy if HIV is present.

Rhabdomyosarcomas (RMS) are malignant tumors that arise from immature skeletal muscle cells in children. They account for approximately 4% of all pediatric cancers and occur most commonly between the ages of two to five years old . There are four main histological subtypes of RMS: embryonal, alveolar, pleomorphic, and spindle cell. Embryonal is the most common type, accounting for about half of all cases, while alveolar accounts for around one-third. Pleomorphic and spindle cell types are less frequent, making up only about 5–10% each .

The most common presenting symptom of pediatric soft tissue sarcoma is pain or swelling in the affected area. Other possible signs include limping due to hip pain, weakness, difficulty walking, or gait disturbance; abdominal distension with palpable mass; and lump or swelling that may be painful or tender to touch.

Treatment of pediatric soft tissue sarcoma (STS) is multimodal and involves surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy depending upon the tumor type, grade, stage, size, location, histology, and patient age . The treatment plan is determined by an interdisciplinary team that includes surgeons, radiologists, pathologists, pediatricians, and oncologists.

Adult Hodgkin's Lymphoma (HL) is a type of cancer that affects the lymphatic system in adults. It is characterized by large multinucleated cells called Reed-Sternberg cells. The exact cause of HL is unknown but it may be related to certain viral or bacterial infections.

There are several ongoing studies in adults with relapsed or refractory classical HL (cHL) that have been conducted by the National Cancer Institute (NCI), including NCT03298651, which is evaluating brentuximab vedotin plus bendamustine versus brentuximab vedotin alone as first-line treatment for cHL patients who are not candidates for ASCT; NCT04712841, which is assessing the efficacy of nivolumab plus AVD chemotherapy compared to AVD alone as frontline therapy for cHL patients unsuitable for ASCT; and NCT03606549, which is investigating the safety and efficacy of pembrolizumab plus AVD followed by pembrolizumab consolidation vs. AVD plus placebo followed by placebo consolidation as frontline therapy for cHL patients eligible for ASCT. Other studies include NCT03316540, which is examining the effectiveness of lenalidomide maintenance after ASCT in cHL patients at high risk of posttransplant relapse, and NCT03708324, which is comparing the efficacy of nivolumab plus doxorubicin, vinblastine, dacarbazine, and procarbazine

There are several known factors that can increase the risk of developing adult non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) including age, family history, certain viral or bacterial infections, autoimmune disorders, prior chemotherapy treatment, radiation exposure, smoking tobacco products, drinking alcohol, being overweight, having diabetes mellitus, and having a weakened immune system due to underlying diseases such as HIV infection .

The treatment of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) depends on several factors such as age, overall health status, type of NHL, stage or extent of disease, whether it is an initial diagnosis or relapse, and personal preferences. In general, there are four main types of cancer treatment: chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell transplantation.

The different stages of HIV-associated lymphoma (HAL) include indolent B cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL), aggressive B cell NHL, primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL), Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL), and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD).

The overall prognosis of mycosis fungoides (MF) depends on its stage at diagnosis. Patients diagnosed with early-stage MF have an excellent prognosis with 5-year survival rates exceeding 90%. However, advanced-stage MF has a poorer prognosis, with 5-year survival rates dropping to around 40% .

Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) is a rare type of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma that develops in the brain or spinal cord. It can occur at any age but is more common among adults aged 50 to 70 years old. PCNSL has been associated with several risk factors including HIV infection, autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis, chronic inflammatory conditions like vasculitis, prior history of immunosuppressive therapy, and exposure to certain chemicals or radiation. People who have had previous chemotherapy treatment also have an increased risk of developing this cancer.

Childhood Hodgkin's Lymphoma (cHL) is a type of cancer that affects the lymphatic system in children aged 15 years or younger. It is characterized by the presence of large cells known as Reed-Sternberg cells within the affected tissues. The exact cause of cHL remains unknown but it has been linked to certain genetic factors and viral infections such as Epstein Barr virus (EBV). Symptoms may include enlarged lymph nodes, fever, weight loss, anemia, fatigue, and night sweats. Diagnosis involves a combination of physical examination, imaging tests, blood tests, and biopsy of affected tissue. Treatment typically includes chemotherapy followed by radiation therapy. Prognosis for patients with cHL has improved significantly over time due to advances in treatment and early detection.

Childhood Hodgkin's Lymphoma (cHL) is staged using the Ann Arbor Staging System for adults with lymphomas . The system classifies cHL into four stages based on the extent of disease involvement at diagnosis. Stage I involves one region or organ; stage II involves two regions or organs on the same side of diaphragm; stage III involves three or more regions or organs on the same side of diaphragm; and stage IV involves lymphoma cells that spread to distant organs throughout the body.

The diagnosis of childhood Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (NHL) is made by performing a combination of physical examination, laboratory testing, imaging studies such as computed tomography scans or magnetic resonance imaging, and biopsy with histopathological evaluation. Laboratory tests that may be done include complete blood count, urinalysis, lactate dehydrogenase, serum electrolytes, beta 2 microglobulin, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and specific immunologic markers depending upon the clinical presentation . Imaging studies can help determine if there has been any spread from the primary site. A biopsy of the affected area is also necessary for confirmation of NHL.

Anal cancer is a type of cancer that originates in or around the anus. It can be caused by various factors such as human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, smoking, high lifetime number of sexual partners, and a family history of colorectal cancer . The most common symptom of anal cancer is rectal bleeding, but other symptoms may include pain with bowel movements, lump felt inside the body, weight loss, constipation, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.

Anal cancer is staged according to the TNM system (Tumor, Node, Metastasis). Stage 0 indicates that abnormal cells have been detected in the anus but not yet formed into tumors. Stages I-IV represent increasing levels of spread or invasion of the disease, with stage IV being the most advanced.

The incidence rate for brain tumors is higher in men than women (10.2 per 100,000 vs. 7.8 per 100,000) . In addition to gender differences, there are also age-related variations in the occurrence of these neoplasms. For example, children aged 5–9 years have the highest rates of primary CNS malignancies compared to other age groups .

The classification of brain tumors is based on their histopathological features. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), there are four grades for gliomas in adults: Grade I pilocytic astrocytoma, grade II diffuse astrocytoma, grade III anaplastic oligodendroglioma or anaplastic astrocytoma, and grade IV glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). GBMs are considered the most aggressive type of primary brain cancer with a poor prognosis.

The most common symptom in children with brain or spinal cord tumor is headache. Other signs include vomiting, drowsiness, lethargy, seizures, visual disturbances, weakness, numbness, back pain, neck stiffness, difficulty walking, loss of balance, speech problems, hearing difficulties, facial paralysis, and hydrocephalus .

An astrocytoma is a type of primary brain tumor that arises from star-shaped glial cells known as astrocytes. These tumors can occur at any age but are most common in adults. Astrocytomas account for approximately 30% of all glioblastomas (GBMs), which are the most frequent malignant central nervous system tumors .

The prognosis of pediatric low-grade glioma (LGG) or pilocytic astrocytoma depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, tumor location, extent of resection, presence of malignant transformation, and compliance to chemotherapy . Five-year overall survival rates range from 80% for patients younger than five years old to approximately 50% for those older than ten years old .

The exact cause of AT/RT is unknown but it has been associated with certain genetic mutations that affect cell growth and development. Some studies have suggested that exposure to environmental chemicals such as pesticides or solvents may increase the risk of developing this type of brain tumor in children. Other possible risk factors include having a family history of cancer, particularly if there is a history of inherited syndromes such as neurofibromatosis or Li-Fraumeni syndrome.

There have been several ongoing studies to develop more effective treatments for CNS ATRTs. One such study (NCT01542637) evaluated the use of chemotherapy with irinotecan in combination with temozolomide and radiotherapy as an adjuvant treatment after surgery. The results showed that this regimen was well tolerated but did not improve overall survival compared to standard therapy alone . Another trial (NCT02891723) investigated the efficacy of combining vincristine, lomustine, and cisplatin with radiation therapy. This study found that while the addition of these drugs improved progression-free survival, it also increased toxicity without improving overall survival .

The most common presenting symptom of pediatric brainstem glioma is cranial nerve deficits such as facial weakness or paralysis (VII), diplopia (VI), ptosis (III), ataxia (V), dysarthria (IX-X), and loss of vision (II). Other signs include headache, vomiting, balance problems, gait disturbance, and nausea.

The treatment of pediatric brainstem glioma is complex and requires multidisciplinary care involving neurosurgeons, radiation oncologists, chemotherapists, neurologists, physiotherapists, speech pathologists, nutritionists, social workers, and other healthcare professionals.

The outcomes of pediatric CNS embryonal tumours vary depending on the type of tumour involved. Medulloblastoma has been associated with good prognosis in children when treated by chemotherapy and craniospinal irradiation . However, patients with high-risk medulloblastomas have poorer survival rates despite aggressive treatment regimens .

Childhood central nervous system (CNS) germ cell tumors are rare brain or spinal cord tumors that arise from cells of the embryonic neural tube during early fetal development . The exact cause is unknown but may be related to abnormal migration of primordial germ cells during early fetal development. Certain genetic conditions such as neurofibromatosis type 1, Carney complex, tuberous sclerosis, and familial teratomas may also increase the risk of developing these tumors. Exposure to radiation has been associated with an increased risk of CNS germ cell tumors, particularly for medulloblastoma .

The treatment of pediatric CNS germ cell tumors is multimodal and typically involves surgical resection followed by chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy depending on the extent of the disease at diagnosis. For patients who present with metastatic disease, combination chemotherapy regimens including cisplatin, etoposide, bleomycin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, ifosfamide, and carboplatin have been used in various combinations to achieve remission prior to surgery .

The overall 5-year survival rate of pediatric patients with craniopharyngioma is approximately 90%, although it can vary depending on tumor size, location, and patient age at diagnosis . Children who have undergone surgical resection may experience neurologic deficits such as endocrine dysfunction, visual impairment, or hypothalamic obesity due to damage to adjacent structures during surgery.

Childhood ependymoma is a brain tumor that arises from cells in the central nervous system (CNS). The exact cause of this type of cancer remains unknown; however, several risk factors have been identified. These include exposure to radiation, genetic predisposition, and certain environmental exposures such as pesticides and solvents . In addition, some studies suggest that there may be an association between childhood ependymoma and viral infection with JC virus or enterovirus .

Ependymoma is a type of brain tumor that develops from cells called ependyma, which line the ventricles of the brain. It can occur at any age but is more common in children under 3 years old. The exact cause of this disease is unknown, but some factors such as exposure to radiation or certain chemicals may increase the risk.

The most common diagnostic test for primary liver cancer is ultrasound (US). US can detect nodules that may be indicative of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), which is the most common type of primary liver cancer. If an abnormality is detected by US, further imaging with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be performed to confirm the diagnosis. CT and MRI can provide more detailed images than US and help determine the size, location, and extent of any tumors present. In addition to imaging studies, blood tests such as alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels may also be useful in diagnosing HCC. AFP is a protein produced by some types of liver cancer cells and elevated levels have been associated with increased risk of developing HCC. However, it is important to note that while these tests can suggest the presence of liver cancer, they cannot definitively diagnose it. For this reason, biopsy is often required to obtain tissue samples from suspicious lesions and evaluate them under a microscope to make a final diagnosis.

Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) refers to cancer that arises from bile duct cells called cholangiocytes. It can occur in any part of the biliary tree including the intrahepatic or perihilar bile ducts, also known as hepatocellular carcinoma; extra-hepatic bile ducts such as distal common bile duct, gallbladder, ampulla of Vater, papilla of Vater, and pancreaticobiliary junction. The most prevalent type of CCA is found within the intrahepatic bile ducts with an incidence rate of 2–3 cases per 100,000 people annually .

There are several ongoing phase II clinical trials investigating various treatment options in patients with advanced biliary tract cancer (BTC) including cholangiocarcinoma. These include studies evaluating combination therapies such as chemotherapy plus immunotherapies like atezolizumab + nab-paclitaxel 150 mg/m2 q3w × 4 cycles followed by atezolizumab monotherapy 1200 mg Q3W × 6 cycles (NCT03798125), durvalumab + gemcitabine + cisplatin , pembrolizumab + gemcitabine + cisplatin , and ipilimumab + nivolumab . Other combinations of targeted agents and immunomodulators are also being studied, including regorafenib + nivolumab , lenvatinib + pembrolizumab , and cabozantinib + nivolumab . Additionally, there is an open label single arm study to evaluate the efficacy of pemigatinib in adult patients with previously treated unresectable locally advanced, recurrent, or metastatic BTC (NCT03767582).

The most common symptom of childhood liver cancer is pain in the right upper quadrant (RUQ). Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, jaundice, weight loss, abdominal mass or distension, fatigue, pale stools, dark urine, palpable spleen, ascites, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, chills, diarrhea, constipation, pruritus, skin rash, edema, easy bruising, bleeding gums, petechial hemorrhages, lymphadenopathy, hernias, weakness, and muscle wasting .

There are several ongoing clinical trials for childhood liver cancer in children at different stages of development. Some examples include NCT03967528 (NCT number), which is evaluating the safety and efficacy of combining nivolumab with irinotecan hydrochloride or temozolomide in treating relapsed or refractory solid tumors in pediatric patients; NCT04107723, which is assessing the safety and efficacy of pembrolizumab plus gemcitabine or capecitabine in treating recurrent hepatoblastoma in children; and NCT04566067, which is investigating the safety and efficacy of cediranib in combination with chemotherapy as first-line treatment for localized hepatoblastoma. It is important to note that this list is not exhaustive and more information can be found on ClinicalTrials.gov using the search term “liver cancer” and limiting results by age group (“all ages” or “child”) and phase (“phase 3” or “phase 4”).

Ewing Sarcoma (ES) is a type of cancer that originates in the bone or soft tissues around it. It affects mainly children and young adults but can occur at any age group. ES cells usually arise from neural tissue precursors known as neuroblasts . The most common sites for primary tumor development include the pelvis, ribs, femur, and vertebrae; however, they may also develop in other parts of the body such as the gastrointestinal tract, parotid gland, kidney, lung, heart, and retroperitoneum .

The mainstay of treatment for localized Ewing Sarcoma is multimodal therapy consisting of chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation. Chemotherapy typically involves a combination of doxorubicin (Adriamycin), vincristine, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, etoposide, and dactinomycin. Surgery may involve limb-sparing resection or amputation depending on the location of the tumor. Radiation therapy may be used after surgical resection to help prevent recurrence. For patients with metastatic disease at diagnosis, chemotherapy remains the primary form of treatment.

The diagnosis of osteosarcoma or MFH requires a combination of clinical history, physical examination, imaging studies such as X-rays, computed tomography scans, magnetic resonance imaging scans, positron emission tomography scans, and biopsy with pathological evaluation.

Gastrointestinal (GI) carcinoid tumors are rare neuroendocrine neoplasms that originate from cells in the lining of the GI tract. They can occur anywhere along the digestive system but most commonly develop in the small intestine or colon. These tumors are slow-growing and typically do not cause symptoms early on. As they grow larger, patients may experience diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and other nonspecific symptoms. Diagnosis is often made through endoscopy with biopsy, imaging tests such as CT scans, and blood tests to measure levels of certain hormones produced by the tumor. Treatment usually involves surgical removal of the tumor followed by monitoring for recurrence.

The stages of gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors are as follows: Stage 0 - confined to the mucosa; Stage I - invasion into submucosal layer; Stage IIA - invasion through muscularis propria into pericolonic tissues; Stage IIB - extension beyond the serosa into adjacent organs or structures; Stage III - metastasis to regional lymph nodes; and Stage IV - distant metastases. Their progression is characterized by an increase in size with subsequent invasion into deeper layers of the bowel wall (T-stage) and involvement of local lymph nodes (N-stage). Metastatic spread typically occurs via hematogenous dissemination to the liver (M1a), although it can also involve other sites such as bone, lung, or brain (M1b).

Chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are a group of rare hematologic malignancies characterized by clonal proliferation of one or more myeloid lineages in the bone marrow. The three main types of MPNs include polycythemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythemia (ET), and primary myelofibrosis (PMF). Patients with PV have an increased red blood cell mass due to erythrocytosis, while those with ET exhibit an elevated platelet count without leukocytosis. In PMF, there is dysplasia of all three myeloid lineages along with fibrotic changes in the bone marrow .

Polycythemia Vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an overproduction of red blood cells due to clonal proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow . The most common presenting symptom of PV is pruritus or skin rash followed by fatigue, night sweats, weight loss, dyspnea, palpitations, chest pain, headaches, dizziness, visual disturbances, erectile dysfunction, abdominal discomfort, constipation, early satiety, and fever . Less frequently reported signs include splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, leukocytosis with increased neutrophils, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia, and osteosclerosis .

The prognosis of primary myelofibrosis (PMF) varies depending on several factors such as age at diagnosis, risk stratification, presence or absence of constitutional symptoms, and genetic mutations. According to the International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS), patients with PMF are divided into three groups based on their risk of progression to acute leukemia: low-risk (median survival not reached after 10 years of follow-up), intermediate-2 risk (5-year OS rate of approximately 63%), and high-risk (median survival time of less than 4 years). However, it should be noted that this system has been criticized due to its inability to predict outcomes among younger patients.

Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an increase in platelet count above 450 × 109 cells per liter with bone marrow hypercellularity and increased numbers of megakaryocytes . The mainstay treatment for ET involves low-dose aspirin to prevent thromboembolic events and cytoreductive therapy such as hydroxyurea or interferon alpha to reduce the risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia . Other options include ruxolitinib, pegylated IFNα, busulfan, pipobroman, radioactive phosphorus, and allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation .

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL) is a rare type of myeloid malignancy characterized by sustained peripheral blood eosinophilia and bone marrow infiltration with immature eosinophils . The treatment options include chemotherapy, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), targeted therapy, and clinical trials.

Chronic Myelomonocytic Leukemia (CMML) is a type of blood cancer that affects the bone marrow. It causes an overproduction of immature cells called monocytes, which accumulate in the bloodstream. CMML differs from other types of leukemia because it develops slowly without causing any symptoms at first. However, as the disease progresses, patients may experience fatigue, weight loss, bruising, bleeding, enlarged spleen or liver, and increased risk of infection. Diagnosis involves a combination of physical examination, blood tests, bone marrow aspiration, and cytogenetic analysis to determine chromosomal abnormalities. Treatment options include chemotherapy, targeted therapy, stem cell transplantation, and supportive care such as antibiotics for infections. The prognosis varies depending on factors such as age, white blood cell count, and presence of certain genetic mutations.

Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia (JMML), also known as monoblastic or monocytic leukemia of childhood, is a rare hematological malignancy that affects children under 10 years old. It accounts for approximately 2% to 4% of all pediatric acute leukemias . JMML cells originate from immature dendritic cell precursors in the bone marrow and accumulate in peripheral blood, lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and central nervous system. The clinical presentation includes fever, anemia, bruising, bleeding, petechial rashes, enlarged lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological symptoms such as seizures and headaches. Diagnosis requires the presence of at least one major criterion (blasts >5%, CD34+ blasts, abnormal karyotype, somatic mutations affecting RAS pathway genes) plus two minor criteria (leucopenia with absolute neutrophil count <1 × 109/L, thrombocytopenia with platelet count <100 × 109/L, anemia with hemoglobin level <7 g/dL, monocytosis with absolute monocyte count >1 ×

Atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) is a rare subtype of CML that presents with atypical features such as anemia or thrombocytopenia without evidence of increased white blood cell count . The clinical presentation can vary depending on the specific mutation present in the patient's cells. However, some common symptoms include fatigue due to anemia, easy bruising or bleeding due to thrombocytopenia, weight loss, fever, night sweats, abdominal pain, bone pain, enlarged spleen or liver, lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, and other complications related to organ dysfunction . It is important for patients with these symptoms to undergo further testing to rule out any underlying causes including cancer.

Myeloid neoplasms (MN) that cannot be classified into any World Health Organization (WHO)-defined subtype are referred to as MNs unclassifiable (MNU). The diagnosis of an MN requires a combination of morphological assessment of blood or bone marrow cells by microscopy, cytogenetic analysis, molecular testing, flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, and other laboratory tests .

The prognosis for women with endometrial cancer depends on several factors including age at diagnosis, stage of disease, histologic type, grade, myometrial invasion, lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), and pelvic nodal status .

Endometrial cancer can affect any woman with a uterus, including those who have never had their period or been sexually active as well as women who were previously pregnant. The risk increases after menopause and in women with obesity, diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), late age at first birth, long-term unopposed estrogen therapy, tamoxifen use, family history of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) or Lynch Syndrome, radiation to pelvic area, and certain genetic syndromes such as neurofibromatosis type 1 and familial adenomatous polyposis .

The treatment of uterine sarcoma depends on several factors such as type, stage, grade, age, menopausal status, and desire to preserve fertility. For localized disease (stage IA-IIB), surgery is usually performed which may include total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy or modified radical hysterectomy depending on the tumor size, histology, and patient's preference. Radiation therapy can be used in combination with chemotherapy after surgical resection if there are poor prognostic features present.

Pediatric extracranial germ cell tumors (EGCTs) can occur in any location outside of the brain and spinal cord. They most commonly arise from the gonads but may also originate from other sites such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, testis, ovaries, kidneys, thyroid, pancreas, liver, and lymph nodes .

The treatment of childhood extracranial germ cell tumors depends on several factors such as age at diagnosis, sex, location of the tumor, stage of disease, presence or absence of metastasis, and individual patient characteristics . For localized disease (stage I), surgical resection is typically curative in most cases . Chemotherapy may also be used to shrink large tumors prior to surgery or if complete removal of the tumor is not possible due to its proximity to critical structures like blood vessels or nerves . In some situations, chemotherapy alone can lead to significant regression of the tumor without requiring surgery .

Extragonadal germ cell tumors (EGCT) can be diagnosed using various imaging modalities such as ultrasound, computed tomography scan (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT). Imaging studies may also reveal elevated serum markers including alpha fetoprotein (AFP), beta chorionic gonadotropin (βhCG), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). A biopsy is usually required for confirmation of diagnosis.

Uveal melanoma (UM) is an intraocular malignant tumor that arises from melanocytes located within the uvea of the eye. The most common type of UM is ocular melanoma which develops in the choroid layer of the eye. Ocular melanomas account for about 5% of all melanomas .

Uveal melanoma is a rare type of cancer that originates from the pigmented cells (melanocytes) located within the uvea layer of the eye. The uvea consists of three layers: the iris at the front of the eye; the choroid, which lies between the sclera and retina; and the ciliary body, which surrounds the lens .

Retinoblastoma can affect any child regardless of race or family history but it is more common in children with a family history of the disease, particularly if a first-degree relative (parent, sibling, or child) has been diagnosed with retinoblastoma. It is also slightly more common in children who have had radiation exposure, especially at a young age.

Retinoblastoma is treated with chemotherapy in combination with surgery or radiation therapy depending upon the stage of cancer at diagnosis . The treatment plan depends on various factors such as age, size, location, and extent of tumor involvement. Treatment options include chemotherapy alone, surgical removal of the eye followed by chemotherapy (enucleation), cryotherapy, brachytherapy, external beam radiotherapy, and plaque brachytherapy . Chemotherapy may be administered intravenously or orally using drugs such as carboplatin, vincristine, etoposide, topotecan, cisplatin, melphalan, cyclophosphamide, and others .

Ovarian cancer is one of the most common gynecological cancers worldwide . The exact cause of this disease has not yet been identified; however, there are several factors that have been associated with an increased or decreased risk of its development.

The standard treatment for ovarian cancer is surgery followed by chemotherapy. Surgery typically involves hysterectomy (removal of uterus), bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (complete removal of both ovaries and fallopian tubes) with cytoreductive surgery to remove any visible tumors in the abdomen and pelvis. Chemotherapy usually consists of platinum-based drugs such as carboplatin or cisplatin combined with paclitaxel. Other options include targeted therapies such as bevacizumab (Avastin) and PARP inhibitors, which target specific genetic mutations found in some patients with ovarian cancer.

The outcomes of ovarian germ cell tumors depend on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, histologic subtype, age, surgical treatment, and chemotherapy regimen used . In general, patients with early-stage disease have excellent prognosis, while advanced stages carry poorer survival rates. For example, 5-year overall survival (OS) rate for stage I EGCTs is approximately 90%, but it drops to around 70% in more advanced stages .

Ovarian LMP tumors are generally benign or have very low malignancy potential. They can be asymptomatic or may present with nonspecific symptoms such as bloating, pelvic pain, abdominal fullness, early satiety, urinary frequency, irregular menstrual cycles, and infertility . Some women may also experience gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea, constipation, nausea, vomiting, indigestion, and loss of appetite. However, these symptoms are not specific to this condition and could indicate other health problems.

There have been several ongoing studies to investigate the molecular mechanisms of ovarian LMPTs and their role in carcinogenesis. One such study is the “Molecular Pathology of Ovary Low-Grade Tumor (LGOT)” project, which aims to identify genetic alterations that may contribute to the development of these tumors. Another study, titled “The Role of Methylation Patterns in Diagnosis and Prognostication of Ovarian Serous Cystadenomas,” seeks to determine whether methylation patterns can be used as biomarkers for distinguishing benign from malignant serous cystadenoma.

Gallbladder cancer (GBC) refers to malignant tumors that arise from the epithelial cells of the gallbladder. It is also known as cholecystocarcinoma or carcinoma of the gallbladder. GBC is a rare type of biliary tract cancer with an estimated incidence rate of 1 per 50,000 people in the United States . The most common symptom of GBC is acute cholecystitis, which can be mistaken for benign inflammation of the gallbladder. Other symptoms include abdominal pain, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, fever, and dark urine. Diagnosis typically involves imaging tests such as ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, and PET scans, along with tissue biopsy for confirmation. Treatment options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Prognosis depends on several factors including stage at diagnosis, size of the tumor, lymph node involvement, and resectability.

The stages of gallbladder cancer are determined by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) staging system . Stages I to IV range from localized disease with no lymph node involvement or metastases present to distant metastatic disease that has spread beyond regional lymph nodes into other organs such as the liver, peritoneum, lung, bone, etc.

Testicular cancer is typically treated with surgery to remove the tumor followed by chemotherapy or radiation therapy depending on the stage of the disease. The type of surgery used depends on whether it's an early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic) cancer.

Gestational trophoblastic diseases (GTD) include hydatidiform mole, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumor, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors. GTD can occur after any pregnancy, but it occurs more frequently after molar pregnancies. The incidence of postmolar GTD is approximately 15-20% in patients with a complete hydatidiform mole and 3-4% in patients with an incomplete hydatidiform mole . Risk factors associated with developing postmolar GTD include advanced maternal age, prior history of GTD, and biparental triploidy or diandric triploidy fetus .

Gestational trophoblastic diseases (GTDs) include hydatidiform mole, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumor, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors . The treatment of GTD depends on the type and extent of the disease. For low-risk patients with no metastasis or only one lung nodule less than 1 cm in diameter, single-agent chemotherapy is recommended. Methotrexate (MTX), actinomycin D (Act D), dactinomycin (DACT), etoposide plus cisplatin, and vinblastine plus methylprednisolone are all effective agents used to treat GTD .

The diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is typically made through a combination of clinical findings, blood tests, imaging studies such as X-rays, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, and tissue biopsies.

Hypopharyngeal cancer refers to malignant tumors that occur in the lower part of the pharynx, which includes the posterior pharyngeal wall, the Eustachian tube, the tonsillar pillars, and the base of the tongue . It accounts for approximately 3%-4% of all head and neck cancers worldwide . The most common type of hypopharyngeal cancer is squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), followed by adenocarcinomas and undifferentiated carcinomas . Risk factors include smoking, alcohol consumption, human papillomavirus infection, and exposure to certain chemicals such as nitrite compounds and mycotoxins . Symptoms may include difficulty swallowing, pain or discomfort in the throat, voice changes, cough, weight loss, and bleeding from the throat . Diagnosis involves physical examination, imaging tests such as CT scans and MRI, and biopsy of suspicious tissue . Treatment options typically involve surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination of these modalities depending on the stage of the cancer at diagnosis . Prognosis varies widely depending on the specific subtype of hypopharyngeal cancer and the extent of spread at the time of diagnosis .

Hypopharyngeal cancer is staged according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) Tumor Node Metastasis (TNM) classification system . The stages range from stage I for early disease limited to the mucosal lining of the hypopharynx with no evidence of metastases, to stage IVA for advanced disease characterized by tumors that have invaded through the full thickness of the hypopharyngeal wall into adjacent tissues or organs, as well as the presence of regional lymph node metastases.

Laryngeal cancer refers to any type of malignant tumor that develops in the tissues of the larynx. It can occur anywhere within the larynx, including the glottis (the area between the vocal cords), supraglottic region (above the epiglottis), subglottic region (below the cricoid cartilage), and epiglottis. The most common sites for laryngeal cancer are the supraglottic region and glottis .

Laryngeal cancer is staged according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) Tumor-Node-Metastasis (TNM) system. The TNM classification includes three components: T for primary tumour extent (Tx-unevaluable; T1a-tumour limited to the true vocal folds; T1b-extension to the anterior commissure or cricoid cartilage; T2-extension beyond the anterior commisure or cricoid cartilage with no involvement of the thyroid cartilage; T3-extension through the thyroid cartilage but not involving the prevertebral muscles; T4-extension to adjacent structures), N for nodal status (N0-no regional lymph node metastases; N1-metastatic unilateral level II–IV nodes; N2-bilateral level II–IV nodes; N3-level I, V, VI nodes), M for distant metastasis (M0-absence of distant metastasis; M1-presence of distant metastasis).

Cancer of the lips and oral cavity can present with various signs and symptoms including a mouth ulcer that does not heal, unexplained numbness or pain in the face, difficulty moving the facial muscles, bleeding from the gums, loosening of teeth, a lump inside the cheek, trouble opening the mouth, a sore throat, voice changes, coughing up blood, problems swallowing, and weight loss.

There are several ongoing clinical trials investigating new treatments for lip and oral cavity cancer (OC). These include phase III trials evaluating the efficacy of pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy or cetuximab as first-line therapy for patients with recurrent or metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck (R/M SCCHN) , and the use of nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus standard platinum-based chemotherapy for untreated R/M SCCHN . Other phase II trials are assessing the effectiveness of immunotherapies such as nivolumab  and atezolizumab  alone or in combination with other agents including durvalumab , tremelimumab , and radiotherapy . Additionally, there is an open label trial examining the safety and efficacy of combining radiation therapy with photodynamic therapy using talaporfin sodium in patients with locally advanced OC .

Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck (HNSCC) without an identified primary tumor is classified as stage IVA according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). The AJCC recommends that these cases be staged using the same criteria used for other HNSCCs, including clinical examination, imaging studies such as computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging, and biopsy if necessary.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a type of head and neck malignancy that originates from the epithelial cells lining the nasopharynx. The most common presenting symptom of NPC is a painless mass or swelling in the neck, which may be mistaken for an enlarged lymph node. Other common symptoms include nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, hearing loss, otitis media, facial numbness, and cranial nerve palsies. Less frequently, patients with NPC can experience more severe symptoms such as dysarthria, ataxia, seizures, and coma due to brainstem involvement.

Currently, there are several ongoing phase I-III clinical trials in China that aim to evaluate new treatment strategies for patients with NPC. These include studies of targeted therapies such as anti-EGFR antibodies (cetuximab), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (erlotinib), and PI3K/mTOR inhibitor (everolimus) combined with chemotherapy regimen (gemcitabine plus cisplatin). Other studies are evaluating immunotherapies including immune checkpoint blockade agents (anti-PD1 and anti-CTLA4 monoclonal antibody) alone or in combination with other treatments. Additionally, there is also an ongoing trial investigating the efficacy of concurrent chemoradiation therapy versus sequential chemoradiotherapy followed by adjuvant chemotherapy for locally advanced NPC .

The overall 5-year survival rate of patients diagnosed with oropharyngeal cancer depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, human papillomavirus (HPV) status, presence of metastasis, and type of treatment received. In general, the 5-year relative survival rates range from approximately 80% in stages I and II to less than 20% in stage IV . HPV positive tumors have better outcomes compared to HPV negative ones, with 5-year survival rates ranging from about 70–90%, even in advanced stages . However, it is important to note that these statistics can vary depending on the specific subsite within the oropharynx where the tumor originated. For example, tongue base cancers tend to have worse outcomes compared to other sites such as tonsil and soft palate . Overall, early detection and intervention are crucial for improving patient outcomes.

Paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity cancers occur more frequently in men than women. The most common age group affected by these types of cancers ranges from 50 to 70 years old. Tobacco smoking has been identified as one of the major risk factors for developing paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity cancers. Exposure to secondhand smoke also increases the risk of these cancers. Other potential risk factors include occupational exposure to wood dust or formaldehyde, radiation therapy to the head or neck area, certain chemicals such as nickel compounds, chromium salts, and asbestos, and some viruses like human papillomavirus (HPV). People with chronic inflammatory conditions of the nose, such as chronic rhinitis or nasal polyps, may be at increased risk for these cancers.

The treatment of paranasal sinus and nasal cavity cancers depends on various factors such as stage at diagnosis, tumor location, size, histology, patient age, general health status, and preferences. For early-stage disease (I or II), endoscopic surgery with adjuvant radiation therapy is often recommended. More advanced stages may require open surgical resection followed by chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy. In some cases, definitive chemoradiation without surgery may be used.

A doctor may use several methods to evaluate possible salivary gland tumors (SGT). These include physical examination of the head and neck region, imaging studies such as ultrasound or CT scans, fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB), and in some cases, surgical exploration. The diagnosis is confirmed by histopathological analysis of tissue samples obtained during FNAB or surgery. Imaging techniques like MRI and PET-CT scan may also be employed for staging purposes after the initial diagnosis has been made.

There are several ways to reduce one's risk of developing oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancers. These include avoiding tobacco use (including smoking and smokeless tobacco), limiting alcohol consumption, maintaining good overall health through regular exercise and a balanced diet, consuming foods that may have chemopreventive properties such as fruits and vegetables rich in antioxidants, brushing your teeth twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, using mouthwash regularly, practicing good dental hygiene by flossing every day, seeing your dentist for routine check-ups at least once a year, and getting screened if you have any symptoms or signs suggestive of oral cancer.

The most common diagnostic test for pancreatic cancer is an abdominal ultrasound (US), which can detect tumors larger than 2 cm. However, it has low sensitivity when identifying small lesions. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) is more sensitive than US but requires insertion of a thin tube through the mouth into the stomach to visualize the pancreas. Computed tomography (CT) scan is another imaging modality that can be used to identify suspicious masses in the pancreas. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) may also be used to evaluate the pancreas.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs), also known as pancreatic endocrine tumors or pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinomas, are rare malignant neoplasms that originate from cells in the pancreas that produce hormones . These tumors can be functional or non-functional depending on whether they secrete hormones that cause specific symptoms such as diarrhea, flushing, sweating, or weight loss. Non-functional tumors do not have these characteristics and may only present with vague signs of abdominal pain, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, anemia, fatigue, and weight loss .

Pancreatic NETs can be treated with surgery, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or a combination of these approaches depending on the stage and grade of the tumor. Surgery is typically recommended as the first line of treatment for localized disease, while systemic therapies such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) may be used in patients with advanced or metastatic disease .

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to renal cell carcinoma (RCC). One of these is NCT03291548 which aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of nivolumab plus ipilimumab in patients with advanced RCC who have not received prior systemic therapy. Another trial, NCT03677751, is evaluating the combination of cabozantinib and atezolizumab as first-line treatment for metastatic clear cell RCC. The third one, NCT03829506, is assessing the effectiveness of pembrolizumab in treating patients with previously treated advanced RCC. These trials are still actively recruiting participants at this time.

Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is a type of urinary bladder cancer that originates from the cells lining the urothelium or transitional epithelium. It can occur in any part of the urinary tract system including the kidney, renal pelvis, ureters, and bladder. The exact cause of TCC remains unknown but several risk factors have been identified such as smoking, exposure to aromatic amines, chronic irritation due to stones or infection, and family history of bladder cancer .

The most common symptom of Wilms tumor is an abdominal mass that can be palpated or detected by ultrasound in children under 5 years old . Other symptoms include pain in the flank, back, or abdomen; fever; vomiting; loss of appetite; weight loss; weakness; fatigue; hypertension due to hyperreninemia; anemia from blood loss if there is bleeding into the peritoneal cavity; and swelling (edema) of the legs, face, or belly.

There are ongoing studies investigating new treatments for pediatric solid tumors including those of the kidneys. The Children's Oncology Group (COG) is conducting a phase I trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of APR-246 in combination with irinotecan hydrochloride temozolomide phosphate (NCT03915785). Another COG study is evaluating the effectiveness of pembrolizumab as maintenance therapy after upfront chemotherapy treatment for relapsed or refractory solid tumors (NCT03317292).

The most common symptom of breast cancer is a painless lump or mass in the breast that appears suddenly. Other signs include changes to the shape or size of the breast, thickening or peeling of the skin, nipple retraction (turning inward), redness or scaling of the nipples, discharge from the nipples without squeezing, and a change in the feel or appearance of the nipple. Less frequent symptoms can also be indicative of breast cancer including swelling of the lymph nodes under the arms, a feeling of heat in the breasts, and pain in one breast that does not go away. It’s important for women to note that these symptoms may also occur due to other causes such as benign tumors, so it’s crucial to consult with a healthcare provider if any of them are present.

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to breast cancer treatment and management. One of these is the TAILORx trial (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01272037), which aims to determine whether chemotherapy can be safely avoided in patients with early-stage hormone receptor positive disease who have low risk recurrence scores according to Oncotype DX testing. Another study, the MINDACT trial (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01165489) is evaluating the use of 70 gene signature from the MammaPrint assay as an indicator for systemic therapy in women with node negative or one to three involved nodes after surgery. The I-SPY 2 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01042379) is assessing the efficacy of neoadjuvant targeted therapies in women with HER2+ locally advanced breast cancer.
Breast cancer is rare in men but can be diagnosed with mammography or ultrasound imaging of the breasts. A biopsy may also be performed if abnormalities are found during these screening methods.

Skin cancer can affect anyone but certain factors increase the risk of developing it. The main risk factor for skin cancer is exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight or artificial sources such as tanning beds. People who have fair skin, hair, and eyes; live close to the equator; work outdoors; have a history of sunburns; and have many moles or freckles are more prone to skin cancer. Other risk factors include having a family member with skin cancer, smoking, taking immunosuppressive medications, and having certain genetic syndromes. It's important to protect your skin by seeking shade, wearing protective clothing, using sunscreen, and avoiding sunlamps or tanning beds. Early detection through regular self-examination and seeing a healthcare provider if you notice any changes in your skin can also help reduce the risk of developing skin cancer.

There are several ongoing clinical trials related to skin cancer prevention and treatment. One such trial is NCT03976582 which aims to evaluate the efficacy of imiquimod 5% cream in treating actinic keratosis (a precancerous form of squamous cell carcinoma). Another study, NCT04198716, is investigating the use of pembrolizumab as an adjuvant therapy for melanoma after complete surgical resection. Additionally, there is also a phase III randomized controlled trial examining the effectiveness of nivolumab versus ipilimumab plus nivolumab as first-line treatments for advanced melanoma (NCT03323813). Furthermore, a phase II trial is evaluating the safety and efficacy of cemiplimab in patients with metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (NCT03465540). These are only some examples of current studies being conducted; interested readers can visit ClinicalTrials.gov for more information about these and other ongoing trials.

Melanoma skin cancer usually appears as an abnormal growth or sore that changes color or texture. It may be black, blue, brown, tan, pink, red, gray, or white. Over time, it can grow larger than 1 mm (about 1/4 inch) in diameter.

Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is an aggressive skin cancer that typically affects older adults over 60 years old, but can occur in younger individuals as well . Risk factors include fair skin, sun exposure, immunosuppression, HIV infection, organ transplantation, and genetic syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum or dysplastic nevus syndrome . Males may be more susceptible than females due to higher occupational UV radiation exposure .

The mainstay of treatment for Merkel cell carcinoma is surgical excision with wide margins to prevent local recurrence. Lymph node dissection may be performed if there is clinically detectable lymphadenopathy or involvement of resected nodes. Radiation therapy can also be used as adjuvant treatment after surgery in patients who have positive margins or high-risk features such as perineural invasion or extracapsular extension. Systemic chemotherapy is recommended for patients with metastatic disease but has limited efficacy. Immunotherapies targeting programmed death 1 (PD-1) pathway have shown promising results in clinical trials and are being investigated further.

The most commonly performed diagnostic test for multiple myeloma is serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) which identifies monoclonal proteins in blood. Immunofixation of SPEP further confirms the presence of M-protein by identifying its unique immunoglobulin class and light chain type. Urine analysis can also detect abnormal amounts of monoclonal proteins excreted into urine as Bence Jones protein. Other laboratory findings include anemia, low levels of platelets, elevated creatinine, calcium, lactate dehydrogenase, β2 microglobulin, and chromosomal abnormality such as t(14;16).

Neuroblastoma (NB) is a pediatric cancer that arises from immature cells of the sympathetic nervous system called neural crest cells . It can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain but most commonly presents in the abdomen or adrenal gland. NB accounts for about 10% of all childhood cancers and occurs more frequently in males than females with an incidence rate of approximately 2–5 cases per million children under five years old worldwide . The exact cause of this disease remains unknown; however, several risk factors have been identified such as family history of NB, prematurity, genetic syndromes, exposure to certain chemicals, and radiation .

Neuroblastoma is classified into four main groups according to its histopathological features (International Neuroblastoma Staging System): 1) localized tumors with low-risk clinical behavior; 2) localized high-risk tumor; 3) metastatic disease in infants less than one year old with low risk; and 4) metastatic or disseminated disease in children older than one year with intermediate or high risk.

Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is more common in men than women. Risk factors include smoking tobacco products, exposure to secondhand smoke, radon gas, asbestos, air pollution, coal dust, and other chemicals. People with a family history of lung cancer may also be at increased risk. Other risk factors that can increase the chances of developing NSCLC include chronic inflammation from conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiectasis, or aspiration pneumonia.

Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) is one of the most common types of cancers worldwide with an estimated 1.8 million new cases diagnosed each year . The treatment options depend on several factors such as stage at diagnosis, age, overall health status, and personal preferences. For early stages (stage IA), surgical resection remains the preferred option with or without adjuvant chemotherapy. Radiation therapy may also be used in some patients who cannot undergo surgery. In locally advanced NSCLC (stages IIB to IIIB), concurrent chemoradiation followed by consolidation chemotherapy is recommended. Immunotherapy alone or combined with chemotherapy is now considered standard care for metastatic disease after failure of first line platinum-based chemotherapy. Targeted therapies including tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have become increasingly important in recent years due to their efficacy and tolerability profile compared to traditional cytotoxic agents.

Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is diagnosed by biopsy of tissue from the lungs followed by pathological examination under a microscope. Imaging studies such as chest X-ray, computed tomography scan (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), bone scintigraphy, and ultrasound may be performed in addition to blood work for tumor markers like neuron specific enolase (NSE).

There are several ways to reduce your risk of developing lung cancer, including not smoking or quitting smoking if you currently smoke; avoiding exposure to secondhand smoke; limiting alcohol consumption; eating healthy foods such as fruits and vegetables that contain antioxidants; maintaining a healthy weight; exercising regularly; and reducing exposure to other potential carcinogens such as radon gas, asbestos, and air pollution. Additionally, getting vaccinated against influenza and pneumonia can help protect your lungs from infection, which may also lower your risk for lung cancer. Finally, it is important to talk with your doctor about screening tests such as low-dose CT scans, which can help detect lung cancer early when it is most treatable.

Parathyroid cancer can be diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of suspected nodules. However, FNAC has low sensitivity for detecting parathyroid carcinoma due to its rarity and overlapping histologic features with benign parathyroid lesions. Therefore, it should not replace surgical exploration when there is a high clinical suspicion of malignancy.

Penile cancer refers to any malignant tumor arising from the tissues of the penis. It can occur at any age but is more common in older men over 50 years old. The exact cause of penile cancer remains unknown; however, certain risk factors have been identified such as smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, phimosis, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, poor hygiene, chronic inflammation or irritation due to tight-fitting clothing, and other sexually transmitted diseases. Early detection through regular screening and treatment of HPV infection may help prevent the development of penile cancer. If detected early, surgical removal of the cancerous tissue along with some healthy surrounding tissue may be sufficient for cure. However, if left untreated or diagnosed late, it can spread to other parts of the body resulting in metastatic disease that becomes difficult to treat .

Penile cancer is classified into four clinical stages (I-IV) according to the TNM staging system for cancers. The T stands for tumor size, N for lymph node involvement, and M for distant metastasis. Stage I refers to a small primary lesion without regional or distant spread. As the disease progresses, there may be enlargement of the primary tumor with or without local invasion (Stage II), involvement of inguinal lymph nodes (Stage III), or presence of distant metastases (Stage IV).

Pituitary tumors can cause several signs and symptoms depending on the type and size of the tumor. The most common presenting symptom is headache, which occurs in about 50% of patients with pituitary adenomas . Other frequent symptoms include vision changes (blurred or double vision), fatigue, weakness, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, amenorrhea, irregular menstruation, infertility, loss of body hair, weight gain or loss, increased sweating, dizziness, fainting spells, and anemia due to iron deficiency from heavy menstrual bleeding . Some patients may also experience hypopituitarism, leading to additional symptoms such as growth retardation, low blood pressure, and reduced stress response .

I am unable to provide information about current clinical trials as my knowledge cutoff is 2019. However, you can check ClinicalTrials.gov (https://clinicaltrials.gov/) for up-to-date information regarding ongoing clinical trials related to pituitary tumors.

Breast cancer is staged according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM system using the tumor-node-metastasis classification . The stages range from 0 to IV, with Stage 0 being noninvasive or in situ carcinoma and Stage IV being metastatic disease. Stages I through III represent invasive cancers that differ by increasing extent of local invasion and possible lymph node involvement.

Colorectal cancer (CRC), also known as colon or bowel cancer, is a type of malignant tumor that arises from cells lining the large intestine . It is one of the most common types of cancers worldwide, with an estimated 1.9 million new cases diagnosed in 2020 alone . The exact cause of CRC remains unknown; however, several risk factors have been identified, including age, family history of CRC, inflammatory bowel disease, smoking, obesity, physical inactivity, and dietary habits such as high consumption of red meat and processed meats .

The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system for CRC classifies it into eight stages ranging from 0 to IV.
